definition: To leave someone or something completely, or to give up a plan or activity before finishing it.
extra_senses: give up with the intent of never claiming again
leave behind empty; move out of
examples: The driver abandoned his broken-down car on the highway and walked to a petrol station.
Many pets are abandoned on the street when their owners move to a new city.
We had to abandon the picnic when it began to pour with rain.
After three failed attempts, she still did not abandon her dream of becoming a doctor.
Villagers abandoned their homes and moved to higher ground as the flood waters rose.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: Our landlord is abandoning the old parking lot to build a small park.
Abandoning a half-finished project can damage your reputation at work.
Ritu abandons her morning jog whenever it rains heavily.
The abandonment of the old railway line made the town much quieter.

definition: Left behind and no longer used, wanted or cared for.
extra_senses: unrestrained and uninhibited
examples: Children should not play inside the abandoned factory because the roof is unsafe.
We found an abandoned kitten shivering outside the shop in the rain.
An abandoned car stood by the roadside for months with flat tyres.
After the river changed its course, the abandoned village slowly filled with weeds.
She felt abandoned when all her friends moved to other cities.

definition: To lower someone's dignity, rank or self-respect, or to behave in a way that humbles yourself.
examples: He refused to abase himself by begging his rival for a favor.
Some employees abase themselves before the boss, laughing at every joke to keep their jobs.
The cruel remarks were meant to abase her in front of her classmates.
A leader should never abase the people who work for him.
Don't abase yourself by lying about your marks; honesty earns more respect.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: He abased himself before the judges and begged for another chance.
His pride has been abased by the embarrassing loss.
The bully is abasing younger students with cruel jokes in the playground.
Abasing yourself before a rude boss rarely earns respect.
Cruel teasing abases the victim and makes them feel worthless.

definition: To make someone feel embarrassed, ashamed or uncomfortable.
examples: Nothing seemed to abash the child, who sang loudly in front of the whole school.
Rafi was abashed when the teacher read his poor answer aloud to the class.
She was not abashed by the interviewer's tough questions and answered every one calmly.
The unexpected praise abashed the shy new employee, who blushed and looked at the floor.
The loud ringtone in the silent hall abashed him, and he fumbled to switch off the phone.

form_sentences.sentence: The stranger's loud praise is abashing the shy boy in front of his friends.
Abashing people with sarcasm is never a good way to win an argument.
Nothing abashes my grandmother, not even a question about her age.

definition: To become less strong, intense or widespread over time.
extra_senses: become less in amount or intensity
examples: After two hours, the heavy monsoon rain finally began to abate, and we walked home.
The pain in my knee did not abate until the doctor changed my medicine.
Public anger over the sudden price rise has not abated, even after the apology.
We waited at the airport until the storm abated enough for planes to take off.
Her nervousness abated once she realized the exam questions were ones she had practiced.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The heavy rain is finally abating, and Dhaka's traffic has started moving again.
Abating the noise from the construction site is the contractor's responsibility.
The pain in her knee abates after a few days of rest.
The city government announced new measures for the abatement of traffic noise near schools.

definition: To give up a position of power, such as a throne, or to fail to accept a duty.
examples: The old king abdicated in favor of his daughter after a long illness.
Parents who let children do whatever they like have abdicated their responsibility.
The club president abdicated his role after losing the members' trust.
You cannot abdicate your duty to check the facts just because the news came from a friend.
The team leader abdicated all responsibility for the failed project and blamed the interns.

form_sentences.sentence: The captain is abdicating his duties to the new deputy this week.
Abdicating responsibility for the group project upset the whole team.
The lazy manager abdicates every hard decision to his assistant.
Some leaders prefer to abdicate their duties instead of making tough choices.
The abdication of responsibility by the committee delayed the repair work.

definition: Different from what is normal, expected or accepted, often in a worrying way.
extra_senses: one whose behavior departs substantially from the norm of a group
examples: The bank's software flagged an aberrant transaction and blocked the card until the owner called.
The doctor was concerned by the aberrant results in the blood test and ordered a second one.
Teachers noticed aberrant behavior in the usually cheerful boy and spoke gently to his parents.
One aberrant data point can distort the average, so check it before drawing conclusions.
The app began showing aberrant behavior after the update, closing itself every few minutes.

form_sentences.sentence: The test results seemed aberrant, so the doctor ordered them again.
This month's sales figures are more aberrant than anything we saw last year.

definition: Something that is unusual and different from what is normal or expected.
extra_senses: a disorder in one's mental state
an optical phenomenon resulting from the failure of a lens or mirror to produce a good image
examples: Her low score was an aberration, since she normally tops the class.
A cold day in the middle of summer is a weather aberration.
The sudden jump in sales proved to be an aberration, not a lasting trend.
He later called his angry outburst an aberration and apologized to everyone.
The one failed test looked like an aberration compared with the other nine.

form_sentences.sentence: Those few late assignments were aberrations in an otherwise punctual class.
The aberrant reading on the machine was caused by a loose cable.

definition: To help or encourage someone to do something wrong, especially to commit a crime.
examples: The police said the driver had abetted the thieves by waiting outside with the engine running.
A student who helps a classmate cheat in an exam is abetting dishonesty.
The man was charged with aiding and abetting a fraud against elderly customers.
Anyone who knowingly buys stolen phones abets the thieves who steal them.
The report said the clerk had abetted the scheme by ignoring false invoices.

form_sentences.sentence: The manager abetted the fraud by ignoring the warning signs for months.
Abetting a crime, even by staying silent, can lead to serious legal trouble.
The officer was accused of conspiring to abet the smuggling of phones.
The police arrested the abettor who had helped the thieves escape.

definition: A state of temporary inactivity, when something is paused and not being used or decided.
examples: Construction of the footbridge has been in abeyance since the city ran out of funds.
Our family rule about phones at dinner fell into abeyance during the holidays.
The company held the new hiring policy in abeyance until the board could meet next month.
The dispute between the two neighbors has lain in abeyance since the fence was repaired.
Her plans to study abroad were in abeyance while her father recovered from surgery.

definition: To hate something very strongly, usually for moral reasons or because it disgusts you.
examples: I abhor cruelty to animals, so I could not watch that film.
Nadia abhors waste and always saves leftover rice for the next meal.
Most teachers abhor cheating because it makes honest students feel cheated.
He abhors the smell of fish, so he never visits the market.
Most Dhaka commuters abhor the evening jam on the main road.

form_sentences.sentence: Most readers abhorred the villain's cruel tricks in the novel.
I have always abhorred cruelty to animals, especially on the city streets.
Many citizens are abhorring the plastic waste piling up along the canal.
Abhorring cruelty is a value that most families try to teach their children.
Honest people tend to abhor lying, even when it would help them.

definition: A feeling of very strong hatred and disgust towards something.
examples: She has a deep abhorrence of cruelty to animals.
He looked at the dirty river with abhorrence.
Many people regard cheating in exams with abhorrence.
The community's abhorrence of violence led them to organise a peace march.
Her abhorrence of waste means she never throws away leftover food.

form_sentences.sentence: Historians describe the wars of that century as abhorrences that must never return.
Child labor is an abhorrent practice that every responsible company must end.
I abhor the way some people sell fake reviews online.

definition: The skill, power or talent needed to do something.
extra_senses: possession of the qualities (especially mental qualities) required to do something or get something done
examples: Her ability to stay calm under pressure helped her during the interview.
He has a natural ability for drawing, though he never took art classes.
Doing your best means working to the best of your ability, not being perfect.
The test measures students' ability to read and understand long English passages.
Dogs have an amazing ability to find their way home from far away.
collocations: to the best of my ability

form_sentences.sentence: Students have different abilities, so teachers must plan lessons carefully.

definition: Extremely bad, hopeless and humiliating, as in very great poverty or failure.
extra_senses: most unfortunate or miserable
showing utter resignation or hopelessness
examples: Millions of people around the world still live in abject poverty.
The team's abject failure in the final left the fans in silence.
He gave an abject apology, begging his neighbor to forgive him.
Years of drought left the farmers in abject misery.
She felt abject shame when she realized she had forgotten her friend's birthday.

form_sentences.sentence: Living conditions in the camp grew more abject as the rains continued.
He apologised abjectly, begging the teacher to give him one more chance.

definition: To formally promise to give up a belief, habit or claim, often in public or under oath.
examples: After his illness, he abjured smoking and promised his family he would never touch a cigarette again.
The new member abjured all her old loyalties and swore to follow only the club's rules.
She publicly abjured her earlier statements and apologized to the committee.
Both sides signed a pledge to abjure violence and settle the dispute by talking.
The athlete abjured sugar and fried food for the whole training season.

form_sentences.sentence: The former smoker has abjured cigarettes after a serious illness.
She is abjuring all junk food and sugary drinks this summer.
Abjuring old habits takes patience, but it can change your life.
He abjures late-night snacking and drinks only water after nine.

definition: Having the skill, power, time or chance to do something.
extra_senses: have the skills and qualifications to do things well
having inherent physical or mental ability or capacity
examples: After the operation, my grandfather was able to walk without a stick.
Will you be able to join us for dinner on Friday?
She is an able manager who solves problems quickly.
I was not able to open the file because it had been damaged.
Babies are able to recognise their mother's voice a few days after birth.

form_sentences.sentence: The new group of students is more able than the last one in math.
Her ability to stay calm under pressure impressed the interview panel.
The young nurse handled the emergency ably, and the patient recovered quickly.

definition: To give up or deny yourself something, such as a pleasure, a right or a belief.
extra_senses: surrender (power or a position)
deny or renounce
examples: Monks abnegate worldly comforts to live a simple life of study and quiet work.
A leader cannot abnegate responsibility when a project fails; he must answer for it.
During exam season, Rafi abnegated video games and parties to focus on his books.
In the story, the old king abnegated his throne so that his daughter could rule.
Some athletes abnegate their social lives for years to prepare for a major competition.

form_sentences.sentence: My cousin has abnegated sweets and fried snacks while preparing for the admission test.
She is abnegating her weekend shopping trips to save money for university.
Abnegating your own comfort can sometimes be the price of a good career.
Ahmed abnegates his evening phone time whenever his exam is close.
Many students try to abnegate social media during the final exam week.

definition: Different from what is usual, expected or healthy, often in a worrying way.
extra_senses: departing from the normal in e.g. intelligence and development
much greater than the normal
examples: The doctor ordered more tests because my blood pressure was abnormal.
It is abnormal for the river to rise this early in the season.
The security system detected abnormal activity on my account and blocked the payment.
The scan showed no abnormal growth, and the doctor smiled with relief.
Abnormal heat in February worried the farmers about their winter crops.

form_sentences.sentence: Doctors said his blood test results were more abnormal than last month.
The engineer found an abnormality in the bridge's steel supports.
The stock price moved abnormally during the first hour of trading.

definition: Something that is hated or considered shockingly bad, wicked or disgusting.
extra_senses: hate coupled with disgust
an action that is vicious or vile; an action that arouses disgust or abhorrence
examples: The new office building, covered in orange panels, was considered an abomination by the neighbors.
To a chef, putting ketchup on a fine steak is an abomination.
He called the dirty public toilet an abomination and demanded that the council fix it.
Cruelty to animals is an abomination to most people.
The film was such an abomination that critics begged readers to avoid it.

form_sentences.sentence: Critics described the poor road repairs as abominations that endangered every commuter.
I abominate wasteful packaging, and I always refuse plastic bags at the shop.

definition: Existing in a place from the earliest times, or belonging to the first people who lived there.
extra_senses: characteristic of or relating to people inhabiting a region from the beginning
having existed from the beginning; in an earliest or original stage or state
examples: Aboriginal communities in the hills have lived there for hundreds of years.
The museum displays aboriginal tools made from stone and wood.
Scientists are studying the aboriginal plants of the island to protect them.
The book explains the aboriginal languages that existed before newcomers arrived.
Aboriginal peoples around the world have their own stories about the land.

form_sentences.sentence: The wetland's bird species seem aboriginal, present there long before any town appeared.

definition: A member of the earliest known people of a region; now often replaced by "Indigenous person".
extra_senses: a member of the people living in Australia when Europeans arrived
examples: The museum has an exhibition about the traditional art of the region's aborigines.
Anthropologists studied how the aborigines of the island had lived for thousands of years.
The documentary showed how an aborigine elder passed old stories to younger generations.
Many aborigines lost their land when settlers arrived, a history that the country now acknowledges.
In her history class, Nadia wrote an essay on the rights of aborigines around the world.

form_sentences.sentence: The travel guide described the aboriginal traditions of the island with great respect.

definition: Failing to reach the intended result, so that the attempt has to be stopped or given up.
examples: After two abortive attempts to start the old generator, we gave up and waited for the electrician.
The company's abortive launch of its new app cost it thousands of users.
Her abortive plan to surprise her sister with a trip ended when the tickets sold out.
Rain forced the team to end their abortive effort to climb the hill before sunset.
The abortive peace talks broke down after only one day, according to news reports.

form_sentences.sentence: The first attempt to repair the router seemed abortive, so we called support.
The second rescue attempt was more abortive than the first, ending in confusion.
Mission control had to abort the rocket launch at the final second.
The protest ended abortively when the organisers ran out of permits.
The software crashed, forcing an abort of the entire upload process.

definition: To exist in large numbers or amounts; to be plentiful.
extra_senses: be in a state of movement or action
examples: Wildflowers abound along the hiking trail in early spring.
Bargains abound in the city's markets in the weeks before Eid.
Rumors abound whenever the school announces a surprise holiday.
Job opportunities abound for people with strong computer skills.
Spelling mistakes abound in the first draft of my essay.

form_sentences.sentence: Mangoes abounded in our village orchard during the summer of my childhood.
Bargain offers have abounded all week, so compare prices before you buy.
Fresh ideas are abounding in the university's new innovation lab this semester.
Abounding in natural beauty is the main reason tourists visit the hills.
The lake abounds with rohu and catfish, so local families spend weekends there.

definition: Harsh and rough, either scraping a surface or irritating people with an unkind manner.
extra_senses: causing abrasion
sharply disagreeable; rigorous
examples: Do not use abrasive cleaners on the new sink, or they will scratch the surface.
The manager's abrasive style made new employees afraid to ask questions.
Sandpaper is an abrasive material used to smooth rough wood.
His abrasive reply to the waiter embarrassed everyone at the table.
A face scrub that is too abrasive can irritate sensitive skin.

form_sentences.sentence: The new soap is more abrasive than the old one, so use gloves.
Rough sand can abrade the surface of soft plastic over time.
The abrasion on his knee from the fall needed a clean bandage.

definition: Fully informed about the latest news, changes or developments in a subject, used with of.
extra_senses: alongside each other, facing in the same direction
examples: Good journalists try to keep abreast of events in every part of the country.
Doctors must stay abreast of new research so they can treat patients with the best methods.
I read the news every morning to keep abreast of changes in exam rules.
Our manager keeps us abreast of any changes to the delivery schedule by sending a daily text.
Students who stay abreast of technology find it easier to get internships.

form_sentences.sentence: She became more abreast of the new rules after reading the circular.

definition: To make a book, text or speech shorter by cutting parts while keeping the main ideas.
extra_senses: lessen, diminish, or curtail
examples: The publisher abridged the thick novel so that younger readers could finish it quickly.
Can you abridge your speech to five minutes? We are short of time.
The film abridges the long book by leaving out several minor characters.
The editor abridged her article by cutting two long examples.
The story was abridged for the school textbook, with most of the long descriptions removed.

form_sentences.sentence: The publisher is abridging the novel for younger readers this year.
Abridging a long report helps busy managers read the key points.
I need to abridge my essay because the word limit is only five hundred.
The abridgement of the textbook made it easier to carry to class.

definition: In or to a foreign country.
extra_senses: in a foreign country
far away from home or one's usual surroundings
examples: Many Bangladeshi students dream of studying abroad after finishing their degree.
She has lived abroad for six years, but she still misses her mother's cooking.
Does your phone plan work when you travel abroad?
Travelling abroad for the first time can feel exciting and a little scary.
Her cousin returned from abroad with gifts for the whole family.

definition: To officially cancel or end a law, agreement or right.
examples: The council voted to abrogate the old rule that banned street vendors from the main road.
The company abrogated the contract after the supplier missed three deadlines.
A new law abrogated the earlier regulation about school uniforms.
Neither side can abrogate the agreement without giving ninety days’ notice.
He accused his landlord of trying to abrogate the lease so that he could raise the rent.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The government has abrogated the old rule that limited night-time deliveries.
The council is abrogating a contract that no longer serves local residents.
Abrogating an agreement without notice can damage trust between business partners.
The new law abrogates the earlier policy, so all old permits become invalid.

definition: The natural process by which a plant drops its leaves, flowers or fruit.
extra_senses: the act of cutting something off
examples: Leaf abscission happens in autumn, when trees seal off the stems and let the leaves drop.
Dry weather can speed up the abscission of mango flowers, which lowers the harvest.
The biology teacher drew a diagram showing how abscission separates a leaf from its branch.
A plant hormone called ethylene helps control the abscission of ripe fruit.
Gardeners watched the abscission of the yellow leaves and swept them up each morning.

definition: To leave a place suddenly and secretly, usually to avoid arrest or to take something that is not yours.
examples: The cashier absconded with the shop's weekly earnings and has not been seen since.
The accused man absconded while out on bail, so the police are searching for him.
A tenant absconded in the night without paying three months' rent.
Two students absconded from the boarding house after the warden confiscated their phones.
The scammer absconded to another city after taking deposits for flats that did not exist.

form_sentences.sentence: The cashier has absconded with the shop's savings, police said on Monday.
My little brother is absconding with my pens again, so I locked my bag today.
Absconding with company property can lead to a long prison sentence.
The dishonest broker absconds with clients' deposits and disappears overnight.
Two prisoners tried to abscond from the jail during the heavy monsoon rain.

definition: The fact of not being present in a place, or the time when someone is away.
extra_senses: failure to be present
the time interval during which something or somebody is away
examples: Her absence from class for a week meant she missed two important tests.
In the manager's absence, his assistant handled all the customer calls.
The school sends parents a text message after every absence.
Frequent absence from work can cost you your job.
My father's long absence abroad made every homecoming special for us.

form_sentences.sentence: Frequent absences from class can lower your grades in the final exam.
The absent students will receive the notes by email this afternoon.
He chose to absent himself from the meeting after the argument with his manager.

definition: Not present in a place where you are expected to be.
extra_senses: go away or leave
nonexistent
examples: Three students were absent from class today because of the flu.
My father was absent from work for two days after the operation.
She marks every absent child in the register at the start of the lesson.
The captain was absent from the final match because of an injury.
Please sign the form if you will be absent from the meeting on Sunday.

form_sentences.sentence: Her absence from the team meeting was noticed by everyone.

definition: Complete and total, with no limits, conditions or exceptions.
extra_senses: complete and without restriction or qualification; sometimes used informally as intensifiers

something that is conceived or that exists independently and not in relation to other things; something that does not depend on anything else and is beyond human control; something that is not relative
examples: The exam hall was in absolute silence except for the sound of pens moving on paper.
I have absolute trust in my sister, so I told her everything.
Getting the scholarship was an absolute joy for the whole family.
Under the old law, the owner had absolute power to fire anyone without giving a reason.
The film was an absolute waste of money, and half the audience left early.

form_sentences.sentence: Silence in the exam hall must be absolute, or the candidates will be disturbed.
The mobile app is absolutely free to download, with no hidden charges.

definition: Completely and without any doubt; used to add strength to what you say.
extra_senses: totally and definitely; without question
examples: The view from the hilltop was absolutely beautiful at sunrise.
You absolutely must wear a helmet when riding a motorbike.
I am absolutely sure that I locked the door before leaving.
Are you coming to the party? Absolutely, I would not miss it!
The soup was absolutely delicious, so I asked for the recipe.

form_sentences.sentence: Absolute silence fell over the classroom when the exam started.

definition: To declare officially that someone is free from blame, guilt or a duty.
extra_senses: let off the hook
examples: The investigation absolved the driver of any blame for the accident.
The new rule does not absolve parents of responsibility for their children's safety.
A written apology cannot absolve you of the duty to repay what you borrowed.
The committee absolved the student of cheating after checking the camera footage.
Telling the truth late does not absolve him from the damage the lie caused.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The inquiry has absolved the nurse of any blame for the mix-up.
The committee is absolving the staff member after reviewing all the evidence.
Absolving the driver without a proper inquiry would anger the families involved.
The judge absolves the defendant when no solid evidence remains.
Years later, he still sought absolution for the mistake that cost his friend the job.

definition: To take something in, such as liquid, heat, light or information, and hold it inside.
extra_senses: take up mentally
take up, as of debts or payments
examples: A sponge can absorb a surprising amount of water in a few seconds.
Dark clothes absorb more heat from the sun, so they feel hotter in summer.
The dry soil quickly absorbed the first rain of the season.
Young children absorb new words very quickly when they hear them every day.
The body absorbs most of the medicine within an hour of swallowing it.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The sponge has absorbed all the spilled juice in less than a minute.
The soil is absorbing heavy rain, so the streets are not flooding yet.
Absorbing new vocabulary every day is easier when you use it in sentences.
Cotton is absorbent, so it is a good choice for towels and shirts.
The absorption of vitamin D depends on how much sunlight you get.

definition: To choose not to do or have something, especially something enjoyable or unhealthy, or to choose not to vote.
extra_senses: choose not to consume
examples: Doctors advise patients with high blood pressure to abstain from salty food.
Three members abstained from the vote because they had not read the proposal.
She abstained from social media during exam week to focus on her studies.
Athletes must abstain from certain medicines before a competition.
I abstained from replying to the angry message until I had calmed down.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: She has abstained from social media during the entire exam season.
The students are abstaining from fast food during the month-long challenge.
Abstaining from loud music during study hours helps me concentrate.
My cousin abstains from coffee after noon so he can sleep well.
He remained abstinent from alcohol for the whole year of training.

definition: Careful to eat and drink only small amounts and to avoid indulging yourself.
extra_senses: marked by temperance in indulgence
examples: My grandfather is abstemious: he eats one small meal at night and never touches sweets.
Training for the marathon made her far more abstemious about food and late nights.
Though he was wealthy, the old judge led an abstemious life and drank only water.
After the Eid feasts, many families return to a more abstemious routine of simple meals.
Be abstemious at the buffet tonight, because you have an early swim meet tomorrow.

form_sentences.sentence: After the wedding, he became more abstemious and drank only plain water.

definition: Deliberately avoiding something enjoyable, such as alcohol or sweets, usually for health or moral reasons.
extra_senses: self-restraining; not indulging an appetite especially for food or drink
examples: He has been abstinent from sugary drinks since his doctor warned him about diabetes.
Many athletes stay abstinent from alcohol during the training season.
After his heart attack, my uncle became abstinent and no longer touches fried food.
She remained abstinent from social media for a month to focus on her exams.
The abstinent diner refused dessert and drank only plain water.

form_sentences.sentence: Athletes in training are often more abstinent about junk food than their friends.
Some students abstain from energy drinks before the exam to sleep better.
Abstinence from late-night phone use improved her sleep and her grades.

definition: Existing as an idea or quality rather than as a physical object, or too general to relate to real situations.
extra_senses: existing only in the mind; separated from embodiment
a concept or idea not associated with any specific instance
examples: Words like freedom and justice are abstract, so children need examples to understand them.
The lesson was too abstract for the class until the teacher showed a real bridge model.
She prefers practical tasks to abstract discussions about what might happen.
Abstract thinking helps mathematicians solve problems that have no direct link to daily life.
Beauty is an abstract quality that people describe in very different ways.

form_sentences.sentence: Her explanation became more abstract as the lecture went on.
The abstraction of the maths lesson confused most students in the first hour.
The professor described the theory abstractly, without any real examples.

definition: Difficult to understand because it is deep, complex or very specialized.
examples: The professor's abstruse explanation of the theory left most of us confused.
Without a dictionary, the abstruse legal language was impossible to follow.
Quantum physics can seem abstruse until you see it explained with simple pictures.
He avoids abstruse words when he writes for young readers.
I skipped the abstruse chapter on philosophy and went straight to the summary.

form_sentences.sentence: This physics textbook is more abstruse than the lecture notes.

definition: A very large quantity of something; more than enough.
extra_senses: (physics) the ratio of the number of atoms of a specific isotope of an element to the total number of isotopes present
(chemistry) the ratio of the total mass of an element in the earth's crust to the total mass of the earth's crust; expressed as a percentage or in parts per million
examples: The market had an abundance of fresh vegetables after the harvest.
Bangladesh has an abundance of rivers, which makes the land rich and green.
Flowers grew in abundance along the roadside after the first monsoon rains.
With an abundance of free online courses, anyone can learn a new skill.
She was grateful for the abundance of love in her family.

form_sentences.sentence: The village has abundant rice fields and clean water all year round.

definition: To use something in a wrong or harmful way, or to treat someone cruelly.
extra_senses: change the inherent purpose or function of something
cruel or inhumane treatment
examples: Some officials abuse their power by asking for money before doing their job.
It is cruel to abuse animals, and the law punishes people who do it.
Teenagers who abuse painkillers can seriously damage their health.
Customers sometimes abuse the free return policy by sending back worn clothes.
He abused her trust by sharing her private messages with his friends.

form_sentences.sentence: Their trust has been abused by a dishonest employee.
The manager is abusing his power by asking staff to work unpaid overtime.
Abusing a free trial to avoid paying for software is unfair to the developers.
The shady app abuses user data by selling it to advertisers, so be careful.
The abusive language in the comments led to several accounts being blocked.

definition: Extremely bad or poor in quality; terrible, wretched and hopeless.
extra_senses: resembling an abyss in depth; so deep as to be unmeasurable
examples: The team's abysmal performance in the final match disappointed all its supporters.
The hostel food was abysmal, so students began cooking in their rooms.
The road is in abysmal condition, full of holes that damage every vehicle.
Her abysmal marks in physics worried her parents, so they hired a tutor.
The customer service was abysmal; nobody answered the phone or replied to emails.

form_sentences.sentence: The bus service this winter has been more abysmal than ever.
Without a savings plan, many families fall into a financial abyss.
The students performed abysmally on the practice test last week.

definition: A very deep hole or space that seems to have no bottom, or a huge gap or depth of feeling.
examples: The climbers looked down into a dark abyss beside the narrow mountain path.

Long ago, people in the village travelled mostly by boat.

definition: To worry or think painfully for a long time before making a decision.

form_sentences.sentence: She has agonized over her choice of university for three long weeks.

Agonizing over small decisions can waste hours that you could spend studying.

Try not to agonize over each mistake in your practice test because everyone makes some.

definition: Relating to farming or to the ownership and use of farmland.
examples: Bangladesh was largely an agrarian society for centuries, with most families living off the land.

form_sentences.sentence: Life in the district remains agrarian, with most families growing rice and vegetables.

definition: To have the same opinion as someone, or to say yes to a plan or request.
extra_senses: consent or assent to a condition, or agree to do something
be compatible, similar or consistent; coincide in their characteristics

The two shopkeepers agreed on a fair price after some discussion.
Most doctors agree that regular exercise helps prevent many illnesses.

form_sentences.sentence: The landlord and the tenant have agreed on a fair rent for next year.

definition: A decision or arrangement that two or more people or groups have accepted together.
extra_senses: compatibility of observations
harmony of people's opinions or actions or characters
examples: The tenant and the landlord signed a one-year rental agreement.

Please read the agreement carefully before you sign it.
The agreement between the farmers and the company guarantees a fixed price for rice.

form_sentences.sentence: The two companies signed several agreements about shipping routes.

definition: In front of someone or something, or further forward in space or time.
extra_senses: toward the future; forward in time
in a forward direction

Our team is ahead by two goals at half time.
It is smart to plan ahead before the exam week starts.
Rafi walked ahead to find a place for us to sit.

definition: Help or support given to someone who needs it, or a thing that makes a task easier.
extra_senses: a person or thing that is a resource that helps make something easier or possible to do
the activity of contributing to the fulfillment of a need or furtherance of an effort or purpose
examples: With the aid of a ladder, the boy climbed up to rescue the kitten.

A calculator is a useful aid in maths, but you must learn the method first.

Foreign aid arrived quickly after the cyclone, including food, water and tents.

definition: The purpose of what you are doing; the result you hope to achieve.
extra_senses: point or cause to go (blows, weapons, or objects such as photographic equipment) towards
propose or intend
examples: My main aim this year is to score above eighty percent in every subject.
The aim of the campaign is to teach children to wash their hands.

The aim of the meeting is to choose a date for the school picnic.

definition: The mixture of gases around the Earth that people and animals breathe.
extra_senses: the region above the ground
a distinctive but intangible quality surrounding a person or thing
examples: I opened the window to let some fresh air into the room.
The air in the city is thick with smoke in the winter.
Plants need air, water and sunlight to grow.
There was a smell of fried snacks in the air near the tea stall.
Pump more air into the tyre before you start cycling.

definition: A vehicle that can fly, such as an aeroplane or a helicopter.
examples: The aircraft landed safely despite the strong winds.
A small aircraft flew over our village, and the children ran outside to look.
Engineers check every aircraft carefully before it takes off.
The airline bought three new aircraft to fly to more cities.

definition: A place where aircraft take off and land, with buildings for passengers.
examples: We reached the airport three hours before our flight.
My uncle picked me up from the airport in his car.
The airport was crowded with families returning home before Eid.
Security officers check every bag at the airport entrance.
A new airport is being built near the coast to serve the growing number of tourists.

form_sentences.sentence: Large cities usually have several airports that serve different types of flights.

definition: Taking place outdoors, in the open air, especially when talking about a meal.
examples: On sunny weekends the cafe by the lake offers al fresco dining under colorful umbrellas.

Nadia loves al fresco breakfasts on the rooftop terrace before the city gets hot.

The restaurant's al fresco seating fills up quickly whenever the weather is pleasant.

form_sentences.sentence: Our dinner was al fresco, under the big mango tree in the courtyard.

definition: Quick and cheerful readiness to do something.
examples: When Mom asked for help carrying the shopping, my brother agreed with alacrity.

Nadia took up the offer of a free ticket to the science fair with alacrity.
The neighbors helped rebuild the fallen fence with alacrity after the storm.
He answered every email with alacrity in his first week, hoping to impress his new boss.

definition: A device or signal that makes a loud noise to warn people of danger or to wake them up.
extra_senses: a device that signals the occurrence of some undesirable event
fill with apprehension or alarm; cause to be unpleasantly surprised
examples: I set my alarm for five o'clock so that I could revise before school.

A car alarm started ringing loudly in the middle of the night.

The shop owner installed an alarm after thieves broke in last month.

definition: Feeling worried or frightened because you think something bad may happen.
examples: We were alarmed when the lights suddenly went out during the exam.
She felt alarmed by the sound of someone knocking on the door late at night.
The parents were alarmed to hear that their son had not come home.
Doctors are alarmed at the rise in cases of dengue fever this monsoon.
Do not be alarmed if you see smoke; the cook is only frying fish.

form_sentences.sentence: The alarmed parents called the school after hearing about the storm.
The residents became more alarmed when the water level rose again.

definition: Causing worry or fear because it seems dangerous or serious.
examples: An alarming number of students admit to sleeping less than five hours a night.
Prices of vegetables have risen at an alarming rate this month.
The doctor found an alarming change in the patient's blood pressure.
It is alarming how quickly a small fire can spread in a crowded market.
The alarming cracks in the old wall made the owners call an engineer.

form_sentences.sentence: The rise in dengue cases is more alarming than last year's figures suggested.
Prices have risen alarmingly in the last three months, according to the report.

definition: Used to introduce a word or phrase that makes the previous statement less strong or less certain.
examples: He passed the exam, albeit with the lowest score in the class.
The hotel was comfortable, albeit a little noisy at night.
She finally agreed to help, albeit reluctantly.
The company made a profit this year, albeit a small one.
We reached the village before dark, albeit tired and covered in mud.

definition: A process that changes something into something better in a way that seems almost magical.
extra_senses: a pseudoscientific forerunner of chemistry in medieval times
examples: It was pure alchemy: she turned a pile of scrap cloth into a stunning dress.
The alchemy of spices and slow cooking turned simple lentils into a rich dish.
Medieval alchemy tried, without success, to turn lead into gold.
The coach's alchemy turned a group of beginners into a winning team.
Some writers have a kind of alchemy: they turn ordinary events into unforgettable stories.

form_sentences.sentence: Her alchemical gift for turning cheap ingredients into rich, memorable meals amazed guests.
Our chemistry teacher is a true alchemist, turning dull lessons into exciting experiments.
She hopes to alchemize her frustration into a strong essay for the admission test.

definition: Drinks such as beer, wine and whisky that can make people drunk.
extra_senses: any of a series of volatile hydroxyl compounds that are made from hydrocarbons by distillation
examples: Doctors warn that too much alcohol can damage the liver.
The shop is not allowed to sell alcohol to anyone under eighteen.
Drivers who have drunk alcohol must never get behind the wheel.
Some medicines should not be taken together with alcohol.
Many people choose to avoid alcohol for health and personal reasons.

form_sentences.sentence: Ethanol and methanol are two alcohols with very different effects on the body.
Alcoholic drinks are banned in many public places during the festival.

definition: Containing alcohol, or relating to drinks that have alcohol in them.
extra_senses: characteristic of or containing alcohol
addicted to alcohol
examples: Alcoholic drinks are not served in the school canteen.
This fruit juice is not alcoholic, so children can drink it safely.
The restaurant offers a wide menu of both alcoholic and soft drinks.
Alcoholic drinks cannot be sold near a hospital or a school.
The doctor told him to avoid alcoholic drinks while he is taking antibiotics.

form_sentences.sentence: Some wines are more alcoholic than beer, so check the label before you drink.

definition: To make someone feel unfriendly, distant or unwelcome, so that they no longer like or support you.
extra_senses: transfer property or ownership
make withdrawn or isolated or emotionally dissociated
examples: Constant bragging can alienate even your closest friends.
The shop alienated loyal customers by suddenly doubling its prices.
Her harsh criticism alienated the new team members, and several of them quit.
Parents who never listen may alienate their teenage children.
The long, confusing form alienates people who want to apply for the scholarship.

Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: Many new students feel alienated by the long and confusing registration forms.
The rude manager is alienating his best staff with constant criticism.
Alienating customers with rude replies will hurt your shop's reputation.

definition: Living, not dead; still breathing and able to survive.
extra_senses: (often followed by `with') full of life and spirit
having life or vigor or spirit
examples: Rescue workers found two people alive under the fallen building.
My grandfather is eighty and still alive and healthy.
The fish was still alive when the fisherman put it into the bucket.
Plants need sunlight and water to stay alive.
Doctors worked all night to keep the injured man alive.

form_sentences.sentence: The city feels more alive during the festival season.

definition: Satisfactory or acceptable; also safe or in good health.
extra_senses: an expression of agreement normally occurring at the beginning of a sentence
without doubt (used to reinforce an assertion)
examples: Is it all right if I borrow your pen for the test?
Are you all right? You look very pale.
The food at the new cafe is all right, but nothing special.
It is all right to make mistakes while you are learning a language.
Everything will be all right after you take some rest.

form_sentences.sentence: The rightness of the decision was clear after we checked all the facts.
You rightly pointed out the error in my calculation, and I thank you.

definition: To reduce or calm a feeling such as fear, worry or doubt.
extra_senses: satisfy (thirst)
examples: The doctor spoke gently to allay the patient's fear before the operation.

The airline's safety report helped allay passengers' doubts about the new plane.
To allay his nervousness before the interview, Imran practiced his answers in front of the mirror.

form_sentences.sentence: The doctor's calm voice has allayed my fears about the surgery.
The bank is allaying customers' worries with clear updates on the transfer.
Allaying parents' concerns about safety is the school's top priority.
Her warm smile allays my nerves before every presentation I give.

definition: To state that someone did something wrong, without giving proof.
examples: The report alleges that the company dumped waste into the river at night.

definition: Said to be true or to have happened, but not yet proved.
extra_senses: doubtful or suspect
examples: The police are investigating the alleged theft of three motorbikes from the market.
The alleged cheating in the exam hall led the school to hold an inquiry.
The company denied the alleged pollution of the river.
Nobody has seen proof of the alleged meeting between the two companies.
The alleged mistake in the bill was later shown to be a printing error.

form_sentences.sentence: The charge remains alleged until the court announces its verdict.
The driver allegedly ran the red light, according to the police report.

definition: Loyalty and support that you give to a person, group, country or cause.
extra_senses: the loyalty that citizens owe to their country (or subjects to their sovereign)

The two directors changed their allegiance to the new owner once the company was sold.
Employees with strong allegiance to the company often stay for decades.

form_sentences.sentence: Shifting allegiances among local clubs made the league table hard to predict.

definition: A story, poem or picture in which characters and events stand for deeper ideas, often about morals or society.
extra_senses: a visible symbol representing an abstract idea
an expressive style that uses fictional characters and events to describe some subject by suggestive resemblances; an extended metaphor
examples: The story of the tortoise and the hare is a simple allegory about steady effort.

form_sentences.sentence: The novel is full of allegories about greed, power and the cost of ambition.

definition: To make pain, difficulty or a problem less severe.

of or relating to or denoting the Allies in World War I

definition: A metal made by mixing two or more metals, or a metal and another element.

definition: A person, group or country that helps and supports another, especially in a difficult situation.

definition: Very close to something, but not completely or exactly so.

definition: Without any other people; by yourself.

definition: Next to or at the side of something or someone.

definition: In a voice that other people can hear, not silently.

definition: A set of letters in a fixed order that is used to write a language.

definition: Unselfish concern for the welfare of others, shown through helpful actions.
examples: Donating blood to strangers is an act of pure altruism.

definition: To combine two or more organizations, groups or things into one.

His letter described the anguish of leaving his village and everyone he loved.

form_sentences.sentence: The novel explores the different anguishes that soldiers carry home after long wars.

definition: A living creature, other than a human, that can move and feel and usually eats food.
extra_senses: marked by the appetites and passions of the body
examples: A cow is a farm animal that gives milk, and many families keep one in the village.
Dogs and cats are the most common animals people keep as pets in cities.
Please do not feed the wild animals in the park, because they may become sick.
Our science book has a chapter about how each animal adapts to its habitat.
The zoo has a new area where visitors can watch elephants and other large animals.

definition: Strong dislike or ill will toward someone that often leads to open hostility.
examples: There was no animosity between the two rivals, who shook hands after the match.
Years of arguments over land created deep animosity between the two families.
She felt no animosity toward the classmate who had beaten her for first place.
A calm talk with a neutral friend helped the roommates end their animosity.
The animosity between the two companies grew when each accused the other of stealing ideas.

form_sentences.sentence: Old animosities between the two neighbouring villages finally ended after the new bridge opened.

definition: The joint that connects the foot to the leg, just above the foot.
examples: I twisted my ankle while running for the bus and could not walk properly.
The doctor wrapped my ankle in a bandage and told me to rest for a week.
Wear shoes with good support, because a weak ankle can easily be injured on rough ground.
She slipped on the wet stairs and hurt her ankle badly during the rainy season.
The footballer had an ankle injury, so he sat out the final match of the season.

form_sentences.sentence: Both ankles were swollen after the long hike up the hill.
She wore a silver anklet with tiny bells that rang when she walked.

definition: To add something to a larger thing, especially to take control of land and make it part of a bigger area.
extra_senses: take (territory) as if by conquest
attach to
examples: The city plans to annex several nearby villages to expand its boundaries.
The neighbouring country annexed the island in the nineteenth century.
The university annexed the old hospital building to create more classrooms.
Writers sometimes annex a short glossary to the end of a long report.
The company annexed a smaller firm to extend its customer base.

The hospital annexes a nearby building whenever its wards become overcrowded.

definition: To destroy something or someone completely, so that nothing is left.
examples: Our team annihilated the opposition and won the school final by six goals.
A strong pesticide can annihilate the insects that attack the rice crop.
A faulty update annihilated every file on my old computer.
Scientists warn that a huge asteroid could annihilate life on Earth.

example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The flood has annihilated the crops in several low-lying villages.

Annihilating every bad habit at once is impossible, so start with the biggest one.

definition: The date each year that marks when a special event happened in an earlier year.
examples: My parents celebrated their twenty-fifth wedding anniversary with a small family dinner.
The school will hold a special programme on the anniversary of its founding.
We bought flowers for our grandparents to mark their golden wedding anniversary.
Today is the anniversary of the day our town received electricity for the first time.
On the anniversary of the country's independence, the streets are decorated with flags.

form_sentences.sentence: Our parents celebrated several wedding anniversaries with a family dinner.

definition: To add short notes or comments to a text or diagram to explain it.
extra_senses: provide interlinear explanations for words or phrases
examples: Our teacher asked us to annotate the poem with notes on its main ideas.

The editor annotated the draft with questions in the margin.
Engineers annotate the drawings with measurements for the builders.
Scholars annotated the old manuscript to help modern readers understand its language.

form_sentences.sentence: She has annotated every page of her grammar book with examples.
Our teacher is annotating the sample essay for the class discussion.
Annotating maps helps travelers remember important routes and landmarks.
This app annotates every PDF you upload with highlights and sticky notes.

definition: To tell people about something publicly or officially, especially a decision or news.
extra_senses: announce publicly or officially
give the names of
examples: The university will announce the admission test results on its website next Friday.

The airline announced a delay of two hours because of the fog at the airport.
My sister announced her engagement at the family dinner, and everyone cheered.
The government announced a new scheme for students who need help with their fees.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The results have been announced on the university website this morning.
The principal is announcing new rules for the lab during the assembly.
Announcing the winners on social media helps the contest reach more people.
The airline announces delays through text messages and the mobile app.
The announcer read the list of results in a clear, calm voice.

definition: To make someone slightly angry or impatient by repeated small actions or words.
examples: The loud music from the next flat annoys me when I am trying to study.
Please stop tapping your pen on the desk, because it really annoys everyone in class.
Constant notifications on my phone annoy me during the lecture every afternoon.
The rickshaw puller's horn annoyed the passengers stuck in the long traffic jam.
My little brother keeps asking questions, and sometimes it really annoys me.

The noise from the construction site is annoying everyone on our street.
Annoying your neighbors is easy, but building good relationships takes effort.
Try not to annoy your classmates with loud noises during the quiet hour.

definition: Slightly angry or impatient because of something that has bothered you.
extra_senses: troubled persistently especially with petty annoyances
examples: I was annoyed when the shop forgot my order, even after I had called twice.
She looked annoyed because her friend arrived forty minutes late for the movie.
The teacher was annoyed that half the class had not finished the homework.
Many commuters felt annoyed by the long wait at the bus stop in the heat.
He sounded annoyed when he said the internet had stopped again during the exam.

form_sentences.sentence: The annoyed passengers complained to the driver about the long delay.
After the third delay, the commuters were more annoyed than before.

definition: Causing slight anger or impatience, usually because it is repeated or unnecessary.
extra_senses: the act of troubling or annoying someone
examples: The buzzing of the mosquito near my ear is very annoying at night.
It is annoying when people talk loudly in the library during the exam period.
Losing the pen you just bought is annoying, but it is not a serious problem.
Her annoying habit of checking her phone during dinner made the meal feel long.
The constant ringing of the mobile in the bus was very annoying for everyone.

form_sentences.sentence: The new ringtone is more annoying than the old one, so I changed it.
Loud music late at night can annoy neighbors and disturb their sleep.
The phone kept buzzing annoyingly during the lecture, so I switched it off.

definition: Happening once every year, or covering a period of one year.
extra_senses: (botany) a plant that completes its entire life cycle within the space of a year
a reference book that is published regularly once every year
examples: The school holds its annual sports day every winter.
The annual fee for the library membership is five hundred taka.
The company publishes its annual report to show how much profit it made.
My family takes an annual trip to the village during the Eid holidays.
Doctors recommend an annual health check for people over forty.

form_sentences.sentence: The sports day is annual, held every October for all students.
The festival is held annually, attracting visitors from across the country.

definition: Once every year, or as a yearly event or payment.
extra_senses: by the year; every year (usually with reference to a sum of money paid or received)
examples: The university publishes its admission notice annually, usually in the early winter.
Our family pays the insurance premium annually instead of every month.
The book fair is held annually in the Bangla Academy premises in February.
My cousin receives a scholarship annually from a foundation that supports poor students.
The company reviews its salary structure annually to keep up with living costs.

form_sentences.sentence: The annual sports day is the biggest event of the school year.

definition: A fixed sum of money paid to someone each year, often after retirement, from an insurance plan or investment.
examples: After retiring, he bought an annuity that pays him a fixed amount every year.
Her grandmother lives on a small annuity from her late husband's insurance plan.
An annuity can protect retired people from running out of money.
The bank advisor explained the difference between an annuity and a savings account.
Her annuity pays out once a year, so she plans her spending carefully.

form_sentences.sentence: Several annuities from the insurance company helped the couple pay for their retirement.

definition: To officially declare that a law, contract, marriage or result is no longer valid.
extra_senses: cancel officially
examples: The court annulled the contract because one side had hidden important facts.
The exam board annulled the results after finding that the questions had leaked.
The couple asked a judge to annul their marriage after only one month.
The club annulled the election and ordered a new vote.
The government can annul a license if the owner breaks the safety rules.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The court annulled the contract after it found that the signature was forged.
The university has annulled the exam result after finding cheating in the hall.
The council is annulling several old licenses that were never renewed.

The referee annuls any goal that is scored after the whistle.

definition: A medicine or other thing that eases pain or comforts someone in distress.
extra_senses: capable of relieving pain
examples: Doctors once used opium as an anodyne for severe pain.
For the grieving family, kind words from neighbors were the only anodyne.
Music is her anodyne after a stressful day at work.
The herbal tea was a mild anodyne that eased his toothache for a few hours.
He found work an anodyne for loneliness after moving to a new city.

form_sentences.sentence: Doctors prescribed two anodynes for the pain after the surgery.

definition: To rub oil or ointment on someone, especially in a ceremony, or to choose them for an important role.
extra_senses: administer an oil or ointment to; often in a religious ceremony of blessing
examples: The therapist anointed her tired shoulders with warm herbal oil.
The grandmother anointed the baby's head with a little coconut oil before the bath.
In the old tradition, a ruler was anointed with oil during the coronation ceremony.
The media anointed the young striker the next big star after only two matches.
The retiring founder anointed his daughter as his successor at the company dinner.

form_sentences.sentence: The coach is anointing a young player as the new team captain.
Anointing someone as a leader before they prove themselves can cause resentment.
Every semester, our department anoints one student as its top researcher.
Many people wanted to anoint her as the new class representative.

definition: Different from what is normal or expected, so that it is hard to explain.
examples: The scientist rechecked the anomalous reading, which was far higher than all the other measurements.
It is anomalous for the river to be this low in the middle of the monsoon.
The auditor noticed several anomalous entries in the shop's accounts.
Doctors were puzzled by the anomalous heart rhythm in an otherwise healthy teenager.
The network team investigated anomalous traffic on the server that did not match any normal pattern.

form_sentences.sentence: The sales data from the Chittagong branch was more anomalous than anything before.
The anomaly in the pricing system was fixed after the software update.

definition: Something that is different from what is normal or expected and cannot easily be explained.
extra_senses: a person who is unusual
(astronomy) position of a planet as defined by its angular distance from its perihelion (as observed from the sun)
examples: One strange result in the experiment was an anomaly that the students could not explain.
A snowfall in this warm region would be a real anomaly.
The accountant noticed an anomaly in the bank statement and called the branch.
It seems an anomaly that such a busy shopping street has no pharmacy.
Her low mark in math was an anomaly, since she normally scored near the top.

form_sentences.sentence: The bank noticed several anomalies in her account, so it froze the card.
The anomalous readings from the weather station were removed before the report.

definition: One more person or thing of the same kind, or a different one.
examples: Could I have another cup of tea, please, because this one is already cold?
We need another chair in the living room for the guests coming tonight.
The bus was full, so we waited for another one that came twenty minutes later.
If the first plan fails, we can try another approach next week.
Let us meet another day, because I have an exam tomorrow morning.

definition: Something you say or write in reply to a question, request or problem.
extra_senses: a statement (either spoken or written) that is made to reply to a question or request or criticism or accusation
a statement that solves a problem or explains how to solve the problem
examples: The student wrote a clear answer to the second question in the English paper.

Her answer to the complaint was polite, but it did not solve the problem.
The correct answer to this maths problem is twenty-four, so check your working.
He gave an honest answer when the manager asked why the delivery was late.

form_sentences.sentence: Sadly, not every question is answerable with the data we currently have.

definition: To make someone angry or hostile towards you by what you say or do.
extra_senses: act in opposition to
examples: Don't antagonize the security guard; he is only following the rules.

Loud music late at night will antagonize your neighbors.
The coach antagonized the players by shouting at them in front of their parents.

definition: Something or someone that came before, and from which a later thing or person developed.
extra_senses: a preceding occurrence or cause or event
preceding in time or order
examples: The bicycle was an early antecedent of the modern motorbike.

The village fair, with its stalls and folk songs, is an antecedent of today’s big shopping festivals.

definition: To come earlier in time than something else.
extra_senses: establish something as being earlier relative to something else
examples: The old fort antedates the nearby town by several centuries.

Some ancient tools are believed to antedate the first farming settlements.

definition: Situated at or near the front of something, especially a body or an organ.
extra_senses: a tooth situated at the front of the mouth
earlier in time

definition: A published collection of poems, stories or songs by different writers, or chosen from one writer's work.

definition: To expect something to happen and be ready for it, or to see it coming.

definition: A set of rooms for living in, usually on one floor of a larger building.

definition: Showing little interest, enthusiasm or concern about anything.
extra_senses: marked by a lack of interest

definition: A lack of interest, enthusiasm or concern about things that should matter.

definition: A small opening or hole in something, especially one that lets light or air pass through.

examples: Sunlight streamed through a narrow aperture in the wall of the old storeroom.

definition: The highest point of something, or the point where it is at its most successful.

definition: A short, clever saying that expresses a general truth.

definition: The total destruction of the world, or any disaster so terrible that it feels like the end of everything.
extra_senses: the last book of the New Testament; contains visionary descriptions of heaven and of conflicts between good and evil and of the end of the world; attributed to Saint John the Apostle
examples: The film is set in a world after a nuclear apocalypse, where survivors search for clean water.

form_sentences.sentence: Writers have imagined many apocalypses, from plague-filled cities to climate-driven floods.
