definition: Widely told as if it were true, but probably not true and never proven to be real.
extra_senses: of or belonging to the Apocrypha
examples: The story that he walked ten miles to school every day is probably apocryphal.
Many apocryphal quotes spread online are wrongly credited to famous scientists.
It is an apocryphal tale, but the whole village still tells it to visitors.
The apocryphal rumor that the school would close early spread through the hostel in minutes.
Her grandmother's tale of a talking fish is apocryphal, yet the children love it.

form_sentences.sentence: The story about a lost gold coin became more apocryphal with each retelling.

definition: The highest or most successful point of something; also the point in an orbit farthest from Earth.
extra_senses: apoapsis in Earth orbit; the point in its orbit where a satellite is at the greatest distance from the Earth
examples: The satellite is farthest from Earth at its apogee, then slowly falls closer again.
When the moon is at apogee, it looks slightly smaller in the sky.
His career reached its apogee when he became head of the hospital.
The empire's power was at its apogee in the seventeenth century.
For many fans, the nineties were the apogee of the band's popularity.

form_sentences.sentence: Engineers track the satellite's apogees to plan each of its orbital adjustments.

definition: To say that you are sorry for something wrong you have done or said.
extra_senses: defend, explain, clear away, or make excuses for by reasoning
examples: I need to apologize to my friend for forgetting her birthday last Thursday.
The shopkeeper apologized for the delay and gave us a discount on the next visit.
Please apologize to your teacher if you missed the deadline without telling her.
He apologized sincerely after he realised that his joke had hurt his classmate.
The airline apologized to passengers for the long wait at the airport gate.

form_sentences.sentence: The company has apologized for the delay and offered a small refund.
The waiter is apologizing for the mistake and bringing a new plate.
Apologizing quickly after a mistake often helps you keep a friend.
He apologizes to everyone he hurts, which is one reason people trust him.
She sent a short apology after she missed the group meeting.

definition: An old-fashioned word for a stroke, a sudden loss of movement and awareness caused by a problem with blood supply to the brain.
examples: In the old novel, the wealthy merchant dies suddenly of apoplexy at the dinner table.
Doctors once called a stroke apoplexy, because it struck without any warning.
Apoplexy can leave a patient paralysed on one side of the body.
My great-grandfather was said to have died of apoplexy, though today we would call it a stroke.
Historical records show that the king's death was caused by apoplexy after years of high blood pressure.

form_sentences.sentence: My father became apoplectic when he saw the bill for the broken window.

definition: The abandonment of a belief, faith, party or cause that you once strongly supported.
extra_senses: the act of abandoning a party for cause
examples: Fans called it apostasy when the captain left his boyhood club to join its fiercest rival.
In his memoir, he describes his apostasy from the party he had supported for decades.
Some scientists saw her move away from the old theory as apostasy, but others praised her courage.
In some communities, leaving the faith of one’s birth has been condemned as apostasy.
My uncle thought it apostasy that I switched from the family’s favorite newspaper to online news.

form_sentences.sentence: Fans called the coach's repeated apostasies from the club's style unforgivable.

definition: A person who gives up a belief, cause or group that they once strongly supported.
extra_senses: not faithful to religion or party or cause
examples: His old teammates called him an apostate when he joined their rival club.
The environmental group treated the former member as an apostate after he took a job at a polluting factory.
In the novel, the hero is branded an apostate for leaving the secret society he once led.
The apostate from the writers' circle published a book criticizing its founders.
Fans of the old band saw her new solo style as the act of an apostate.

definition: A strong and enthusiastic supporter or promoter of a new idea, cause or belief.
extra_senses: any important early teacher of Christianity or a Christian missionary to a people
(New Testament) one of the original 12 disciples chosen by Christ to preach his gospel
examples: She became an apostle of recycling and convinced the whole street to sort its rubbish.
The doctor was an apostle of handwashing, teaching children the right way in every school.
As an apostle of free education, he built a night school for working children.
My uncle is an apostle of cycling and rides to work in all weather.
The teacher acted as an apostle of reading, giving a book to every student at the end of the year.

form_sentences.sentence: Several apostles of the new cycling movement spoke at the event.

definition: The perfect example or highest point of something; originally, the raising of a person to the status of a god.
extra_senses: the elevation of a person (as to the status of a god)
examples: For many football fans, that final goal was the apotheosis of the whole tournament.
The kacchi biryani at that old Dhaka restaurant is, for many locals, the apotheosis of the dish.
Her graduation speech was the apotheosis of four years of hard work and late-night study.
Critics called the new phone the apotheosis of minimalist design, with no buttons or visible ports.
The concert, with its perfect sound and lights, marked the apotheosis of the band's long career.

form_sentences.sentence: Critics saw the final scenes of the film as the apotheoses of its main themes.

definition: Shocking and very bad, causing horror or strong disapproval.
extra_senses: an experience that appalls
examples: The appalling smell from the broken drain made it hard to eat lunch.
Living conditions in the old hostel were appalling, with leaking roofs and no clean water.
It was appalling to see so much food thrown away after the party.
The team's appalling defense lost them the match by six goals.
Her appalling rudeness to the waiter embarrassed all her friends.

form_sentences.sentence: The landlord's behavior was the most appalling thing I have seen this year.
The hostel kitchen was appallingly dirty, and nobody cleaned it.

definition: A loyal official in a large organization or party who follows orders without question.
extra_senses: a communist who was a member of the administrative system of a communist party
examples: The new director was a loyal apparatchik who never questioned a single order from the head office.
Nobody expected the old apparatchik to propose any bold ideas for the company.
Reporters described him as a cautious apparatchik who had never given an interview without approval.
The club's committee is full of apparatchiks who care more about rules than about members.
Rafi refused to become a faceless apparatchik and left the department to start his own firm.

definition: Easy to see or understand; clear to everyone.
extra_senses: appearing as such but not necessarily so
examples: It soon became apparent that the old bus would not reach the town.
The tiredness on his face was apparent to everyone in the room.
Her disappointment was apparent when she read the results.
There is no apparent reason for the sudden delay.
It was apparent from the long queue that the shop was running a sale.

form_sentences.sentence: Her improvement in English became more apparent after a month of daily reading.
Apparently, the shop will close early today because of the strike.

definition: Used to say that something seems to be true, although you are not completely sure.
extra_senses: unmistakably (`plain' is often used informally for `plainly')
examples: Apparently, the match has been postponed because of the rain.
He apparently forgot the meeting, since he never turned up.
The shop is apparently closed today; there is no one inside.
My brother is apparently learning to cook, though he has never made rice.
Her phone is apparently broken, which is why she has not replied.

form_sentences.sentence: The apparent cause of the delay was a broken signal at the station.

definition: A ghost, or a strange image of a person or thing that suddenly appears.
extra_senses: the appearance of a ghostlike figure
something existing in perception only
examples: In the old story, an apparition in white walks along the river bank at midnight.
Through the thick fog, the lone rickshaw looked like an apparition.
She screamed when a pale apparition appeared at the window, but it was only a curtain.
The children told scary tales about an apparition in the abandoned school.
The tall figure standing in the dark corridor seemed an apparition to the sleepy guard.

form_sentences.sentence: Old villagers told stories of apparitions seen near the abandoned mill at night.

definition: A strong, urgent request for help, money or support, often made to the public.
extra_senses: attractiveness that interests or pleases or stimulates

(law) a legal proceeding in which the appellant resorts to a higher court for the purpose of obtaining a review of a lower court decision and a reversal of the lower court's judgment or the granting of a new trial
examples: The charity launched an appeal for blankets to help families during the cold winter.
The police made a public appeal for anyone who had seen the missing boy.
Her tearful appeal for help brought dozens of volunteers to the flood shelter.
The university issued an appeal for donations to build a new library.
The mayor made an appeal for calm after the storm damaged hundreds of homes.

form_sentences.sentence: The appealing design of the new app attracted many younger users.
The appellant asked the court to review the case after new evidence appeared.

definition: To seem to be a particular way, or to come into view and become visible.
extra_senses: come into sight or view
be issued or published
examples: The sky began to appear grey as storm clouds gathered over the river.
She appears calm, but I can tell she is nervous about the interview.
A new message appeared on my phone screen just as the lecture ended.
Your name does not appear on the list, so please check with the office again.
The problem appears simple, but it takes several steps to solve properly.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The old problem has appeared again after the software update.
New buildings are appearing along the highway every month.
Appearing confident in an interview can make a good impression.
Her appearance on the morning show made her school famous across the district.

definition: The way that a person or thing looks to other people when you see them.
extra_senses: the event of coming into sight
formal attendance (in court or at a hearing) of a party in an action
examples: Good manners and a neat appearance can make a strong first impression at work.
The old house had a tired appearance, but the fresh paint made it look new.
The actor made a surprise appearance on stage, and the audience cheered loudly.
Despite the rain, the appearance of a rainbow over the Padma delighted everyone on the ferry.
Doctors noticed a change in my father's appearance, so they ran some tests.

form_sentences.sentence: The actor made several appearances on television this year.
The rash began to appear after I ate the seafood, so I stopped eating it.

definition: To calm an angry or demanding person by giving them what they want.
extra_senses: overcome or allay
make peace with
examples: The airline offered free meals to appease passengers angry about the long delay.
To appease her crying baby brother, Nadia gave him her last biscuit.
Teachers know that giving in to a bully's demands may appease him briefly but never stops him.
He bought flowers to appease his wife after forgetting their anniversary.
The committee changed the loudspeaker hours at the festival to appease neighbors who had complained about the noise.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The shop owner appeased angry customers with a small discount.
Her mother has appeased the noisy neighbors with a box of sweets.
The manager is appeasing an upset client by offering a free service.
Appeasing every demand can make a team lose focus on its real goal.
My uncle appeases his hungry kids with puffed rice before dinner.

definition: A name or title by which a person or thing is known.
extra_senses: a geographical indication used to identify where the grapes for a wine are grown
examples: The professor preferred the appellation Doctor, since he had worked hard for the degree.
The town earned the appellation “City of Lakes” because of its many ponds.
Nobody used his formal appellation; everyone just called him Uncle Jamal.
The cricketer was given the appellation “the Rock” for his strong defense.
The shop's appellation, Golden Spoon, appeared above the door in large green letters.

form_sentences.sentence: Many of the old streets in Dhaka carry appellations that reflect their trades.

definition: To add something extra to the end of a piece of writing, a list or a document.
extra_senses: fix to; attach
state or say further
examples: Please append your certificates to the application form before sending it.
The author appended a short list of sources to the end of the article.
I appended a note to the email asking my teacher for a longer deadline.
You can append new rows to the table by pressing the Tab key.
The lawyer appended a signed statement to the contract.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The report has appended a list of sources, including all the survey questions.
The editor is appending a short glossary to the end of the textbook.
Appending signatures to the form took longer than the students expected.
Every email the system sends appends a short privacy notice at the bottom.
A small appendage of the old house, a tin shed, was used to store firewood.

definition: Something attached to a larger or more important thing, such as a limb or an extra part.
extra_senses: a natural prolongation or projection from a part of an organism either animal or plant
a part that is joined to something larger
examples: A tail is a useful appendage that helps a monkey keep its balance.
The small shed behind the house was an appendage built many years after the main building.
Octopuses use their eight arms as flexible appendages for catching food.
The smaller department was treated as an appendage of the head office and received little attention.
The printer was just an appendage to the old computer, plugged in only when needed.

definition: To clap your hands to show that you enjoyed something, or to praise it.
extra_senses: express approval of
examples: The audience stood up to applaud the young singer.
Parents applauded loudly when their children finished the school play.
I applaud your decision to apologise to your friend.
The community applauded the doctor who treated patients for free.
Passengers applauded the pilot after the smooth landing in heavy rain.

form_sentences.sentence: The audience has applauded the young dancers twice during the show.
Parents are applauding the teachers for their hard work during the exam season.
Applauding every small win helps children feel confident about learning.
The judge applauds clear thinking and honest answers from every witness.

definition: A round, crisp fruit with smooth skin, usually red, green or yellow, that grows on trees.
extra_senses: native Eurasian tree widely cultivated in many varieties for its firm rounded edible fruits
examples: My mother packed an apple and two biscuits in my lunch box for the school trip.
A red apple makes a healthy snack when you are studying late at night.
The Shimla apples at the market were fresh and crisp, although a little expensive.
He cut the apple into thin slices and shared them with his younger sister.
The apple tree in our backyard gave so much fruit this year that neighbours took some.

definition: A formal written request, often on a form, asking for a job, place, loan or permission.
extra_senses: a verbal or written request for assistance or employment or admission to a school
the work of applying something
examples: I submitted my application for the scholarship just before the deadline on Sunday night.
Please fill in the application form in black ink and attach two passport photographs.
Over two thousand students sent an application for the twenty places in the programme.
The company received many applications for the marketing job, so the interviews took weeks.
Her application to the university was accepted, and she will start classes in January.

form_sentences.sentence: Students must apply before the deadline if they want a place in the program.

definition: To make a formal request for a job, place, loan or permission.
extra_senses: be pertinent or relevant or applicable
ask (for something)
examples: Many students apply to Dhaka University every year, hoping for a seat in their chosen subject.
I plan to apply for a part-time job at the bookshop near my flat this summer.
You can apply online for a new passport, but you still need to visit the office once.
My brother applied for a bank loan to start a small tea stall near the bus station.
She applied to three universities abroad and is waiting to hear back from all of them.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: She has applied for a scholarship to study in Japan next year.
Hundreds of students are applying for the same twenty places this year.
Applying for a job online saves time, but a personal visit can help too.
The rule applies to all students, including those in the evening program.
Please check which discount is applicable to your order before you pay.

definition: To choose someone for a job or position, or to name a person to take on a role.
extra_senses: assign a duty, responsibility or obligation to
furnish
examples: The university appointed a new vice-chancellor who will begin work next month.
Our class teacher appointed me as the leader for the science fair project.
The school committee appointed two experienced teachers to supervise the admission test.
The company appointed a new manager to lead the sales team after the old one retired.
My aunt was appointed as a doctor at the district hospital last year.

form_sentences.sentence: The board is appointing a new head of the finance department this month.
Appointing the right person for the job takes time and careful checks.
The director appoints a new team leader every two years.
The club voted to appoint a new coach before the next season.
The appointee will start work on Monday after completing the training.

definition: An arrangement to meet someone, or to be seen by someone, at a fixed time.
extra_senses: a meeting arranged in advance
(usually in the plural) furnishings and equipment (especially for a ship or hotel)
examples: I made an appointment with the dentist for Thursday morning because my tooth hurts.
Please do not miss your appointment at the passport office on Monday morning.
My mother had a doctor's appointment, so she left work early and took a rickshaw.
The visa office gave me an appointment for the interview at nine o'clock next week.
The lawyer cancelled our appointment because she was stuck in heavy traffic.

form_sentences.sentence: Doctors' appointments are often booked weeks in advance in big cities.
The company will appoint a new manager once the interviews are over.

definition: To divide something and share it out among people according to a plan, need or fairness.
extra_senses: give out as one's portion or share
examples: The teacher apportioned the work equally among the four members of the group.
The will apportioned the family land among the three children.
Insurance companies apportion blame after an accident to decide who pays.
The city apportions its water supply fairly among all districts during dry months.
Mother apportioned the biryani onto six plates so everyone got the same amount.

form_sentences.sentence: The study budget was apportioned equally among the five research teams.
The manager is apportioning household chores according to each person's free time.
Apportioning the work fairly is harder than it sounds in a busy team.
The committee met to apportion the remaining funds among the community groups.

definition: Very suitable and relevant to the situation or subject being discussed.
examples: The teacher gave an apposite example that made the difficult rule easy to understand.
Her apposite comment on the poem helped the class see its real meaning.
A proverb about patience was apposite, since we had been waiting for hours.
The lawyer quoted an apposite case from last year to support his argument.
He chose an apposite gift: a fine pen for his friend who loves writing.

form_sentences.sentence: Her example about the storm was more apposite than the speaker's joke.

definition: To judge the value, quality or importance of something carefully, usually as an expert.
extra_senses: consider in a comprehensive way
examples: An expert came to appraise the antique clock before the family sold it.
The bank sent a surveyor to appraise the house before approving the loan.
Teachers appraise each student's progress at the end of the term.
Before buying a used motorbike, ask a mechanic to appraise its condition.
The manager appraised the new employee's work and gave honest feedback.

form_sentences.sentence: The jeweler has appraised the necklace at about two lakh taka.
The bank is appraising our flat before approving the home loan.
Appraising old furniture takes an expert eye and a good knowledge of history.
The valuer appraises each painting by its age, condition, and artist.
The appraiser checked the house's roof and walls before writing the report.

definition: Large enough to be noticed or measured; noticeable and significant.
examples: After a month of practice, there was an appreciable improvement in his handwriting.
The new pump made no appreciable difference to the water pressure.
Drinking green tea had no appreciable effect on her sleep.
An appreciable number of students arrived late because of the road works.
The bakery saw an appreciable rise in sales during the festival week.

form_sentences.sentence: The price difference is appreciable, so compare the two shops carefully.
After three weeks of practice, my pronunciation improved to a more appreciable level.
Her English has improved appreciably since she joined the speaking club.

definition: To increase in value over time.
extra_senses: be fully aware of; realize fully
hold dear
examples: Land near the new highway has appreciated sharply since the project was announced.
Antique furniture usually appreciates in value, while a new phone loses value every month.
The taka appreciated slightly against the dollar this week, making imports a little cheaper.
Gold has appreciated steadily over the past five years, so my aunt kept her jewelry.
Rafi hopes the old coins he collects will appreciate enough to help pay for his studies.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: Property prices in Dhaka's outer areas are appreciating every year.
Appreciating in value over time is why many families buy land early.
The appreciative audience gave the orchestra a standing ovation.
Every good concert needs a true appreciator of classical music in the audience.

definition: A worried feeling that something unpleasant may happen in the future.
extra_senses: the cognitive condition of someone who understands
painful expectation
examples: She felt a growing apprehension as she waited outside the interview room.
Many parents voiced apprehension about the new exam system.
He opened the medical report with some apprehension.
There was widespread apprehension in the village as the river kept rising.
Rafi boarded his first flight with a mixture of excitement and apprehension.

form_sentences.sentence: Her apprehensions about the interview faded once she started speaking.
The apprehensive parents waited outside the hall for the admission results.
Officers were quick to apprehend the suspect after the chase.

definition: Worried or fearful that something bad may happen.
extra_senses: mentally upset over possible misfortune or danger etc
in fear or dread of possible evil or harm
examples: Nadia felt apprehensive before her first day at the new school.
Passengers grew apprehensive as the plane shook in the storm.
He was apprehensive about the test results and could not eat breakfast.
Many people are apprehensive about visiting the dentist, even for a simple check.
The farmers were apprehensive when the river kept rising during the heavy rain.

form_sentences.sentence: An apprehensive student asked whether the exam would be harder this year.
She felt more apprehensive as the flight date came closer.
Police managed to apprehend the thief near the railway station.

definition: To tell someone about something, especially recent news or changes.
extra_senses: make aware of
gain in value
examples: Please apprise me of any changes to the exam schedule as soon as you hear.
The doctor apprised the family of the risks before the operation.
The team leader kept the clients apprised of progress through a weekly email.
I was not apprised of the room change, so I waited outside the wrong classroom.
The bank apprised customers of the new fees by text message last week.

form_sentences.sentence: The manager is apprising staff of the new holiday schedule.
Apprising the team of problems early helps everyone plan better.
The school's website apprises parents of exam dates through regular emails.
The officer was asked to apprise the families of the accident.

definition: A way of dealing with a problem, task or person.
extra_senses: ideas or actions intended to deal with a problem or situation
the act of drawing spatially closer to something
examples: The teacher takes a patient approach with students who are afraid of speaking English in class.
A simple approach to saving money is to set aside a fixed amount on payday.
The hospital's new approach to booking appointments has cut the queue at the front desk in half.
Our team is trying a more careful approach to testing the app before every release.
Her calm approach to family arguments usually stops them from getting out of hand.

form_sentences.sentence: Our head teacher is approachable, so students feel comfortable asking questions.

definition: To approve of something officially or formally.
extra_senses: accept (documents) as valid
examples: The board will approbate the new budget at its monthly meeting on Sunday.
The ministry must approbate the textbook before schools are allowed to use it.
Only after the committee approbated the proposal could the engineers begin building.
Parents were asked to approbate the school trip by signing the permission form.
The city council has formally approbated the plan for a new public park.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The committee has approbated the new curriculum after two months of review.
The principal is approbating the proposal for a new science lab.
Approbating a project without reading the full plan is a risky habit.
The university senate approbates each final thesis before it is printed.
The approval of the new bus route took three months.

definition: Formal approval or praise, especially from someone in authority.
extra_senses: official recognition or approval
examples: The council's plan won the approbation of residents after a public meeting.
She waited anxiously for her teacher's approbation after reading her essay aloud.
The audience's warm approbation was clear from the long applause at the end of the play.
The new safety rules received the approbation of both workers and managers.
He nodded in approbation as his son carefully packed the shop's orders.

form_sentences.sentence: The board must approve the new budget before the end of the month.

definition: To take something for your own use, often without permission, or to officially set money aside for a purpose.
extra_senses: give or assign a resource to a particular person or cause
take possession of by force, as after an invasion
examples: The city appropriated money for new streetlights at the end of the budget meeting.
A coworker appropriated my idea and presented it to the boss as his own.
The college appropriated half of this year's budget for new science labs.
My brother appropriated my phone charger again without asking, so mine was gone.
The musician was criticized for appropriating a folk song without crediting the villagers who created it.

form_sentences.sentence: The land near the river was appropriated for a new flood shelter.
The council is appropriating money for better drainage in old Dhaka lanes.
The university appropriates funds for new laboratories every year.
She refused to appropriate her classmate's essay for her own assignment.
The appropriateness of the dress code was discussed at the staff meeting.

definition: Official permission or agreement that something is acceptable and may go ahead.
extra_senses: a feeling of liking something or someone good
acceptance as satisfactory
examples: The principal gave her approval for the class trip to the Sundarbans next month.
We need approval from the building owner before we can paint the outer wall.
The project cannot start until the government gives its final approval.
Official approval for the new road came only after the engineers finished the safety tests.
Without the head teacher's approval, the sports day could not be moved to Friday.

form_sentences.sentence: The project needed approvals from three different government offices.
The committee will approve the budget at the next meeting on Thursday.

definition: To agree officially to something, or to decide that a plan or request is acceptable.
extra_senses: judge to be right or commendable; think well of
examples: The board approved the plan to build a new library next to the science block.
The bank will not approve the loan until we show proof of a steady income.
My mother does not approve of staying up late, especially during exam week.
The city council approved a new bus route to reduce the long waits in traffic.
The examiners approved his research topic after a short discussion with his supervisor.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The new bridge design has been approved by the city engineers.
The school board is approving new textbooks for the next academic year.
Approving a loan requires a careful review of the applicant's income.
The manager approves every leave request within twenty-four hours.

definition: Showing that you think someone or something is good, right or acceptable.
extra_senses: expressing or manifesting praise or approval
examples: My teacher gave me an approving smile when I answered the difficult question correctly.
The manager gave a quick, approving nod when he saw the finished report.
Her parents were approving of her choice to study medicine, so she felt relieved.
The audience gave the speaker an approving murmur when he finished his speech.
Our neighbour looked at the new gate with an approving expression and said it was lovely.

form_sentences.sentence: After the demo, the director looked more approving than she had all week.
I approve of your plan, and I will sign the form tomorrow.

definition: Close to the exact amount or figure, but not completely exact.
extra_senses: not quite exact or correct
judge tentatively or form an estimate of (quantities or time)
examples: The approximate cost of the repairs is around twenty thousand taka.
What is your approximate arrival time, so I can plan lunch?
These are only approximate figures; the final numbers will be published next week.
The tailor gave me an approximate date, but he warned that it might change.
The approximate distance from Dhaka to Cox's Bazar is four hundred kilometers by road.

form_sentences.sentence: The cost of the trip is approximate, depending on the number of people.
The journey takes approximately three hours by bus, depending on traffic.

definition: Roughly, or close to a particular number or amount, but not exactly.
examples: The journey from Dhaka to Chattogram takes approximately six hours by bus.
Approximately two hundred students applied for the scholarship this year.
The shop sells rice at approximately sixty taka per kilogram, depending on the quality.
The meeting will start at approximately nine o'clock, so please arrive a little early.
The phone battery lasts approximately ten hours with normal use, according to the box.

definition: An extra item or feature that belongs to something larger and is usually less important than it.
extra_senses: a supplementary component that improves capability
examples: The deed lists the house and all its appurtenances, including the garden shed and the well.
A silk scarf was just another appurtenance of her carefully styled look.
Gold chains and fancy cars were the appurtenances of his new wealth.
Besides the main machine, the kit includes all the necessary appurtenances, such as cables and filters.
A mobile charger is a necessary appurtenance of modern travel.

definition: Suitable for a particular situation or moment; fitting and relevant.
extra_senses: at an opportune time
introducing a different topic
examples: Her comment about saving money was apropos, since we were about to book the trip.
The song playing as we left school seemed perfectly apropos.
A warm scarf is an apropos gift for someone moving to a cold city.
He found a story apropos to the topic and shared it in class.
The manager's reminder about deadlines was apropos, given how late the team had been.

form_sentences.sentence: The teacher made an apropos remark about the importance of sleep before exams.

definition: Suitable for a particular situation, or likely to behave or happen in a certain way.
extra_senses: at risk of or subject to experiencing something usually unpleasant
mentally quick and resourceful
examples: Metal is apt to rust quickly in the humid weather near the coast.
Lazy is not an apt description of a student who studies every night.
Young children are apt to forget instructions when they are excited.
Her apt comment about the traffic jam made everyone on the bus laugh.
The title Rainy Days is an apt name for a book about the monsoon.

form_sentences.sentence: Of all the candidates, she seemed the most apt for the role of project lead.

definition: To one side, or away from use, so that something can be kept for later.

definition: To say something as a question to get information, or to request something from someone.

definition: In a way that shows doubt, suspicion or disapproval, usually in the phrase look askance at.

lacking sensation

definition: One particular part or feature of a situation, idea or problem.

the visual percept of a region

definition: The season between summer and winter, when the weather becomes cooler and leaves often change colour.
examples: In Bangladesh, autumn brings clear blue skies and white kash flowers along the riverbanks.
Our family visits the village every autumn to harvest the rice and enjoy the cool weather.
Many maple trees in Canada turn bright red and orange every autumn before the first snow.
In many countries, the autumn term begins in September, when students return to school.
The autumn winds bring cooler nights, and I need a light blanket to sleep comfortably.

form_sentences.sentence: Dhaka's autumns are short, with pleasant weather after the monsoon rains.
The park has an autumnal colour now, with orange and red leaves everywhere.

definition: Giving extra help or support; used as a second or backup when the main one is not enough.
extra_senses: functioning in a supporting capacity
furnishing added support
examples: The hospital switched to an auxiliary generator when the power cut began.
In the sentence "She is reading," the word "is" is an auxiliary verb.
Auxiliary staff such as cleaners and guards keep the school running every day.
The ship carried an auxiliary engine in case the main one failed.
The college added auxiliary classes in the evenings for students who needed extra help.

form_sentences.sentence: The backup generator is auxiliary, so it only runs when the main power fails.
The new road became more auxiliary once the main bridge was repaired.

definition: To be of use or help to someone in achieving something.
extra_senses: a means of serving
be of use to, be useful to
examples: Neither apologies nor gifts availed, and she stayed angry for a week.
Crying and begging did not avail with the strict guard.
No amount of cheering could avail the team once rain flooded the pitch.
His expensive tutor's lessons availed him little because he never practised.
Locks and alarms will not avail you if you leave the window open.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: Many students have availed themselves of the free tutoring sessions this term.
Our neighbours are availing themselves of the new bus route to reach work.
Availing oneself of free advice can save students a lot of costly mistakes.
Extra revision avails little if your study method is wrong, so change it.
The seats are available on a first-come, first-served basis at the front desk.

definition: Able to be obtained, used or reached, or free to do something.
extra_senses: not busy; not otherwise committed
convenient for use or disposal
examples: Are there any seats available on the night bus to Sylhet?
The doctor is available on weekdays between ten and two.
Fresh mangoes are available in the local market only during the summer months.
I'm not available on Friday afternoon because I have a driving lesson.
The final report will be available online as soon as the committee approves it.

form_sentences.sentence: The available seats were near the back, so we sat there.
After the new branch opened, the service became more available to rural families.
Students can avail themselves of free counselling before the exams.
The availability of clean water is limited in some parts of the district.

definition: Extreme greed for money or possessions.
extra_senses: extreme greed for material wealth
examples: The landlord's avarice led him to raise the rent every few months.
Avarice made the businessman cheat his own partners for a little extra profit.
In the old story, the king's avarice leads to his ruin.
Her avarice was clear when she refused to share even a small part of her prize money.
Charity can be a good answer to avarice, because giving teaches us to need less.

form_sentences.sentence: The avaricious landlord raised the rent again before the lease ended.

definition: To state something firmly and confidently as being true.
extra_senses: to declare or affirm solemnly and formally as true
examples: The witness averred that she had seen the driver run the red light.
He averred that he had never copied anyone's homework, and the teacher believed him.
The company averred in its statement that the product is safe for children.
My grandmother avers that a pinch of salt in the tea improves the taste.
The shopkeeper averred that the phone was brand new and had never been repaired.

form_sentences.sentence: The witness averred that she had seen the car leave before midnight.
The company has averred that no customer data was lost in the attack.
The landlord is averring that the rent was paid late, but we have the receipts.
Averring something under oath without proof can land you in serious trouble.
The witness was ready to aver that the car was blue.

definition: Typical or ordinary, neither especially good nor especially bad in quality or amount.
extra_senses: amount to or come to an average, without loss or gain
a statistic describing the location of a distribution
examples: My brother is an average student, but he works hard and improves a little every term.
The average temperature in Dhaka during the monsoon is much higher than in winter.
The restaurant food was average, neither delicious nor bad, so we did not go back there.
An average family in the village earns less in one month than a city worker earns in a week.
Her marks were above average, which gave her a good chance of winning the scholarship.

form_sentences.sentence: The second half of the match was more average than the exciting first half.

definition: Strongly unwilling or opposed to something; not liking it at all.
examples: I am not averse to a short walk after dinner.
Many young entrepreneurs are averse to taking out large loans.
She is averse to spicy food, so we ordered something mild.
The manager was averse to changing a plan that had worked for years.
Rafi is averse to speaking in public, so he asked Nadia to present.

form_sentences.sentence: The risk-averse investors chose safe government bonds over stocks.
My grandmother is more averse to online shopping than my father is.

definition: A strong feeling of dislike for something, which makes you want to avoid it.
extra_senses: the act of turning yourself (or your gaze) away
examples: Many children have an aversion to bitter vegetables like bitter gourd.
He developed an aversion to crowded buses after being stuck in one for hours.
Her aversion to public speaking made group presentations stressful.
I have a strong aversion to loud music when I am trying to study.
The company's aversion to risk keeps it from trying new ideas.

form_sentences.sentence: Many children develop strong aversions to vegetables, which worries many parents.
Careful planning can avert many problems before they start.

definition: To prevent something bad from happening, or to turn your eyes away from something.
extra_senses: turn away or aside
examples: A quick-thinking driver averted a crash by braking just in time.
Talks between the workers and the company averted a strike.
Vaccines help avert serious illness in young children.
She averted her eyes when the scary scene began in the film.
Clearing the drains early helped avert flooding in our street.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The quick response has averted a serious crisis at the power plant.
Volunteers are averting a flood by clearing blocked drains across the city.
Averting a crisis often depends on clear communication and quick decisions.
Wearing a helmet averts serious head injuries in road accidents.
Her aversion to spicy food surprised her friends at the restaurant.

definition: Very enthusiastic and eager about a hobby or activity, and doing it with great interest.
extra_senses: marked by active interest and enthusiasm
examples: My sister is an avid reader and finishes about three novels a month.
He is an avid cricket fan who never misses a live match on television.
The avid gardener spends every weekend planting flowers on her rooftop.
Avid travelers book their tickets months in advance to get cheaper fares.
As an avid photographer, she carried her camera everywhere.

form_sentences.sentence: My cousin is avid about cricket and never misses a match.
She became more avid about gardening after she moved to the countryside.
The children avidly followed the rocket launch on television.

definition: To keep away from something or someone, or to stop something from happening.
extra_senses: prevent the occurrence of; prevent from happening
refrain from doing something
examples: Please avoid the main road in the afternoon, because the traffic near the bridge is terrible.
I try to avoid sugary drinks, especially in the hot summer months when I feel thirsty.
Students should avoid last-minute cramming, because it often leads to tired and careless mistakes.
She has avoided her neighbour since their argument about the parking space last week.
Farmers planted the paddy early this year to avoid damage from the sudden floods.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The driver avoided the flooded road by taking a longer route through the village.
I am avoiding sugary drinks this month to improve my energy levels.
Avoiding late-night snacks helped me sleep better during exam week.
My father avoids heavy lunches before driving, because he feels sleepy.
Avoidance of junk food is easier when healthy snacks are kept at home.

definition: Possible to prevent or stop from happening.
examples: Most road accidents are avoidable if drivers follow the traffic rules.
The delay was avoidable, because the tickets could have been booked earlier.
Many illnesses in children are avoidable with clean water and vaccines.
Losing the project file was an avoidable mistake; I should have saved a backup.
Wasting food is an avoidable problem in most households.

form_sentences.sentence: Smoking is among the most avoidable causes of illness in the world.
Drink plenty of water to avoid headaches during long study sessions.

definition: To state something openly and firmly, or to admit something publicly.
extra_senses: admit openly and bluntly; make no bones about
examples: At the wedding, he avowed his love for her in front of all their relatives.
The player avowed that he had made a mistake and apologized to his teammates.
She avowed her determination to finish the degree, whatever the cost.
The company avowed that it would never sell customer data to other firms.
Rafi openly avowed that he was nervous, which made the other candidates relax.

form_sentences.sentence: The chef has avowed never to use frozen vegetables in his restaurant.
She is avowing her commitment to honest reporting in every article she writes.
Avowing a clear goal can make a long study plan feel less overwhelming.
Our coach avows that practice matters more than talent in every sport.
He was brave enough to avow his mistake in front of the whole class.

definition: Kind, friendly and generous toward younger people, in the way a good uncle would be.
extra_senses: being or relating to an uncle
examples: The avuncular shopkeeper always slipped an extra toffee into the children's bags.
Our new boss has an avuncular manner that quickly puts nervous interns at ease.
He gave her an avuncular pat on the shoulder and told her not to worry about the exam.
The avuncular doctor chatted with the frightened boy about cricket before he checked his throat.
With an avuncular smile, the old bus conductor helped the students find their seats.

form_sentences.sentence: Our neighbour seemed avuncular, always bringing sweets for the children on the street.
Our history teacher became more avuncular with the nervous first-year students each week.

definition: To wait for something that is going to happen or be given to you.
examples: Thousands of students nervously await their admission test results.
A warm welcome awaits visitors at every village house in the countryside.
We awaited the arrival of the train at the crowded station.
The patient is awaiting the doctor's call about the blood test.
Millions of farmers await the monsoon with hope each year.

form_sentences.sentence: The results have been awaited by thousands of students since morning.
Awaiting the results of the admission test was nerve-racking.
The students are ready to await the verdict in silence.

definition: Not sleeping, or fully conscious and alert to what is happening around you.
extra_senses: stop sleeping
mentally perceptive and responsive
examples: I stayed awake until midnight, reading my notes for the chemistry exam the next day.
The baby was awake early, so we took her for a short walk in the garden.
Drink some water if you feel sleepy, because it helps you stay awake during long lectures.
The noise from the construction next door kept me awake for most of the night.
Are you awake yet? The bus will leave the station in about fifteen minutes.

form_sentences.sentence: After a strong cup of tea, I felt more awake for the morning lecture.
The awakening of the city began at dawn with the call of the birds.

definition: A prize or certificate given to recognise someone's achievement or excellence.
extra_senses: give, especially as an honor or reward
a tangible symbol signifying approval or distinction
examples: Our class teacher received an award for her outstanding work with rural schools.
My cousin won an award for the best short story in the national writing competition.
The school held an award ceremony to honour the students who topped their classes.
The film received an award for best screenplay at the international festival last year.
The company gives a small award each month to the employee who helps customers most.

definition: Knowing that something exists or is happening; having knowledge of it.
extra_senses: bearing in mind; attentive to
examples: Are you aware that the library closes early on Fridays?
Most drivers are aware of the dangers of using a phone while driving.
I wasn't aware of the new rule until the guard stopped me at the gate.
She became aware of a strange noise coming from the engine.
Parents should be aware of what their children watch online.

form_sentences.sentence: After the workshop, the students became more aware of online scams.
Public awareness of road safety has grown since the new campaign began.

definition: Not at a particular place, or at a distance from it.
extra_senses: from one's possession
out of the way (especially away from one's thoughts)
examples: My parents are away in Sylhet this week, so I am staying at my aunt's flat.
The office is far away from the station, so I usually take a rickshaw in the morning.
The doctor is away on holiday, so the clinic will reopen next Monday.
Keep the medicine away from small children, because they might swallow the tablets by mistake.
The festival is still two months away, but the shops are already selling decorations.

definition: A feeling of great respect and wonder, sometimes mixed with fear, caused by something very impressive or powerful.
extra_senses: inspire awe in
a feeling of profound respect for someone or something
examples: The children stared in awe at the huge skeleton of a blue whale in the museum.
We watched the sun rise over the sea at Cox's Bazar in awe.
She was in awe of her professor, who had written over twenty books.
The crowd fell silent in awe as the rocket lifted into the sky.
He listened in awe as the old fisherman described a storm at sea.

definition: Very bad, unpleasant or of poor quality.
extra_senses: used as intensifiers
causing fear or dread or terror
examples: The soup tasted awful because someone had added too much salt.
We had an awful journey: the bus broke down twice.
She felt awful about forgetting her friend's birthday.
The awful smell from the drain made us close the windows.
He had an awful cold and stayed home from work.

form_sentences.sentence: This week's traffic jam was more awful than the one we had last month.
The awfulness of the food at the hostel made everyone skip dinner.
The bus was awfully crowded, so we walked the last two kilometers.

definition: Very or extremely, often used informally to strengthen the meaning of a word.
extra_senses: of a dreadful kind
in a terrible manner
examples: Thank you so much for helping me, I am awfully grateful for your kindness.
The test was awfully difficult, and most of my friends could not finish it on time.
I am awfully sorry that I missed your birthday party last Friday evening.
The tea at that stall is awfully sweet, so ask for less sugar if you do not like it.
The new road is awfully crowded at lunchtime, so take the back lane instead.

form_sentences.sentence: The weather was awful during the trip, so we stayed indoors and played cards.

definition: Causing embarrassment or unease, or difficult to deal with in social situations.
extra_senses: lacking grace or skill in manner or movement or performance
difficult to handle or manage especially because of shape
examples: There was an awkward silence after the teacher asked why the student had come late again.
The waiter made an awkward joke about our late order, and nobody knew how to respond.
It is awkward to ask a neighbour for money, but we had no other choice that month.
He felt awkward when his friends began talking about a party he had not been invited to.
She gave an awkward smile when the teacher praised her in front of the whole class.

form_sentences.sentence: The silence became more awkward after she mentioned her exam results.
The awkwardness of the first meeting faded after we shared some tea.
She sat awkwardly on the small chair, trying not to disturb anyone.

definition: In a clumsy or embarrassed way, or in a way that is not smooth or comfortable.
examples: He stood awkwardly at the back of the room, not knowing whom to talk to.
She laughed awkwardly when the presenter forgot the name of the speaker.
The old dog moved awkwardly across the wet floor, slipping on almost every step.
The cricketer fell awkwardly after the catch and hurt his shoulder during the match.
The chair was placed awkwardly near the window, so nobody could reach the light switch.

form_sentences.sentence: The awkward angle of the bookshelf made it hard to fit through the door.

definition: Not as planned; wrong, off course or out of place.
extra_senses: away from the correct or expected course
not functioning properly
examples: Our plans for the picnic went awry when it began to rain heavily.
Something is awry with the printer, because it keeps ejecting blank pages.
Rafi checked the numbers again, certain that something had gone awry in the calculation.
His tie was awry, and his hair was messy after the long bus ride.
When the power cut came during the live stream, the whole event went awry.

form_sentences.sentence: The weekend trip grew more awry with every delay, every missed train and every wrong turn.

definition: A statement that is accepted as true without proof, and used as a starting point for reasoning.
extra_senses: (logic) a proposition that is not susceptible of proof or disproof; its truth is assumed to be self-evident
examples: It is a basic axiom of geometry that two points define exactly one straight line.
My father lives by the axiom that honesty is the best policy.
That the customer is always right was an axiom in the old shop, though it was not always true.
In science, no axiom is safe forever if new evidence shows it to be wrong.
Teachers accept the axiom that students learn best when they feel safe.

form_sentences.sentence: Mathematicians build proofs from several axioms that they accept without proof.
It is axiomatic that practice improves performance, so practise daily.

definition: A very young child, especially one that is not yet walking or talking.
extra_senses: the youngest member of a group (not necessarily young)
treat with excessive indulgence
examples: The newborn baby slept peacefully in her mother's arms during the long train journey.
My cousin gave birth to a healthy baby boy at the hospital in Mymensingh last week.
Please keep the baby's bottle clean, because germs can easily cause stomach problems.
The baby laughed whenever her grandfather made funny faces at her from across the room.
Parents should check the baby's temperature if she cries a lot and seems unusually hot.

form_sentences.sentence: The hospital welcomed three healthy babies born during the night shift.
Her babyhood was spent in a small village near the Padma river.

definition: A wild, noisy party with a lot of drinking, or a person who takes part in one.
extra_senses: used of riotously drunken merrymaking
a drunken reveller; a devotee of Bacchus
examples: The old film shows a Roman bacchanal with music, dancing and wine.
The office party turned into a noisy bacchanal until the manager asked everyone to go home.
The newspaper described the festival's last night as a bacchanal of music and dancing in the streets.
The painting of a bacchanal shows laughing figures dancing around a table full of fruit and wine.
He was a bit of a bacchanal in his youth, but now he drinks only tea.

definition: To or in the place you came from, or returning to a place or state you were in before.
extra_senses: the posterior part of a human (or animal) body from the neck to the end of the spine
at or to or toward the back or rear
examples: I left my umbrella at school, so I had to go back to get it before the rain started.
My cousin comes back from Malaysia every winter to spend time with the family.
Please bring the books back to the library by Friday, or you will have to pay a fine.
After the holidays, the students came back to the classroom with new stories to share.
She walked back home quickly, because the sky looked dark and the wind was getting strong.

form_sentences.sentence: The project received strong backing from the local council and several donors.

definition: To support someone, or to show with evidence that a statement or claim is true.
extra_senses: move backwards from a certain position
establish as valid or genuine
examples: Please back up your argument with facts, because the examiner will not accept guesses.
My friend backed me up when the teacher questioned my answer during the class discussion.
The report backs up what the doctors said, that the new medicine works very well.
The shopkeeper backed up his claim by showing the receipt for the same product.
Our captain backed up the young bowlers after the commentators criticised their performance.

form_sentences.sentence: The engineers have backed up all the project files before installing the update.
Ayesha is backing up her phone photos to the cloud right now.
Backing up files every week saves you from losing important work.
Everyone should remember to back up their laptop once a month.
Keep a backup of your thesis on a separate hard drive.

definition: A person's past experience, education or family situation, which explains who they are.
extra_senses: the part of a scene (or picture) that lies behind objects in the foreground
information that is essential to understanding a situation or problem
examples: Her educational background in chemistry helped her get the research job very quickly.
Employers often ask about a candidate's background before they make the final decision.
The student's humble background made her even more determined to win the scholarship.
My uncle comes from a farming background, so he knows a great deal about growing rice.
Tell me about your work background, because the company is looking for experienced staff.

form_sentences.sentence: Students from different backgrounds often bring fresh ideas to the classroom.
The press office sent a short backgrounder explaining the new tax rules.

definition: Secretly doing or saying something harmful to a person who trusts you, especially to damage their reputation.
examples: There was so much backstabbing in the office that nobody trusted their colleagues.
Nadia was hurt by the backstabbing of a friend who shared her secret with the whole class.
The reality show was full of backstabbing, with contestants plotting against each other.
Backstabbing in the committee ended when the chairperson asked everyone to speak openly.
He climbed the company ladder through flattery and backstabbing, and few people respected him.

definition: Directed or moving towards the back, rather than towards the front.
extra_senses: directed or facing toward the back or rear
in a manner or order or direction the reverse of normal
examples: The driver took a backward glance before reversing the bus out of the narrow lane.
She took a careful backward step when the big dog came running towards her.
The exercise trains your balance by moving slowly in a backward direction without looking.
He turned his chair backward and rested his arms on the back while he talked to us.
My backward landing was too heavy on one foot, so I twisted my ankle during the dance class.

form_sentences.sentence: The rickshaw seemed backward and unsteady after the wheel slipped on the wet road.

definition: Towards the back, or in the reverse of the usual direction or order.
extra_senses: in a manner or order or direction the reverse of normal
examples: The child can count backwards from twenty to one without making a single mistake.
Please do not walk backwards near the edge of the platform, because it is very dangerous.
The car rolled backwards slowly down the hill when the driver forgot to apply the handbrake.
In the magic show, the performer walked backwards across the stage with a big smile.
My younger sister wrote her name backwards on the cover of her notebook, just for fun.

definition: Tiny single-celled living organisms, some of which cause disease while others are useful.
examples: Washing hands with soap helps kill harmful bacteria that can cause stomach infections.
Doctors said the bacteria in the dirty flood water made many children ill last year.
Yogurt contains useful bacteria that help the stomach digest food more easily.
Bacteria grow quickly in warm, moist places, so keep the kitchen dry and clean.
The scientist examined the bacteria under a microscope to find the cause of the infection.

form_sentences.sentence: Doctors said the bacterial infection would clear up after a course of antibiotics.

definition: Of poor quality, unpleasant, or harmful; not good in the way it should be.
extra_senses: very intense
feeling physical discomfort or pain (`tough' is occasionally used colloquially for `bad')
examples: I had a bad cold last week, so I stayed in bed and drank hot water with honey.
The weather was bad during the trip, with heavy rain and strong winds on the highway.
She is bad at remembering phone numbers, so she writes them down in her diary.
The milk smelt bad, so we threw it away before making the tea this morning.
The film had a bad ending, and many people in the cinema complained loudly.

form_sentences.sentence: The traffic on Mirpur Road is worse than usual this morning.
The badness of the smell from the drain forced us to open every window.
She badly needs a holiday after months of working double shifts.

definition: Easily angered, or often in a bad mood and quick to complain.
examples: My uncle is bad-tempered in the morning, so we avoid talking to him until after breakfast.
The shopkeeper was bad-tempered and shouted at the child for touching the mangoes.
The teacher was bad-tempered after the whole class failed the test and started complaining.
After a sleepless night, she became bad-tempered and snapped at her little brother.
Our bus conductor was bad-tempered at first, but he was helpful when passengers needed directions.

form_sentences.sentence: The bad-tempered cashier shouted at every customer who asked a question.
My uncle becomes bad-tempered whenever the power cuts off during dinner.
After the long bus journey through Dhaka traffic, passengers were more bad-tempered than usual.
He took the bad news badly and slammed the door of his room.

definition: In a poor or unsatisfactory way, or to a serious degree.
extra_senses: (`ill' is often used as a combining form) in a poor or improper or unsatisfactory manner; not well
evilly or wickedly
examples: The old bridge was badly damaged by the floodwater, so buses cannot cross it now.
He did badly in the mock test, but he is working harder to improve his score.
She was badly hurt in the accident, so the doctors kept her in hospital for a week.
The students badly need a new library, because the current one has very few books.
The company treated its workers badly, so many of them decided to leave the job.

definition: Unable to understand or explain something, and so confused.
extra_senses: perplexed by many conflicting situations or statements; filled with bewilderment
examples: The baffled students stared at the strange maths problem for ten minutes.
I was baffled when my phone turned off by itself in the middle of a call.
Doctors were baffled by the child's sudden fever and rash.
The tourist looked baffled by the maze of narrow lanes in Old Dhaka.
Baffled by the instructions, he asked his brother to help him assemble the shelf.

form_sentences.sentence: I felt more baffled after reading the instructions a second time.

definition: A flexible container made of cloth, paper, leather or plastic, used for carrying things.
extra_senses: the quantity of game taken in a particular period (usually by one person)
a place that the runner must touch before scoring
examples: I packed my notebooks and pens in my school bag before walking to the bus stop.
Please bring a cloth bag to the market, so we do not need plastic bags for vegetables.
The traveller left his bag on the train, and it contained his passport and his phone.
She carried a heavy bag full of rice, lentils and fresh vegetables from the bazar.
My grandmother keeps her medicines in a small bag beside the bed, so they are easy to find.

form_sentences.sentence: Please keep your bags in the rack above your seat during the flight.

definition: The suitcases and bags that a traveller takes with them on a journey.
extra_senses: a worthless or immoral woman
the portable equipment and supplies of an army
examples: Please check the weight of your baggage at the counter, because the airline allows only twenty kilograms.
We waited at the carousel for almost an hour, but our baggage did not arrive on the flight.
The driver loaded our baggage onto the roof of the bus before the journey to Cox's Bazar began.
Travellers should keep valuables in their hand baggage, not in the large suitcase.
My uncle packed far too much baggage for a short visit, so he had to pay extra fees.

definition: To cook or harden food, such as bread or cakes, or clay, by dry heat, usually in an oven.
extra_senses: prepare with dry heat in an oven
heat by a natural force
examples: My mother likes to bake a sponge cake for my brother's birthday every December.
We baked the chicken with potatoes and onions in the oven for about an hour.
The bakery near our house bakes fresh bread every morning before the shops open.
I want to bake cookies for the school fair, so please buy some butter and sugar.
The potter baked the clay pots in a kiln until they were hard enough to use.

form_sentences.sentence: My sister has baked a chocolate cake for my birthday.
The bakery is baking fresh bread at five every morning.
Baking bread at home is a relaxing weekend habit for many families.
Our local baker opened a new shop near the university last month.

definition: The ability to stay steady and upright, or the state of being evenly supported without falling.
extra_senses: bring into balance or equilibrium
equality between the totals of the credit and debit sides of an account
examples: The cyclist lost his balance on the wet road and fell onto the grass beside the path.
Please hold the handrail so you can keep your balance when the bus suddenly brakes.
The tall tower stays upright because its weight is spread evenly to keep a perfect balance.
Carrying a heavy bag on one shoulder makes it hard to keep your balance on the stairs.
The gymnast kept her balance on the narrow beam despite the loud cheering of the crowd.

form_sentences.sentence: The phone's battery balancer keeps every cell charging at the same level.

definition: Threatening harm or showing evil intentions.
extra_senses: threatening or foreshadowing evil or tragic developments
examples: The guard gave us a baleful stare when we walked past the gate.
A baleful silence filled the room after the manager read the email.
Dark clouds gathered with a baleful look over the Bay of Bengal.
The cat's baleful eyes watched the pigeons from the windowsill.
Her parents worried about the baleful influence of the gang on their son.

form_sentences.sentence: The stray dog's stare seemed baleful in the dark alley.
His glare grew more baleful when the referee made the call.

definition: To suddenly refuse to do something, or to stop and refuse to go on, because you are unwilling or afraid.
extra_senses: the area on a billiard table behind the balkline
something immaterial that interferes with or delays action or progress
examples: Many people balk at paying extra for a small bag of plain potato chips.
The pony balked at the narrow bridge and would not cross.
She balked when the dentist said she needed three more visits.
Investors balked at the high price and walked away from the deal.
He balked at the idea of waking up at five every morning to study.

form_sentences.sentence: The horse has balked at the bridge twice this morning.
The driver is balking at the steep road and refusing to start.
Balking at the first hurdle is a common mistake for new learners.
Whenever his parents mention homework, Ravi balks and goes quiet.
Many students tend to balk at difficult maths problems.

definition: A round object, often made of rubber, leather or plastic, that is thrown, kicked or hit in games.
extra_senses: a solid projectile that is shot by a musket
an object with a spherical shape
examples: The children were playing with a rubber ball in the courtyard after the rain stopped.
He kicked the ball hard, and it flew over the wall into the neighbour's garden.

form_sentences.sentence: Heavy rain has caused waterlogging on many roads in the city.
The careless driver is causing a traffic jam near the bridge.
Causing damage to public property can lead to a heavy fine.
A single loose wire often causes a fire in an old building.
Poor diet is one of the causative factors of heart disease.

definition: Able to burn or eat away at things chemically, or very bitter and sarcastic in speech.
extra_senses: harsh or corrosive in tone
of a substance, especially a strong acid; capable of destroying or eating away by chemical action
examples: Caustic soda can burn your skin, so wear gloves when you clean the drain.
The critic's caustic review called the film dull, pointless and far too long.
Her caustic reply made everyone in the meeting fall silent.
The old professor was known for caustic comments on careless assignments.
The caustic liquid had eaten away the paint on the old iron gate.

form_sentences.sentence: Her remarks became caustic whenever her brother boasted about his grades.
The chemical is more caustic than bleach and must be handled with gloves.

definition: Showing a careless or arrogant lack of concern about something serious.
extra_senses: given to haughty disregard of others
a royalist supporter of Charles I during the English Civil War
examples: His cavalier attitude to deadlines cost the team an important client.
The doctor was cavalier about the patient’s fears and rushed through the appointment.
She gave a cavalier wave and left without a word of thanks.
It is unwise to be cavalier about road safety, especially on rainy nights.
The manager’s cavalier treatment of staff complaints led several people to resign.

form_sentences.sentence: He grew more cavalier about deadlines after the first month of the job.
The manager cavalierly dismissed our concerns about the unsafe ladder.

definition: To make petty, unnecessary objections or complaints about something that is not really important.
extra_senses: raise trivial objections
examples: Critics cavilled about the colour of the logo and ignored the strength of the main idea.
It is pointless to cavil over tiny errors when the report is excellent overall.
He cavilled at every suggestion his colleagues made, until nobody wanted to work with him.
Some parents cavil about the homework, even though it takes only twenty minutes.
Don't cavil over the bill; the food was good and the service was friendly.

form_sentences.sentence: The critic caviled at the film's pacing, but he praised the acting.
Several members have caviled at every proposal without offering a better idea.
He is caviling about the small details again, instead of helping with the plan.
Caviling over small mistakes can make a team lose sight of the bigger goal.
The editor cavils at every comma, which annoys the writers on her team.

definition: To stop happening or stop doing something; to come to an end.
extra_senses: have an end, in a temporal, spatial, or quantitative sense; either spatial or metaphorical
(`cease' is a noun only in the phrase `without cease') end
examples: The rain did not cease until late in the evening, so the match was cancelled.
The factory will cease production next month because of rising costs.
Talking must cease as soon as the exam papers are handed out.
My phone suddenly ceased working after I dropped it in water.
The two neighbours never ceased arguing about the broken fence.
