The epicure who writes our weekend food column reviews roadside stalls as seriously as hotels.

form_sentences.sentence: She has epicurean tastes, preferring slow-cooked dishes and fine wine.

definition: A short, clever and often funny saying that expresses an idea in a memorable way.
examples: My uncle ended every speech with a funny epigram that guests repeated for weeks.
The poster carried a short epigram about time, saying that lost minutes never return.
She loves collecting epigrams and writes her favorite ones on sticky notes above her desk.
The columnist is famous for turning complicated issues into a single sharp epigram.
To help students remember the rule, the teacher wrote an epigram on the board: look before you leap.

definition: A short section at the end of a book, play or film that gives a final comment or tells what happened later.
extra_senses: a short passage added at the end of a literary work
examples: In the epilogue, the author tells us what happened to the characters ten years later.
The film ends with a short epilogue showing the family back at the old house.
My teacher read the epilogue of the novel aloud, and the class went silent.
The report closes with an epilogue explaining how the project changed the village.
The play's epilogue is spoken directly to the audience by one of the actors.

form_sentences.sentence: Many novels and films include epilogues that reveal what happened to the characters later.

definition: A perfect or typical example of a quality or type of thing.
extra_senses: a brief abstract (as of an article or book)
examples: With her calm voice and patient smile, our teacher is the epitome of kindness.
That glass-fronted mall, full of imported goods, is the epitome of modern city life in Dhaka.
For many students, a quiet library with fast Wi-Fi is the epitome of a good study place.
The fries and sugary soda were the epitome of an unhealthy lunch.
He looked like the epitome of success in his tailored suit, but he was deeply in debt.

form_sentences.sentence: Those two students are the epitomes of hard work and discipline.
Her quiet kindness can epitomize what a good neighbour should be.

definition: A long period of time in history that is marked by important events or changes.
extra_senses: (astronomy) an arbitrarily fixed date that is the point in time relative to which information (as coordinates of a celestial body) is recorded
a unit of geological time that is a subdivision of a period and is itself divided into ages
examples: The invention of the printing press began a new epoch in human communication.
The arrival of the internet marked a new epoch in the way people work.
Historians call that period the epoch of great discoveries.
Moving to a new country was an epoch in her life, and everything changed.
Geologists divide the Earth's history into eras, periods and epochs.

form_sentences.sentence: Mobile banking was an epochal change for millions of people who had no bank account.

definition: Having the same size, amount, value or status as another person or thing.
extra_senses: be identical or equivalent to
a person who is of equal standing with another in a group
examples: Both students scored equal marks in the physics test, so the teacher shared the prize.

Every citizen should have equal rights under the law, regardless of background.
Cut the cake into equal pieces so that nobody feels they got less.
The two candidates were equal in experience, so the interview panel had a tough choice.

form_sentences.sentence: Many people hope for a more equal society where every child can go to school.
Equality of opportunity is important for students from every district.
Do not equate a high salary with a happy life.
The two teams shared the prize money equally after the final match.

definition: In the same amount or degree, or in a way that treats people the same.
extra_senses: in equal amounts or shares; in a balanced or impartial way
examples: Please divide the rice and lentils equally between the three bowls on the table.
Our teacher treats every student equally, whether they are clever or struggling.
Health and education are equally important for building a strong future.
The cost of the trip was shared equally among the five friends.
Both parties were equally blamed for the delay in the joint project.

form_sentences.sentence: Every student deserves an equal chance to win the national quiz.

definition: A calm and balanced state of mind, especially in difficult situations.
examples: She accepted the bad exam result with equanimity and began planning her next attempt.
The pilot's equanimity during the storm helped the passengers stay calm.
He faced the long traffic jam with equanimity, listening to music instead of complaining.
Meditation helped him meet stress at work with greater equanimity.
When the power cut spoiled his stock of ice cream, the shopkeeper took the loss with equanimity.

definition: To consider or treat one thing as being the same as, or equal to, another.
extra_senses: be equivalent or parallel, in mathematics
make equal, uniform, corresponding, or matching
examples: Many people equate expensive gifts with love, but kindness matters far more.
Don't equate a low exam score with a lack of intelligence.
Some parents equate success with becoming a doctor or an engineer.
It is unfair to equate every online seller with a cheat.
Advertisers often try to make us equate a famous brand with happiness.

form_sentences.sentence: Many people equated success with a high salary during the last decade.

Critics are equating screen time with laziness, but the research is more complex.
Equating a cheap phone with a bad phone is an easy mistake to make.
The report equates rising rents with a growing shortage of affordable housing.

definition: Relating to riding horses, especially as a sport or skill.
extra_senses: of or relating to or composed of knights
of or relating to or featuring horseback riding
examples: She won a medal at the national equestrian championship last spring.
The school has an equestrian club where students learn to ride and care for horses.
Equestrian events at the Olympics include jumping and dressage.
A bronze equestrian statue stands in the middle of the park.
My cousin's equestrian training starts at dawn, before the stable gets busy.

form_sentences.sentence: Our holiday resort felt equestrian, with stables, riding trails and horses everywhere.
The new sports centre is more equestrian than its rival, with a larger indoor arena.

definition: Having all sides of the same length, as in a triangle with three equal sides.
extra_senses: having all sides or faces equal
examples: Draw an equilateral triangle and measure each side to check that they match.

In an equilateral triangle, all three angles measure sixty degrees.
We tied three bamboo sticks into an equilateral frame for the kite.

form_sentences.sentence: The triangle on the board seems equilateral, with all three sides the same length.

definition: To provide a person or place with the tools, equipment or skills needed for a task.
extra_senses: provide with abilities or understanding

definition: The tools, machines or other items needed for a particular job or activity.

definition: Fair and reasonable to everyone involved, treating each person or side justly.

definition: To destroy something completely so that none of it remains.

establish the validity of something, as by an example, explanation or experiment

definition: To judge roughly how large, how long or how much something is, without measuring it exactly.

The seller wrapped the fish in a layer of ice to keep it fresh.
Put a bag of ice on your swollen ankle to reduce the pain.
The fridge makes ice in small trays, so we keep a few in the freezer.

definition: A sweet frozen food made from cream, milk and sugar, with flavours added.
examples: The children licked their ice cream quickly before it melted in the heat.
We bought a cone of chocolate ice cream from the shop near the park.
My cousin asked for two scoops of vanilla ice cream at the birthday party.
Too much ice cream every night can make you gain weight, so eat it occasionally.
Summer evenings in Dhaka are perfect for a cold ice cream from a roadside stall.

definition: A person who attacks or rejects widely accepted beliefs, customs or institutions.
extra_senses: someone who attacks cherished ideas or traditional institutions
examples: The young chef is an iconoclast who serves dessert first and mixes foods nobody expects.
As an iconoclast in the art world, she painted portraits using only rubbish and old newspapers.
My uncle, an iconoclast in our traditional family, left his law job to become a farmer.
Every school has an iconoclast who questions rules that everyone else simply follows.
The scientist, an iconoclast, rejected the accepted theory and spent years proving it wrong.

form_sentences.sentence: Some of the best designers are iconoclasts who question every rule in the industry.

definition: Attacking or rejecting traditional beliefs, customs and respected institutions.
extra_senses: destructive of images used in religious worship; said of religions, such as Islam, in which the representation of living things is prohibited
examples: The iconoclastic young chef ignored every traditional recipe and invented dishes of his own.
Her iconoclastic essay challenged the idea that exams are the best way to measure talent.
The magazine is known for its iconoclastic views on fashion, school and family life.
An iconoclastic scientist often faces resistance before the world accepts a new theory.
Rafi's iconoclastic attitude toward office rules annoyed his manager but delighted his colleagues.

form_sentences.sentence: The young architect's design seemed iconoclastic compared with traditional buildings.
Her later films became more iconoclastic and challenged every convention.
The iconoclasm of the young painters shocked the traditional art critics.

definition: A thought, plan or suggestion that someone has in their mind.
extra_senses: your intention; what you intend to do
a personal view
examples: That is a brilliant idea, so let's ask the manager before we start the project.
My sister had a good idea: we can share a taxi to the airport.
The teacher's idea of a group project helped everyone learn to work together.
The idea of a new bridge over the river excited the villagers.
Her idea for a small home bakery became a reality after two years of savings.

form_sentences.sentence: Our team shared several new ideas during the brainstorming session.
The ideal location for the school is near the river and the main road.

definition: Perfect, or exactly the best thing for a particular purpose.
extra_senses: the idea of something that is perfect; something that one hopes to attain
model of excellence or perfection of a kind; one having no equal
examples: The small village near the lake is the ideal place for a quiet holiday.
A room with a window facing east would be ideal for studying in the morning.
The ideal time to buy vegetables is early in the morning, before the crowd arrives.
Our manager describes the ideal employee as punctual, honest and always polite.
For a family dinner, the ideal dish is hilsa curry with steamed rice.

form_sentences.sentence: This flat is more ideal for our family because it has two bedrooms.
The idea of starting a small bakery came to her during the holidays.
Many students idealize life abroad, but it has its own challenges.
Ideally, you should revise a little every day before the exam.

definition: Exactly the same as another thing or person in every detail.
extra_senses: being the exact same one; not any other:
(of twins) derived from a single egg or ovum
examples: These two keys are identical, so you can use either one to open the door.
Identical twins can look so alike that even their friends get confused.
Both answers were identical, so the teacher suspected the students had copied.
Her new phone is identical to mine, down to the same blue cover.
The two apartment blocks are identical, so visitors often walk into the wrong one.

form_sentences.sentence: Her identity was confirmed when she showed her passport at the counter.
The two siblings dress identically, which confuses their teachers every day.

definition: To recognize someone or something and be able to say who or what it is.
extra_senses: give the name or identifying characteristics of; refer to by name or some other identifying characteristic property
consider (oneself) as similar to somebody else
examples: Police asked shoppers to help identify the man seen in the security camera video.
The doctor could not identify the cause of the rash right away.
Can you identify the bird sitting on that branch by its song?
The test helps teachers identify students who need extra support in reading.
Please identify yourself at the gate by showing your student card.

form_sentences.sentence: The doctor identified the cause of the rash after one simple test.

definition: The distinct personality or character that makes a person, group or place what it is.
extra_senses: the individual characteristics by which a thing or person is recognized or known
an operator that leaves unchanged the element on which it operates
examples: Many young Bangladeshis are proud of their cultural identity and their language.

The children's rooms showed their identity with posters, books and paintings.

form_sentences.sentence: The festival celebrates the many cultural identities of the region.
Doctors can identify the infection quickly with a simple blood test.
The twins wore identical shirts to the family wedding.

definition: A system of ideas and beliefs that shapes how a person or group thinks about society, politics or the economy.
extra_senses: imaginary or visionary theorization
examples: The professor compared different political ideologies and explained how each one views the role of government.

The ideology behind the old school system valued obedience more than creativity.
Her essay explains how ideology can shape the way news is reported.

form_sentences.sentence: The debate became ideological, with each side refusing to consider the other's evidence.

definition: A strange or personal habit or way of behaving that is typical of one particular person or thing.
examples: One of my father's idiosyncrasies is that he never eats before he reads the newspaper.
Every old computer has its own idiosyncrasies, such as turning on only after two tries.
Her idiosyncrasy of writing in green ink made her notes easy to spot.
Part of the author's charm is the idiosyncrasy of her spelling and punctuation.
We got used to the teacher's idiosyncrasy of starting each class with a riddle.

form_sentences.sentence: The idiosyncratic style of the author makes her novels easy to recognize.

definition: Excessive, uncritical admiration for a person or thing, as if it deserved to be worshipped.
examples: Some teenagers' idolatry of film stars makes them copy every detail of their lives.
The idolatry of money can make people forget their family and friends.
The fans' idolatry of the team captain turned into anger when he played badly.

definition: Extremely peaceful, simple and beautiful, like a perfect picture of country life.
extra_senses: suggestive of an idyll; charmingly simple and serene
examples: We spent the weekend in an idyllic village with green fields, a quiet pond and no traffic.
The travel poster showed an idyllic beach with white sand and calm blue water.
Her childhood in a small riverside town was idyllic, full of boat rides and mango trees.

He dreams of an idyllic life away from the noise and pollution of the city.

form_sentences.sentence: Our family picnic by the lake was the most idyllic afternoon of the summer.
After the exam, she dreamed of a quiet idyll with books, tea, and no alarm clocks.

definition: Dishonorable, showing low moral standards or selfish motives.
extra_senses: not of the nobility
examples: Taking credit for a coworker's work is an ignoble thing to do.
Spreading false rumours about a classmate just to win the class election is ignoble.

Many people considered it ignoble to cheat the poor out of their last savings.
The team suffered an ignoble defeat, losing by ten goals to a school side.

form_sentences.sentence: Stealing from his own team was the most ignoble thing he could have done.
The contractor ignobly abandoned the half-built school and kept the advance payment.

definition: Public shame and loss of respect caused by something dishonorable.
examples: The team suffered the ignominy of losing by seven goals to nothing against a much smaller school.
He left the company in ignominy after the audit found that he had faked his expense reports.
The official resigned in ignominy after photos of his luxury trips appeared online.
She felt the ignominy of failing the driving test for the third time in front of her cousins.
To avoid the ignominy of being caught cheating, he confessed to the teacher before the results came out.

form_sentences.sentence: Leaked emails revealed a series of ignominies the firm had hidden for years.
The minister's ignominious exit from office shocked his supporters.

definition: A lack of knowledge, education or information about something.
examples: His ignorance of basic first aid made him panic when his friend fainted.
Many illnesses spread because of ignorance about clean drinking water.
Ignorance of the traffic rules is not an excuse when a policeman stops you.
She admitted her ignorance of computers and asked her niece to teach her.
The campaign aims to reduce ignorance about vaccines in rural areas.

form_sentences.sentence: He was ignorant of the new rules, so he parked in the wrong place.
Please do not ignore the warning signs on your car's dashboard.

definition: To deliberately pay no attention to someone or something.
extra_senses: bar from attention or consideration
fail to notice
examples: It is rude to ignore your guests, so please greet them at the door.
My little brother tried to ignore the cartoon, but he kept looking at the screen.
Students who ignore the teacher's warning about plagiarism may face serious penalties.
The shopkeeper ignored the customers waiting in line and kept chatting with a friend.
Doctors advise patients not to ignore chest pain, even when it seems mild.

form_sentences.sentence: The manager has ignored every request for a new computer this year.
The children are ignoring the rain and playing in the puddles.
Ignoring small problems often makes them grow into big ones.
My father ignores the phone while he is reading the newspaper.
Ignorance of the rules is not an excuse for breaking them.

definition: Not in good health, or suffering from an illness.
extra_senses: (`ill' is often used as a combining form) in a poor or improper or unsatisfactory manner; not well
resulting in suffering or adversity
examples: My grandmother fell ill during the winter, so we took her to the clinic.
Several students were ill after eating contaminated street food during the trip.
The manager stayed at home because he was seriously ill with a high fever.

form_sentences.sentence: The ill patient was moved to a quieter room on the third floor.

Illness during the monsoon season is common in crowded neighbourhoods.

definition: Against the law, or not allowed by official rules.
examples: Parking on the footpath is illegal, so the traffic police may fine the driver.

Students should know that cheating in the exam is illegal under university rules.

form_sentences.sentence: The police closed the illegal shop that was selling fake medicines.
Driving without a valid licence is more illegal than parking in the wrong place.

The factory had been dumping waste illegally into the river for years.

definition: In a way that is against the law or against official rules.
examples: Several shops were found selling medicines illegally without a licence.
The driver parked illegally near the bus stop, and the car was towed away.
The company was fined because it dumped waste into the river illegally.
Some people download films illegally, but this can harm the creators of the work.
Nobody should use a neighbour's Wi-Fi illegally, even when the signal is strong.

form_sentences.sentence: The illegal parking near the school gate causes traffic jams every morning.

definition: A narrow-minded unwillingness to accept different ideas, opinions or ways of life.
examples: The illiberality of the committee surprised us, since it refused to listen to any new idea.

definition: Not allowed by law or by the rules of society; illegal or forbidden.
extra_senses: contrary to or forbidden by law
examples: Customs officers seized a large shipment of illicit goods hidden inside the truck.
The police shut down an illicit factory that was making fake medicines.
Selling exam questions before the test is an illicit practice that can end a teacher's career.
Buying electricity through an illicit connection is dangerous as well as against the law.
The company was fined for the illicit dumping of waste into the river.

form_sentences.sentence: Police said the factory's operations seemed illicit, so they sealed the building.

Several shops were illicitly selling unlicensed medicines near the Dhaka bus terminal.

definition: A disease or condition that makes a person or animal feel unwell for a time.
examples: Her illness lasted three weeks, so she missed most of the school term.
Many people in the village suffer from waterborne illness during the flood season.
Keeping the kitchen clean helps prevent illness among children at home.
The insurance policy covers the cost of treatment for a serious illness.
My friend took a few days off work after a sudden illness with a high fever.

form_sentences.sentence: Doctors warn that many common illnesses spread quickly in crowded places.

definition: Not real but seeming real, and likely to deceive you.
examples: The scheme's promise of easy money proved illusive.
Thirst made the lake in the distance seem real, but it was an illusive image.

The advertisement created an illusive picture of a perfect life.

form_sentences.sentence: The true cause of the power failure proved more illusive than the engineers had expected.

definition: To explain or make something clearer by using examples, pictures or diagrams.
extra_senses: depict with an illustration
supply with illustrations
examples: The teacher drew a diagram to illustrate how rainwater becomes a river.

definition: A picture, photograph or reflection of someone or something, or a picture that you form in your mind.

form_sentences.sentence: The travel agency's website shows images of beaches, hotels and mountain resorts.

definition: Existing only in the mind or in stories, and not real.

form_sentences.sentence: The threat was more imaginary than real, as the teacher later explained.

definition: The ability to form pictures or ideas in your mind, especially of things that are not present.
extra_senses: the ability to form mental images of things or events
the ability to deal resourcefully with unusual problems

The architect's imagination gave the new library a design nobody had seen before.

Stop letting your imagination run wild, because the noise was only the wind.

form_sentences.sentence: Children have wild imaginations and can turn a box into a castle.

Can you imagine living without electricity for a whole week?

definition: To form a picture or idea in your mind of something that is not present or not real.

definition: Perfectly clean, neat and tidy, with no mistakes or marks.

definition: At once, without any delay or hesitation.

definition: Morally wrong, or not following accepted standards of right and wrong.

definition: Fair, and not favoring one side or person more than another.

definition: A situation in which no progress is possible because the sides cannot agree.

definition: Showing no emotion or reaction, especially when other people expect you to.

definition: Annoyed by delay or lack of progress, or too eager for something to happen.

definition: To formally accuse a public official of serious wrongdoing, or to challenge someone's honesty.

definition: Perfect and without any fault or mistake.

examples: The waiter's impeccable manners impressed every guest at the wedding dinner.

It was impudent of the waiter to roll his eyes at the customer.
She gave an impudent reply that made her father furious.
The impudent crow stole sandwiches from the picnic table right in front of us.
Nobody expected an impudent question from the quiet new student.

form_sentences.sentence: The intern grew more impudent every week, interrupting managers during important meetings.
The student's impudence toward the examiner got him removed from the hall.

definition: To question or attack someone's honesty, motives or the truth of what they say.
examples: I do not mean to impugn your honesty, but the numbers in your report do not match.
The lawyer tried to impugn the witness's memory by pointing out contradictions in her story.
Nobody wants to impugn the referee's decision, but the replay clearly showed a different result.
She felt hurt when her colleague impugned her motives for suggesting the change.
Critics impugned the study's findings, noting that it had only twelve participants.

form_sentences.sentence: The auditor has impugned the accuracy of the company's accounts.
The lawyer is impugning the witness's memory to weaken the case.
Impugning a colleague's motives without evidence can damage your reputation quickly.
Whenever a rival criticizes the project, the director impugns their motives in public.

definition: Acting suddenly on a feeling, without thinking carefully about what might happen.
extra_senses: without forethought
having the power of driving or impelling
examples: It was an impulsive purchase; I bought the shoes without checking the price.
Rafi is so impulsive that he booked the tickets before asking his parents.
An impulsive reply in anger can hurt a friendship.
The impulsive child jumped into the pond without waiting for anyone.
She made an impulsive decision to quit her job and start a bakery.

form_sentences.sentence: Children are often more impulsive than adults, so they need clear rules.
His impulsiveness made him buy a new laptop without checking the budget.
She impulsively bought a plane ticket to Cox's Bazar and left that evening.

definition: Freedom from punishment, harm or other bad results of your actions.
examples: Drivers who ignore red lights with impunity put every pedestrian at risk.
Online bullies often act with impunity because nobody knows who they are.
Factories dumped waste in the river with impunity until the new inspection team arrived.
The older boy believed he could break school rules with impunity because the teachers were afraid of his father.
Pickpockets work with impunity in crowded markets when the police are far away.

definition: To say that someone or something is responsible for a fault or has a quality, often unfairly.
extra_senses: attribute (responsibility or fault) to a cause or source
examples: Please don't impute bad motives to me; I forgot to call because my phone died.
The manager imputed the sales drop to poor weather, though customer complaints told another story.
People often impute laziness to teenagers who are simply tired from studying late.
The journalist imputed the fire to an electrical fault before the inspectors had finished.
It is unfair to impute the mistake to the new intern when no one trained her.

form_sentences.sentence: The mistake in the report has been imputed to a clerical error, not to fraud.
The critics are imputing the delays to poor planning, not to bad luck.
Imputing blame to others is an easy habit that rarely solves the real problem.
The coach imputes every defeat to the referee, which hides the team's weak defense.
The imputation of fault to the new staff was unfair, as the records show.

definition: A lack of the power, skill or means to do something.
extra_senses: lacking the power to perform
examples: Her inability to focus during long lectures made her take short breaks.
The company's inability to pay its workers on time caused a serious protest.
My grandfather's inability to walk long distances means he now uses a stick.
The doctor showed concern about the patient's inability to sleep for three nights.
Many villagers have an inability to access clean water during the dry season.

definition: Not enough in quantity, or not good enough in quality, for a particular purpose.
extra_senses: of insufficient quantity to meet a need
examples: The village has inadequate medical facilities, so patients must travel to the city.
My salary is inadequate to cover rent, food and transport.
The lighting in the study room is inadequate, so many students strain their eyes.
Many students failed because their preparation was inadequate.
The hotel's inadequate fire exits worried the safety inspectors.

form_sentences.sentence: The old fan became more inadequate each summer as the classroom grew hotter.
The bridge was inadequately repaired, and it closed again after the monsoon.
The inadequacy of the hospital's equipment worried the local doctors and nurses.

definition: Not done on purpose, but happening by accident because of not paying attention.
examples: His inadvertent mistake in the form delayed my visa application by two weeks.
An inadvertent click on the wrong button sent the email to the whole class.
I apologize for the inadvertent noise, because the door slipped from my hand.
Her inadvertent comment about the surprise party nearly ruined the plan.
The doctor said the rash was an inadvertent result of using the wrong soap.

form_sentences.sentence: The damage to the lab equipment was inadvertent, and nobody was blamed.
His mistake seemed more inadvertent once he explained what had happened.
I inadvertently deleted the file, so I had to ask the IT team to restore it.

definition: Without intending to, by accident or because of not paying attention.
examples: I inadvertently deleted the whole folder while trying to clear space on my phone.
She inadvertently took her brother's umbrella instead of her own.
The waiter inadvertently gave us someone else's bill, so we paid far too little.
He inadvertently shared the surprise party plan in the family group chat.
Travelers can inadvertently offend local people by ignoring simple customs, such as removing shoes at the door.

form_sentences.sentence: The inadvertent mistake in the form delayed my visa application.

definition: Impossible to take away or give up, because it belongs to someone by right.
extra_senses: not subject to forfeiture
examples: Every child has an inalienable right to education and safe shelter.
The constitution describes freedom of speech as an inalienable right.
Her ancestors’ land was inalienable under the old village law and could not be sold.
He believes clean drinking water is an inalienable human need that no company should control.
Respect is an inalienable part of any real friendship.

definition: Extremely silly or empty of meaning, showing a lack of sense or intelligence.
examples: He kept asking inane questions during the lecture, and the whole class began to sigh.
I stopped reading the comments under the video because they were so inane.
The sitcom's inane jokes made me switch off the television after ten minutes.
At the family dinner, Uncle filled the silence with inane chatter about the weather.
She gave an inane grin when the teacher asked why her homework was missing.

form_sentences.sentence: The chatbot's replies grew more inane with every question I asked.
The inanity of the advertisement made viewers switch channels within seconds.
The announcer inanely repeated the same weather update for twenty minutes.

definition: Used in the phrase inasmuch as, meaning because of the fact that, or to the extent that.
strong_synonyms: in view of the fact that
examples: The plan is good inasmuch as it saves both time and money.
I am responsible inasmuch as I signed the form without reading it.
She is lucky inasmuch as she has a family that supports her studies.
The test was fair inasmuch as every student received the same questions and the same time.
Inasmuch as the roads were closed by floods, the exam was moved to next week.

definition: To begin or open something officially with a ceremony, or to formally install someone in office.
extra_senses: open ceremoniously or dedicate formally
be a precursor of
examples: The mayor will inaugurate the new bridge with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Friday.
Our school inaugurated its science fair with a speech by the principal.
The company inaugurated its new office with tea, sweets and a short speech.
The chief guest inaugurated the book fair and then walked through the stalls.
The new club president was inaugurated at a small ceremony attended by all the members.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The university is inaugurating a new library building next Friday.
Inaugurating the bridge took less time than the planners had expected.
Each new term, the principal inaugurates a fresh student council in a short ceremony.
The inauguration of the sports complex drew crowds of students and local families.

definition: Glowing brightly because of great heat, or shining with extreme brilliance or intensity.
extra_senses: characterized by ardent emotion or intensity or brilliance
examples: The old incandescent bulb gave off a warm yellow light, but it wasted a lot of electricity.
The blacksmith pulled the incandescent iron rod out of the fire and hammered it into shape.
The incandescent afternoon sun made the tin roofs too hot to touch.
Her incandescent performance in the final left the whole audience on its feet.
He walked out of the meeting incandescent with anger after hearing the unfair decision.

form_sentences.sentence: The metal rod became incandescent in the furnace, glowing a bright orange.
The afternoon sun grew more incandescent as the clouds drifted away.
The incandescence of the lamp filament is what gives an old bulb its warm light.

definition: A set of words spoken or sung as a magic spell.
examples: In the fairy tale, the witch whispered an incantation and the door swung open.
The magician repeated a mysterious incantation before pulling a rabbit out of his hat.
The children made up a silly incantation to stop the rain on the day of the picnic.
In the video game, you must speak the right incantation to defeat the dragon.
His morning incantation, just five more minutes, never got him out of bed on time.

form_sentences.sentence: The old storyteller chanted several incantations before the village festival began.

definition: Causing such serious injury, illness or fear that a person cannot work or do normal activities.
examples: A sudden, incapacitating back pain kept him in bed for two weeks.
The virus can cause an incapacitating fever that leaves patients too weak to stand.
Some people suffer from an incapacitating fear of speaking in public.
The footballer's incapacitating knee injury ended his season.
An incapacitating migraine forced her to miss the whole day at work.

form_sentences.sentence: The pain from the injury was so severe that it felt incapacitating.
A bad flu can be more incapacitating than a simple cold, so rest is important.

definition: Bright red in colour, like blood, or sometimes a fresh pink like flesh.
examples: The sunset turned the whole river incarnadine, and the boatmen paused to watch.
She wore an incarnadine silk sari to the wedding, and everyone noticed its rich red glow.
Shame spread an incarnadine blush across his cheeks when the teacher read out his answer.
In late spring, the hillside was covered with incarnadine flowers that looked like spilled paint.
The chef finished the dish with a drizzle of incarnadine sauce made from beetroot and pomegranate.

form_sentences.sentence: The sky above the harbor looked incarnadine just before sunset.
The silk in the bridal shop was the most incarnadine I have ever seen.

definition: A person who perfectly represents a quality or idea, as if it had taken human form.
extra_senses: (Christianity) the Christian doctrine of the union of God and man in the person of Jesus Christ
time passed in a particular bodily form
examples: Our grandmother is the incarnation of patience; nothing ever seems to upset her.
The new manager is the incarnation of everything the staff wanted in a leader.
Critics called the singer the incarnation of the country's hopes after the difficult year.
In the school play, Nadia was the perfect incarnation of the stubborn but kind village teacher.
Many people saw the old doctor, who treated the poor for free, as the incarnation of generosity.

form_sentences.sentence: The village elders were living incarnations of kindness, always ready to help strangers.
Her teachers hope she will incarnate honesty and courage in every job she takes.

definition: Designed to start fires, or likely to stir up strong anger and conflict.
extra_senses: involving deliberate burning of property
a bomb that is designed to start fires; is most effective against flammable targets (such as fuel)
examples: The fire investigators found an incendiary device near the back door of the warehouse.
His incendiary comments about the neighboring village started a fight at the market.
The editor removed the incendiary headline because it could cause panic.
Posting incendiary messages online can turn a small disagreement into a big quarrel.
The coach's incendiary speech, full of angry attacks on the referee, stirred the crowd into shouting.

form_sentences.sentence: His comments in the meeting sounded incendiary, and several people walked out.
The online posts became more incendiary after every reply, until the forum was closed.

definition: To make someone extremely angry, especially by something unfair or insulting.
extra_senses: perfume especially with a censer
the pleasing scent produced when incense is burned
examples: The unfair penalty incensed the home fans, who started shouting at the referee.
She was incensed when she found that her little brother had read her diary.
The rude reply from the customer service agent incensed him even more.
Residents were incensed by the plan to cut down the old banyan tree in the park.
It incenses me when people throw plastic bottles out of bus windows.

form_sentences.sentence: The new rule is incensing parents, who say it was announced without any warning.
Incensing the public with careless comments is an easy way to lose trust.
The delayed refund was enough to incense even the most patient customers.

definition: Something that encourages a person to do something, such as a reward or a benefit.
extra_senses: an additional payment (or other remuneration) to employees as a means of increasing output
examples: The shop offers a free gift as an incentive to buy two items.
Good marks are a strong incentive for students to keep studying.
Her company gives workers a cash incentive for finishing projects early.
Lower prices for electric bikes may give people an incentive to stop using cars.
He had little incentive to wake up early since the class was optional.

form_sentences.sentence: The company offers incentives such as bonuses and extra holidays to high performers.

definition: Continuing without pause, often in an annoying or tiring way.
examples: The incessant noise from the road made it difficult to sleep.
Her incessant phone calls annoyed everyone in the library.
Incessant rain during the monsoon turned the village paths into mud.
The baby's incessant crying kept the whole family awake all night.
He is tired of the incessant questions from relatives about his marriage plans.

form_sentences.sentence: The traffic noise outside our flat is incessant, especially after midnight.
The rain grew more incessant after the river began to rise.
The phone rang incessantly during our final exam review, so I turned it off.

definition: A unit of length equal to about 2.5 centimetres, or one twelfth of a foot.
extra_senses: a unit of measurement for advertising space
advance slowly, as if by inches
examples: The fish was about twelve inches long, and it weighed nearly a kilogram.
Measure the length of the shelf carefully, because it must be within an inch of the wall.
The water level rose by three inches in an hour and flooded the road.
My father bought a new television with a screen of forty inches.
The tailor measured my waist and sleeves carefully, one inch at a time.

definition: Only just begun and not yet fully formed or clear.
examples: My plan to open a bakery was still inchoate, just a few notes in a notebook.
She felt an inchoate sadness that she could not explain to her friends.
The students' inchoate ideas needed a lot of discussion before they became a proper project.
The rules of the new game were inchoate, so every match brought fresh arguments.
The draft was inchoate, with scattered thoughts and no clear order, so the editor asked for a rewrite.

form_sentences.sentence: The early draft of the proposal was more inchoate than the final version.

definition: The rate or frequency at which something, especially a disease or crime, occurs.
extra_senses: the striking of a light beam on a surface
examples: The incidence of dengue rises sharply in Dhaka after the monsoon rains begin.
There is a high incidence of road accidents near the bus terminal.
Doctors noticed a lower incidence of colds among children who washed their hands often.
The incidence of cheating dropped after teachers began checking bags at the exam hall door.
The insurance company noted a rising incidence of phone theft in crowded markets.

form_sentences.sentence: Officials reported higher incidences of dengue fever after the heavy rains in Dhaka.
In the lab, we measured the angle of incident light on the prism.

definition: A single event, especially one that is unpleasant, unusual or dangerous.
extra_senses: falling or striking of light rays on something
a public disturbance
examples: A small incident at the bus stop left two passengers injured.
The school reported an incident involving a broken window during the sports day.
The newspaper described the incident as a minor fire in the kitchen of a restaurant.
After the strange incident at the office, the manager asked for a written report.
My cousin was shocked by the incident on the rickshaw, but she was not hurt.

form_sentences.sentence: Several minor incidents were reported during the exam, but none affected the results.
The incidence of dengue rises sharply during the rainy season.

definition: Happening as a minor or less important part of something else.
extra_senses: (frequently plural) an expense not budgeted or not specified
an item that is incidental
examples: Please keep receipts for incidental expenses such as taxi fares and snacks.
The music in the film was incidental and barely noticeable.
Reading novels improved my vocabulary as an incidental benefit.
Pay attention to the main point, not the incidental details.
Some loss of data is incidental to moving files between old computers.

form_sentences.sentence: Snacks and tea were more incidental than the bus fare, yet they still added to our costs.
Incidentally, the library is closed on Friday, so plan your visit for another day.

definition: Just beginning to appear or develop, and still in an early stage.
examples: The doctor noticed incipient signs of the disease and started treatment early.
There was an incipient crack in the wall that nobody had noticed.
An incipient friendship began between the two new students on the first day of class.
She felt an incipient headache and took a rest before it got worse.
Farmers saw incipient signs of drought and decided to save water early.

form_sentences.sentence: The disagreement between the two partners is still incipient, so it can be fixed easily.
Doctors found the most incipient signs of the disease during the routine checkup.

definition: Clear, sharp and direct in thinking or expression, showing a deep understanding.
extra_senses: suitable for cutting or piercing
examples: The professor's incisive comments helped me see the real weakness in my argument.
She asked an incisive question that exposed the gap in the plan.
The reporter wrote an incisive article on why food prices keep rising.
He is known for his incisive mind and quick solutions to hard problems.
An incisive review of the film explained exactly why the ending failed.

form_sentences.sentence: The editor's notes seemed incisive, pointing straight to the weakest argument.
The second reviewer's comments were more incisive than the first, and far more useful.
The surgeon made a small incision near the wrist, and the patient recovered quickly.
The carver will incise the names into the wooden panel before the ceremony.

definition: A natural tendency or preference to do, like or choose a particular thing.
extra_senses: (astronomy) the angle between the plane of the orbit and the plane of the ecliptic stated in degrees
(geometry) the angle formed by the x-axis and a given line (measured counterclockwise from the positive half of the x-axis)
examples: He has a natural inclination for music and plays three instruments.
I had no inclination to go out after such a long day at work.
Her inclination is to trust people, which sometimes gets her into trouble.
Students show a growing inclination to use online tools for group study.
Follow your inclination when choosing a subject; you will study harder if you enjoy it.

form_sentences.sentence: Teachers noticed the students' inclinations toward science and mathematics early on.
I incline to trust the second witness, since the evidence supports her story.

definition: To make someone more likely to think or act in a certain way, or to have a tendency to do so.
extra_senses: an elevated geological formation
an inclined surface connecting two levels
examples: I am inclined to agree with you about the new schedule.
Her kind words inclined me to forgive him.
High petrol prices incline many people to use public buses instead.
He is inclined to be late whenever he travels by bus.
Her good grades incline the teachers to trust her.

form_sentences.sentence: The new manager is inclining the team toward faster decisions and fewer meetings.
Inclining people toward healthy habits takes patience, but it can be done.
My father inclines to be cautious, so he always checks the weather before travelling.
The committee hopes to incline the public toward recycling through a new awareness campaign.
She has an inclination toward art, so she spends weekends sketching at the museum.

definition: To have something as one of its parts, or to make something part of a larger whole.
extra_senses: consider as part of something
add as part of something else; put in as part of a set, group, or category
examples: The price of the package includes breakfast, a city tour and airport transfer.
Please include your student ID number on every page of the application form.
The new menu includes several vegetarian dishes, which many customers requested.
The team's plan includes a health check for every worker at the factory.
Did you include my name on the guest list for the wedding?

form_sentences.sentence: The package included a free guide and two practice tests.
The new plan has included free delivery for all students this year.
The coach is including more listening practice in each weekly session.
Including a short summary at the end of an essay can improve its clarity.
The organisers decided to include a quiz after the lecture.

definition: Used to show that something is one of the items in a group or a list.
examples: The bill came to five hundred taka, including the service charge.
Several students, including my cousin, passed the admission test this year.
Every room has a fan, including the bathrooms, so the hotel is quite comfortable.
The team has ten members, including two engineers and a quality tester.
Almost every vegetable, including potatoes and onions, got more expensive this month.

definition: Not clear or logical, so that people cannot understand it.
extra_senses: (physics) of waves having no stable definite or stable phase relation
unable to express yourself clearly or fluently
examples: After the shock, she was so upset that her speech became incoherent.
The essay was incoherent, jumping from one topic to another without any link.
His incoherent explanation made the police officers even more confused.
The phone line was so bad that his message was incoherent.
The patient's incoherent mumbling worried the nurses.

form_sentences.sentence: His explanation became more incoherent as he tried to remember the details.
The driver spoke incoherently after the accident, so the police called an ambulance.
The incoherence of the first draft made the editor ask for a complete rewrite.

definition: The money a person or business receives regularly, especially from work or investments.
examples: Her income from tutoring is small, but it pays for her bus fare and books.
Families with a low income can apply for a scholarship for their children.
My father's income is fixed, so we plan our spending carefully.
Selling vegetables at the roadside is the family's only source of income.
Online freelancing gave him a second income while he was still studying.

form_sentences.sentence: Families with lower incomes often struggle to pay for private tuition.

definition: A lack of fit or harmony between things that seem out of place together.
examples: She wore a torn jacket, and its incongruity with her expensive watch surprised us.
Many people laugh at the incongruity of a fancy wedding dress at a muddy village fair.
The report noticed an incongruity between the company's promises and its actual working conditions.
Comedy often depends on incongruity, such as a very serious teacher wearing a clown nose.
There was a strange incongruity in seeing a man in a formal suit riding a tiny bicycle.

form_sentences.sentence: The room's modern furniture created several incongruities with the ancient wooden walls.
The bright neon sign looked incongruous beside the old stone bridge.

definition: Strange or out of place because it does not fit with its surroundings.
examples: A modern glass tower looked incongruous next to the old wooden houses.
It seemed incongruous to hear loud party music in a quiet hospital waiting room.
His bright orange tie was incongruous with the serious mood of the ceremony.
The incongruous sight of a goat in the office lobby made everyone laugh.
Her cheerful mood was incongruous with the sad news she had just heard.

form_sentences.sentence: A modern glass office looked more incongruous beside the old wooden market each year.
The incongruity of a snowman in the hot desert made the photo very funny.
A large camel stood incongruously in the middle of the busy car park.

definition: Of little or no importance, so not worth worrying about.
extra_senses: not following logically as a consequence
examples: Whether we meet at five or six is inconsequential, so choose whichever time suits you.
Small spelling errors in a text message are inconsequential, but not in a job application.
He dismissed the scratch on his car as an inconsequential problem.
To a three-year-old, losing a toy is never inconsequential, and she cried for an hour.
The difference in price between the two brands is inconsequential, so just buy the one you like.

form_sentences.sentence: The small spelling error seemed more inconsequential than the wrong total in the report.

definition: Not easily seen or noticed; not attracting attention.
examples: The small shop is so inconspicuous that many people walk past it without noticing.
She tried to look inconspicuous at the back of the hall because she was late.
An inconspicuous crack in the wall turned out to be a serious problem.
The security camera was placed in an inconspicuous corner of the ceiling.
He is an inconspicuous man who rarely speaks in meetings but notices everything.

form_sentences.sentence: Wearing a plain grey jacket made him more inconspicuous in the crowded station.

definition: The quality of changing often and being unreliable or not faithful.
extra_senses: the quality of being changeable and variable
examples: The inconstancy of the weather in April makes it hard to plan a picnic.
Her inconstancy in friendships meant she dropped old friends whenever she met new ones.
Investors worry about the inconstancy of the market, where prices swing wildly from day to day.
The coach complained about the team's inconstancy: brilliant one week, careless the next.
I could not rely on him because of his inconstancy; he changed his plans three times in a day.

form_sentences.sentence: Small inconstancies in his moods made it hard for the team to plan.
The inconstant weather in April makes it hard to plan a picnic at the park.

definition: To make something a part of a larger whole, or to include it as one part.
extra_senses: include or contain; have as a component
formed or united into a whole
examples: The teacher asked us to incorporate three new words into our essay.
Our company plans to incorporate customer feedback into the next version of the app.
Try to incorporate more vegetables into your diet, such as spinach and carrots.
The architect incorporated an old brick wall into the design of the new library.
The cook slowly incorporated the eggs into the flour so that the dough stayed smooth.

form_sentences.sentence: The new safety rules have been incorporated into every training manual.
The chef is incorporating local spices into the traditional menu.
Incorporating feedback from students improves every revision of the course.
The new app incorporates a voice search feature for busy users.
The incorporation of the two companies was completed in March.

definition: Having bad habits or faults that cannot be changed or corrected.
extra_senses: difficult or impossible to manage or control
examples: My little brother is an incorrigible prankster who hides my shoes however often he is scolded.
Rafi is an incorrigible latecomer; even with three alarms he arrives after class begins.
The incorrigible gambler borrowed money again, despite all his family's pleas.
She is an incorrigible optimist who still believes the rain will stop before the match.
The teacher sighed at the incorrigible chatterbox in the back row.

form_sentences.sentence: Even after many warnings, my cousin remains incorrigible about leaving lights on.
The old printer has become more incorrigible each week, jamming on almost every page.
The puppy was incorrigibly playful, chewing shoes and running off the moment the gate opened.

definition: To become larger, greater or higher in amount, number or degree.
extra_senses: make bigger or more
a quantity that is added
examples: Bus fares increase every year, and many students now walk to campus.
Visitors to the national park will increase during the winter holidays.
Our monthly electricity bill increased sharply after the summer heat began.
If you study consistently, your exam marks will increase over the semester.
The number of online customers began to increase after the shop launched a website.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: Bus fares have increased by ten percent since last month.
Traffic on the highway is increasing every year during the festival season.
Increasing your daily reading by ten minutes can improve your vocabulary.
The price of rice increases during the monsoon in many local markets.
The company made incremental changes to the app over several months.

definition: More and more, or to a greater and greater extent over time.
examples: Mobile banking is increasingly popular among shopkeepers in small towns.
Students are increasingly using phones to take notes during lectures.
The traffic in Dhaka is becoming increasingly heavy every year.
Older people find it increasingly difficult to climb the stairs of old buildings.
The garden became increasingly green as the rain continued through the monsoon.

form_sentences.sentence: There is an increasing demand for online English tutors across the country.

definition: Unable or unwilling to believe something because it seems too strange or surprising.
examples: She gave an incredulous laugh when he said he had won a car.
The teacher looked incredulous when the whole class said they had finished the homework.
Fans were incredulous when their team scored three goals in five minutes.
I was incredulous when the bill came to ten times what we expected.
He listened with an incredulous expression as the salesman described the miracle cream.

form_sentences.sentence: Her teacher grew more incredulous as the student explained the impossible story.
To everyone's incredulity, the shopkeeper returned the lost wallet without asking for money.

definition: A small increase, especially one of a series of regular increases in pay or amount.
extra_senses: the amount by which something increases
examples: Employees at the bank receive a small increment in their salary every January.
The temperature rose in increments of one degree every ten minutes during the experiment.
She built her savings by adding a modest increment to the account each month.
The teacher raised the difficulty in small increments so that nobody felt lost.
The university announced an increment in tuition fees of five percent for the next session.

form_sentences.sentence: The bank will increase the interest rate by a small margin next quarter.
Our team uses incremental changes to improve the app every two weeks.

definition: To teach an idea, habit or belief firmly by repeating it often.
examples: Good parents inculcate habits like honesty and kindness in their children from an early age.
The school tries to inculcate a love of reading by giving students time to read every day.
My father inculcated the value of saving by giving me a small piggy bank when I was six.
The training program inculcates safe working habits in new factory staff.
Teachers must inculcate respect for others if they want a peaceful classroom.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: Good teachers have inculcated the habit of reading in their students for decades.
Parents are inculcating honesty in their children through daily example and conversation.
Inculcating discipline in young athletes takes patience and consistent coaching.
The inculcation of civic values in school is part of the national curriculum.

definition: Currently holding a job or official position; also, necessary as a duty (incumbent on someone).
extra_senses: lying or leaning on something else
necessary (for someone) as a duty or responsibility; morally binding
examples: The incumbent mayor is asking voters for another four years in office.
It is incumbent on every driver to stop at a red light.
As the incumbent champion, she had to defend her title against younger players.
It is incumbent upon managers to treat all employees fairly.
The incumbent head of the department will retire next year.

definition: A sudden hostile entry into another country or area, especially by armed forces.
extra_senses: an attack that penetrates into enemy territory
the mistake of incurring liability or blame
