definition: A general rule that guides how people should behave or think.
extra_senses: a doctrine that is taught
examples: Honesty is the first precept my grandfather taught his children.
The school lives by the precept that every child can learn.
She lived by the old precept that you should treat others as you want to be treated.
Medical students learn the basic precepts of patient care before they ever treat anyone.
Many proverbs are short precepts passed down from one generation to the next.

definition: To cause something, usually something bad, to happen suddenly or much sooner than expected.
extra_senses: separate as a fine suspension of solid particles
a precipitated solid substance in suspension or after settling or filtering
examples: The sudden rise in fuel prices precipitated protests in several cities last week.
One careless remark precipitated a long argument between the two brothers at dinner.
Skipping meals for days can precipitate a serious health problem.
News of the bank's losses precipitated a panic among customers who rushed to withdraw their savings.
Heavy rain in the hills precipitated a landslide that blocked the main road.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: Heavy rain has precipitated landslides on the hill road near the tea gardens.
The sudden drop in temperature is precipitating heavy rain over the plains.
Precipitating a crisis by rushing the decision was a costly mistake for the firm.
A small spark often precipitates a fire when dry grass is nearby.
The precipitation in the hills was heavy, and the river rose by two metres overnight.

definition: Extremely steep, like a cliff; also used for a very sudden and sharp fall or drop.
extra_senses: extremely steep
examples: The hikers carefully descended the precipitous mountain path, holding onto the rope with both hands.
A precipitous drop in temperature overnight left the whole village shivering.
Online shoppers noticed a precipitous fall in phone prices right after the new model appeared.
The bus crept along a precipitous hill road near Bandarban, and several passengers closed their eyes.
The shop's sales took a precipitous decline after the new supermarket opened next door.

form_sentences.sentence: The path down the hillside was precipitous, so we walked slowly and held the rope.
The road became more precipitous as it climbed toward the Chittagong hills.
The team stood on the precipice of relegation after losing four matches in a row.
A sudden rise in costs could precipitate a crisis for small shops.
Share prices fell precipitously after the company reported a large loss.

definition: A short summary of the main points of a text, speech or argument.
extra_senses: make a summary (of)
examples: Our English teacher asked us to write a precis of the long passage in under a hundred words.
A good precis keeps the main ideas and leaves out the examples.
Before the meeting, Nadia sent the team a one-page precis of the forty-page report.
The lawyer prepared a precis of the contract so that her client could read it quickly.
I wrote a precis of each chapter to help me revise before the final exam.

definition: Exact and accurate in every detail.
extra_senses: (of ideas, images, representations, expressions) characterized by perfect conformity to fact or truth; strictly correct
examples: The recipe needs precise measurements, so use a scale instead of guessing.
Can you tell me the precise time the meeting starts?
She gave precise directions, so we found the house without any trouble.
A good engineer is precise and checks every number twice.
The doctor was precise about how many tablets to take each day.

form_sentences.sentence: The second measurement was more precise, because we used a digital scale.
The clock must be set precisely, or the train timetable will be wrong.

definition: Exactly, accurately, or with great care about the details.
extra_senses: in a precise manner
just as it should be
examples: The train leaves at precisely seven in the morning, so please arrive early.
The doctor measured the medicine precisely, because even a small mistake can be dangerous.
Can you tell me precisely where the bank is, because I am lost in this area?
The chef measured the spices precisely, so the curry tasted the same every time.
The accountant checked the numbers precisely before sending the final report.

form_sentences.sentence: The instructions must be precise, or the machine will not work.

definition: To make something impossible or prevent it from happening.
extra_senses: make impossible, especially beforehand
examples: A knee injury precluded him from playing in the final match.
The contract precludes the company from selling the product in other countries.
Heavy flooding precluded any chance of holding the sports day on schedule.
Her work schedule precludes her from attending evening classes.
Strict airport rules preclude passengers from carrying liquids in their hand luggage.

form_sentences.sentence: The heavy rain has precluded any cricket matches at the ground this week.
The new rule is precluding students from taking the exam twice in one year.
Precluding late applications protects the fairness of the admission test.
The organisers wanted to preclude any delays by checking every ticket at the gate.

definition: Showing skills or mature behavior at a much younger age than usual.
extra_senses: appearing or developing early
examples: A precocious six-year-old in our building can already solve difficult math puzzles.
She was a precocious writer, publishing her first story at the age of twelve.
The precocious boy asked questions that surprised even his teachers.
My cousin's precocious interest in coding began when he was only eight.
The film stars a precocious girl who runs her family's shop while her parents are away.

form_sentences.sentence: Their daughter is precocious, and she was reading full novels at age four.
The younger boy seemed more precocious than his brother at the same age.
The precocity of the young violinist amazed the audience at the concert hall.
The child spoke precociously, using long words that surprised her teachers.

definition: Something or someone that comes before another and prepares the way for it or hints that it is coming.
extra_senses: a person who goes before or announces the coming of another
something that precedes and indicates the approach of something or someone
examples: Dark clouds and a sudden drop in temperature are often the precursors of a storm.
The telegraph was an early precursor of today's instant messaging apps.
Doctors say a persistent cough can be a precursor to more serious lung problems.
Her early volunteer work at the clinic was a precursor to a long career in public health.
The small protest outside the factory proved to be the precursor of a much larger strike.

definition: An animal that hunts and kills other animals for food.
extra_senses: any animal that lives by preying on other animals
examples: The tiger is the top predator in the Sundarbans forest.
Birds build nests high in the trees to hide from predators.
Without natural predators, the deer population grew too large.
The documentary showed a crocodile, a patient predator, waiting by the river.
The owl is a silent predator that hunts mice at night.

definition: A person who held a job or position before someone else, or a thing that came before another.
extra_senses: something that precedes and indicates the approach of something or someone
examples: My manager's predecessor left detailed notes that made the first weeks easy.
The new phone is much faster than its predecessor.
The current principal praised her predecessor for building the school library.
The old tram was the predecessor of today's metro train.
Unlike his predecessor, the coach lets the players choose their own positions.

form_sentences.sentence: Many modern designers acknowledge the ideas of their predecessors in the field.

definition: A difficult or unpleasant situation that is hard to get out of.
examples: I was in a predicament when I lost my wallet in a city where I knew nobody.
The company’s predicament became worse when its biggest customer stopped ordering.
Students in a predicament over fees can ask the office for a payment plan.
She explained her predicament to the teacher: she had two exams on the same day.
The bus broke down in the middle of the road, leaving the passengers in a real predicament.

form_sentences.sentence: Many students face predicaments when their exam dates clash with weddings.

definition: To say what you think will happen in the future, based on knowledge or experience.
extra_senses: indicate, as with a sign or an omen
examples: Weather experts predict heavy rain for the coast this weekend.
No one could predict how many people would come to the fair.
The teacher predicted that the class would find the exam easy.
Economists predict that prices will rise slowly next year.
My grandmother can predict a storm from the ache in her knees.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The rain was predicted for noon, so we moved the match to the afternoon.
The weather office is predicting a heavy monsoon for the whole region.
Predicting the winner of the cricket final is harder than it looks.
The teacher predicts that the test will be easier than last year's.
Doctors use predictive tests to find out which patients may face serious problems later.

definition: The quality of being easy to know or guess in advance.
examples: Farmers value the predictability of the seasonal rains.
Some people enjoy the predictability of a daily routine.
The predictability of the film's ending made it boring.
Salaried workers enjoy greater predictability in their monthly income than street vendors.
The predictability of the train timetable makes it easy to plan the trip.

form_sentences.sentence: The ending of the film was predictable, but the acting was excellent.

definition: A natural or strong liking for something, which you tend to choose.
extra_senses: a strong liking
examples: My brother has a predilection for spicy food and always adds extra chili.
Her predilection for old novels led her to spend every weekend at the secondhand bookstalls.
The manager's predilection for early meetings made life hard for parents on the team.
Rafi's predilection for cricket over studying worried his mother before the exams.
Cats have a predilection for warm spots, which is why mine sleeps on my laptop.

form_sentences.sentence: Old films and jazz are two of my predilections, shaping how I spend weekends.

definition: To make someone more likely to have a certain condition, feeling or behaviour.
examples: A family history of diabetes can predispose you to the disease.
Poor sleep predisposes students to careless mistakes in exams.
His shy nature predisposed him to prefer quiet jobs.
Kind teachers predispose children to enjoy school.
A positive first impression predisposes the interviewer to favour you.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The strict teacher has predisposed her to a fear of public speaking.
Easy credit and impulse shopping are predisposing many families to debt.
Predisposing yourself to disease happens slowly, through years of small habits.
Her natural predisposition to worry made the long train journey feel even longer.

definition: Likely to behave in a certain way or suffer from something because of your nature or background.
examples: Some people are genetically predisposed to diabetes, so they should check their sugar regularly.
The jury must not be predisposed to believe either side before hearing the evidence.
Children raised among books are often predisposed to enjoy reading.
Having lost money once, he was predisposed to distrust every investment offer.
Tired and hungry people are predisposed to argue over small things.

form_sentences.sentence: Patients with a predisposed heart condition need regular checkups every year.
People with a family history are more predisposed to diabetes, so they should check regularly.

definition: Most noticeable or most common; having the greatest influence or power.
extra_senses: having superior power and influence
examples: Green is the predominant colour in the countryside after the monsoon rains.
Rice is the predominant crop in the fields around our village.
The predominant feeling in the class was relief when the exam finished.
Mobile payment has become the predominant way of paying for small purchases in the city.
Safety was the predominant concern among parents at the school meeting.

form_sentences.sentence: Among local shops, small family-run stores were predominant in the old market.
Mobile phone use has become more predominant among students each year.
The predominance of English in the company's emails surprised the visiting client.
In the village, farmers still predominate, though many have moved to towns.
The library is predominantly quiet in the mornings, which makes it ideal for revision.

definition: Better or more important than all others in a particular area.
examples: She is the preeminent heart surgeon in the country, and patients travel for hours to see her.
The university has long been preeminent in engineering education across the region.
Shakespeare is still regarded as the preeminent English playwright.
Her preeminent position in the debate club came from years of winning every competition.
The old bakery is preeminent in the neighborhood, famous for its fresh bakarkhani.

form_sentences.sentence: She is widely considered the most preeminent scientist in the field.
Dhaka's preeminence in trade has drawn workers from across the country for decades.

definition: To prevent something from happening, or to take an advantage for oneself, by acting before others do.
extra_senses: a high bid that is intended to prevent the opposing players from bidding
take the place of or have precedence over
examples: The manager held a short briefing to preempt any complaints about the new schedule.
Rafi apologized before anyone could complain, hoping to preempt an angry reaction.
The bank preempted the problem by sending a text alert before the card expired.
A special news bulletin preempted the evening drama on television.
She preempted her sister's request by cleaning the kitchen before she was asked.

form_sentences.sentence: The company has preempted the rival's launch by releasing its new phone first.
The principal is preempting trouble by talking to the students before the trip.
Preempting a problem is always cheaper than repairing the damage afterwards.
A good plan preempts most problems before they reach the project team.
The hospital took preemptive steps, ordering extra masks before the outbreak spread.

definition: To like one thing or person more than another, or to choose one option over others.
extra_senses: select as an alternative over another
promote over another
examples: I prefer tea to coffee, especially when it is made with fresh ginger.
Most students prefer to study in the library, where the air conditioning is always on.
My mother prefers the old bus route because it avoids the busiest roads.
Would you prefer to pay in cash or by mobile banking?
We prefer to rent a small apartment near the office rather than a large one far away.

form_sentences.sentence: Last year, most students preferred the online test to the paper one.
Many employers have preferred graduates with practical experience.
Many students are preferring online lectures to crowded classrooms now.
Preferring quiet places helps me concentrate on difficult reading.
I would prefer to take the train from Dhaka rather than a crowded bus.

definition: A feeling that you like one thing or option more than another.
extra_senses: a predisposition in favor of something
the right or chance to choose
examples: My sister has a strong preference for cotton clothes during the hot summer months.
The waiter asked about our food preferences before he took the order.
Do you have a preference for a window seat, or do you want the aisle?
Students' preferences for online classes changed after the exams ended.
Our team leader respects each person's preference when assigning tasks for the project.

form_sentences.sentence: Would you prefer tea or coffee at the meeting?
The school gave preferential seating to students with disabilities.

definition: Full of meaning or importance, with much that is felt but not said aloud.
extra_senses: rich in significance or implication
filled with or attended with
examples: There was a pregnant pause before the teacher read out the exam results.
After the manager asked who had made the error, a pregnant silence fell over the meeting.
She gave him a pregnant look that said she knew exactly what had happened.
The old poem is pregnant with meaning, and every line rewards a second reading.
Her pregnant remark about leaving early made everyone wonder what had gone wrong.

form_sentences.sentence: The pause grew more pregnant with unspoken words until the judge finally spoke.

definition: Coming before the main event or action and done to prepare for it.
extra_senses: a minor match preceding the main event
something that serves as a preceding event or introduces what follows
examples: Preliminary results show that the new medicine reduces fever within a day.
She passed the preliminary round of the quiz contest and will compete again tomorrow.
The two countries held preliminary talks before they signed the trade agreement.
Before the main interview, there is a short preliminary test on basic maths.
The architect showed us a preliminary drawing of the new library and asked for comments.

form_sentences.sentence: The results are preliminary, so please do not share them yet.
The committee preliminarily approved the plan, pending a final review next month.

definition: An event or action that comes before something larger and prepares the way for it.
extra_senses: serve as a prelude or opening to
music that precedes a fugue or introduces an act in an opera
examples: The light rain was only a prelude to the heavy storm.
A short quiz is a good prelude to the main lesson.
The first meeting was merely a prelude to months of hard work.
Soft piano music was the prelude to the evening's concert.
Careful planning is a necessary prelude to any successful trip.

form_sentences.sentence: Early warning signs were preludes to the flood that closed the highway for a week.
The doctor ran a few preliminary tests before scheduling the full scan.

definition: Thought about and planned in advance, rather than done suddenly or by accident.
examples: Prosecutors argued that the theft was premeditated, because the thief had studied the guard's schedule.
The judge said it was a premeditated crime, not a sudden act of anger.
Her sharp reply sounded premeditated, as if she had practised it in front of a mirror.
The emails showed that the layoffs were premeditated, although managers had promised there would be no cuts.
The prank on the teacher was carefully premeditated, right down to the hidden speaker in the cupboard.

definition: An idea or statement that is accepted as true and used as the basis for an argument or plan.
extra_senses: set forth beforehand, often as an explanation
furnish with a preface or introduction
examples: The whole plan rests on the premise that more people will take the new bus route.
Your argument fails because its main premise, that everyone has fast internet, is simply untrue.
The class was built on the premise that students learn best by teaching each other.
In logic class, we learned to check each premise before accepting the conclusion of an argument.
The bank approved the loan on the premise that the shop would keep earning the same profit.

form_sentences.sentence: Her two premises were both false, so the conclusion collapsed.

definition: The land and buildings belonging to a business, institution or organisation.
examples: Smoking is not allowed anywhere on the premises of the university hospital.
The guard asked all visitors to sign the register before entering the premises.
Our school has a large playground, a library, and several classrooms on its premises.
Parking is available on the premises for customers who visit the restaurant.
We were told to leave the premises calmly during the fire drill this morning.

definition: Work or action done to get ready for something that is going to happen.
extra_senses: a substance prepared according to a formula
the cognitive process of thinking about what you will do in the event of something happening
examples: Our family is making preparations for Eid, buying new clothes and cooking sweets.
Good preparation is the key to passing the IBA admission test.
The chef's preparation of the meal took almost three hours, but it was delicious.
Careful preparation before a job interview makes you feel calmer on the day.
Our teacher said that preparation for a long trip includes checking the weather.

form_sentences.sentence: Students must prepare carefully for the English section of the test.
The prepared speech was short and clear, so everyone understood it.

definition: To make something or someone ready for a particular use, event or purpose.
extra_senses: prepare for eating by applying heat
to prepare verbally, either for written or spoken delivery
examples: My mother is preparing a big lunch for the guests who are visiting this afternoon.
Students should prepare for the exam by solving past papers every week.
The manager asked the team to prepare the slides before tomorrow's client meeting.
Nurses prepare the patient for the blood test by explaining each step calmly.
We prepared a packed lunch and a flask of tea before setting out on the train.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: I have prepared a list of questions for the job interview.
Preparing for the IBA test requires a steady study plan.
My brother prepares dinner for the whole family on Fridays.
Preparatory classes help students get ready for university entrance exams.
Good preparation makes exam day far less stressful.

definition: Made ready or willing in advance, especially for a task or event.
extra_senses: having made preparations
equipped or prepared with necessary intellectual resources
examples: Please take an umbrella, because you should be prepared for the heavy rain.
Our team was well prepared for the debate, so we answered every question confidently.
My grandmother is always prepared for guests, with snacks and tea ready in the kitchen.
I am not prepared to lend my car, so please ask someone else for a ride.
The chef was fully prepared for the dinner rush and had every ingredient ready.

form_sentences.sentence: The journalist read a prepared statement to the press.
After months of study, I feel more prepared than ever.
The school's preparedness for floods was tested during the monsoon.

definition: A greater number, amount or importance; the fact of being larger or more powerful than others.
extra_senses: a superiority in numbers or amount
exceeding in heaviness; having greater weight
examples: There is a preponderance of women in the nursing profession.
A preponderance of evidence pointed to the cook as the person who left the gas on.
The preponderance of positive reviews convinced me to buy the headphones.
The garden has a preponderance of red flowers, with only a few white ones.
There was a preponderance of first-year students in the audience.

definition: To influence someone's opinion in advance, often favorably, before they have had a chance to judge for themselves.
extra_senses: cause to be preoccupied
make a positive impression (on someone) beforehand
examples: The glowing reviews prepossessed me in favor of the restaurant before I even sat down.
A friend's warning had prepossessed her against the new manager, so she barely gave him a chance.
His polite manner and neat appearance prepossessed the interview panel in his favor.
Teachers should avoid being prepossessed by a student's old test results when grading new work.
A cheerful sales pitch prepossessed the customers in favor of the product long before they saw the price.
collocations: be prepossessed by favor of something
be prepossessed in favor of something

form_sentences.sentence: Bright packaging is prepossessing shoppers before they have even read the label.
Prepossessing a jury with media coverage can make a fair trial harder.
The first impression of a teacher often prepossesses students before any lesson begins.
Reviewers tried not to prepossess readers with their opinions before the story began.

definition: So unreasonable or silly that it is hard to take seriously.
examples: It is preposterous to expect a ten-year-old to carry such a heavy bag.
He gave a preposterous excuse about a dog eating his laptop.
The idea of finishing the whole syllabus in one night is preposterous.
The shop's preposterous prices made us walk out immediately.
She laughed at the preposterous rumour that all exams would be cancelled forever.

form_sentences.sentence: The idea of walking to Cox's Bazar in one day became more preposterous each hour.
The shopkeeper priced the old umbrella preposterously high, asking nearly five thousand taka.

definition: A special right or privilege that belongs to a particular person, position or group.
examples: Choosing the final team is the coach's prerogative, and the players must accept it.
It is my prerogative to change my mind if I find a better offer.
As the owner, she has the prerogative to close the shop whenever she likes.
In many families, deciding the wedding date is the prerogative of the elders.
Choosing which movie to watch is the prerogative of whoever pays for the tickets.

form_sentences.sentence: Senior members of the club enjoy several prerogatives, such as booking the best room.

definition: To be a sign that something, usually bad, is going to happen.
extra_senses: a foreboding about what is about to happen
a sign of something about to happen
examples: Dark clouds in the west presaged a heavy storm before evening.
The sudden drop in sales presaged bigger problems for the company.
His long silence at dinner presaged bad news.
The strange quiet of the sea presaged the cyclone, the fishermen said.
Many people believe a ring around the moon presages rain.

form_sentences.sentence: The dark clouds had presaged the monsoon rain, so we brought our umbrellas.
The falling rupee is presaging a rise in import costs for local businesses.
Presaging a crisis is never easy for economists.
Scientists use satellite data to presage floods before they reach the villages.

definition: Knowing or seeming to know in advance what will happen in the future.
examples: Her prescient decision to save money last year helped her family when the factory closed.
The teacher's prescient warning about the exam topic proved right when the question appeared.
It was prescient of Dad to buy a generator before the long power cuts began.
The engineer's prescient report about the cracks led to repairs before the monsoon arrived.
Investors praised her prescient move into online sales years before it became popular.

form_sentences.sentence: Her warning about the market crash was the most prescient comment in the whole meeting.
The prescience of the old farmers, who stored grain before the drought, kept villages fed.

definition: The state of being in a particular place, or the fact that something exists.
extra_senses: the immediate proximity of someone or something
an invisible spiritual being felt to be nearby
examples: Her calm presence at the hospital helped her worried parents feel much better.
The teacher noticed the presence of a new student at the back of the class.
The presence of a strong network signal makes video calls much clearer.
Rafi's quiet presence in the team made everyone feel supported during a difficult week.
The presence of fog on the river made the ferry journey slow and cautious.

form_sentences.sentence: The present rules on parking are unclear to most residents.

definition: Being in a particular place, such as at a meeting or event, rather than absent.
extra_senses: give an exhibition of to an interested audience
being or existing in a specified place
examples: All the students were present for the morning exam, so the teacher started on time.
My uncle was present at my graduation ceremony, and he took many photos.
Please make sure the manager is present at the meeting before we start the presentation.
Only a few members were present when the committee voted on the new rules.
Is the doctor present in the clinic this afternoon, or should we come tomorrow?

form_sentences.sentence: Only present members can vote in the committee meeting.
The manager is presently reviewing the new budget proposal.

definition: A formal talk or display used to show information or ideas to a group.
extra_senses: a show or display; the act of presenting something to sight or view
the act of making something publicly available; presenting news or other information by broadcasting or printing it
examples: Nadia gave an excellent presentation on climate change to the whole class.
Our group's presentation on the sales report impressed the company's directors.
The presentation of the awards will take place in the auditorium at noon.
The waiter's presentation of the dish was so beautiful that we took photos before eating.
The bank's presentation about savings accounts was clear, so I decided to open one.

form_sentences.sentence: The students gave several presentations about climate change this week.
I will present my research findings at the conference next month.

definition: A strong feeling that something bad is going to happen.
examples: She had a presentiment that something was wrong when her brother did not answer his phone.
A sudden presentiment of danger made him stop and look both ways before crossing the road.
I felt a presentiment of failure the moment I opened the exam paper.
My grandmother often claimed she had a presentiment before any bad news arrived.
Dark clouds and a sudden silence filled the fishermen with a presentiment of a storm.

form_sentences.sentence: Some of the passengers had strange presentiments before the ferry left the port.

definition: To keep something in its original state, or protect it from harm or decay.
extra_senses: keep in safety and protect from harm, decay, loss, or destruction
to keep up and reserve for personal or special use
examples: We should preserve our historical buildings so that children can learn about the past.
My grandmother preserves mango pickle in glass jars so that it lasts all winter.
Please preserve your notes carefully, because they will help you revise for the final exam.
Forests in the hills must be preserved to protect animals and prevent landslides.
The museum uses special cabinets to preserve old manuscripts from light and humidity.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The museum preserved the old manuscripts in a climate-controlled room.
The government is preserving the forest to protect local wildlife.
Preserving old buildings keeps the city's history alive for visitors.
The preservation of historic buildings requires careful funding.
Salt has a strong preservative effect on fish.

definition: The leader of a country, club, company or other organisation, often elected.
extra_senses: the person who holds the office of head of state of the United States government
the chief executive of a republic
examples: Rafi was elected president of the university debating club earlier this year.
The president of our housing society called a meeting to discuss the water supply.
The company president announced a new plan for the next three years.
My cousin's school president asked students to help clean the playground on Friday.
A president must listen to the members before making important decisions.

form_sentences.sentence: Two university presidents attended the conference on higher education.
The presidential suite at the hotel has a view of the lake.
Her presidency of the student club lasted two years.
The judge will preside over the hearing on Monday morning.

definition: To push or squeeze something firmly, often against a surface.
extra_senses: force or impel in an indicated direction
to be oppressive or burdensome
examples: Press the power button for three seconds to restart the old laptop.
My mother pressed the wrinkled shirt with a hot iron before the wedding.
Press the lemon gently on the chopping board to get more juice from it.
The student pressed the photocopier's start button, but the machine would not work.
The passengers pressed against the door as the crowded bus turned the corner.

form_sentences.sentence: Journalists have pressed the minister for a clear answer on the budget.
The nurse at the Dhaka clinic is pressing a clean cloth on the cut.
Pressing the wrong button on the lift caused a short delay this morning.
The chef presses the dough flat before cutting it into small squares.
Remember to press the save button before you close the file.

definition: The force that is applied to something, or the stress caused by demands on a person.
extra_senses: a force that compels
the act of pressing; the exertion of pressure
examples: Students often feel pressure before final exams, so they should take regular breaks.
The tyres on the rickshaw need more air, because the pressure is too low.
Peer pressure can make teenagers try things they would normally refuse.
Under pressure at work, my sister learned to plan her day more carefully.
The doctor checked my blood pressure and said that it was slightly high today.

form_sentences.sentence: Parents may press their children to study harder before the final exams.

ipa: /prəˈzu mə bli, prɪˈzu mə bli, priˈzu mə bli/
definition: Used to say that you think something is probably true, although you are not completely sure.
examples: The lights are off, so presumably everyone has gone home.
You presumably know the way, since you have driven here before.
Presumably, the train is late because of the heavy fog.
He has not replied to my message, presumably because his phone is switched off.
Nadia is not at her desk, presumably because she is in a meeting.

definition: To suppose that something is true because it seems likely, even though you have no proof.
extra_senses: take upon oneself; act presumptuously, without permission
constitute reasonable evidence for
examples: I presume you have already read the notice about tomorrow's holiday.
Since the lights were off, I presumed everyone had gone home.
A person is presumed innocent until a court proves otherwise.
The ship was presumed lost after it failed to reach the port.
From the long queue outside, I presume the shop is having a big sale.

form_sentences.sentence: My teacher is presuming we all read the chapter, so she will skip the summary.
Presuming that every customer knows the rules can lead to confusion at the counter.
The law presumes that a signed contract is valid unless proven otherwise.
It would be wrong to presume that the answer is always the first option.
The doctor gave a presumptive diagnosis of dengue until the blood test was ready.

definition: Accepted as true or likely because of strong evidence, even though it is not yet proved.
extra_senses: affording reasonable grounds for belief or acceptance
examples: The doctor gave a presumptive diagnosis of flu and ordered more tests to be sure.
The captain was the presumptive winner of the club election, since nobody else had applied.
Presumptive evidence, such as muddy shoes, suggested he had walked through the field.

definition: To return something to its usual place, or to store it safely out of sight.
extra_senses: throw or cast away
lock up or confine, in or as in a jail
examples: Please put away your toys before dinner, because the floor is dangerous to walk on.
After the wedding guests left, the family put away the decorations in the storeroom.
She put the winter blankets away in a metal trunk to keep them dry during the monsoon.
My brother never puts away his school uniform, so it always smells damp on Monday.
He put away the documents in a safe drawer before going out for the afternoon meeting.

form_sentences.sentence: The children have put away their toys before dinner time.
Mum is putting away the clean dishes in the kitchen cupboard.
Putting away your clothes each evening keeps the room tidy.
Please remember to put away your books after the lesson.

definition: To return something to the place where it was before, or to delay something to a later time.
extra_senses: cost a certain amount
examples: Please put the library book back on the right shelf, so the next reader can find it.
The manager put the meeting back by two hours because the power had gone off.
After reading the magazine, I put it back in the rack by the window.
The shop put back the price increase until after the festival season had finished.
She put her phone back in her pocket when the teacher walked into the classroom.

form_sentences.sentence: The shop has put back its opening date until next month.
The team is putting back the launch date by two weeks.
Putting back the meeting will give everyone more time to prepare.
Heavy rain often puts back the start of the morning bus service.
They decided to put back the exam until the roads are repaired.

definition: To place something you are carrying on a surface, or to lower something to a flat position.
extra_senses: put in a horizontal position
cause to come to the ground
examples: Please put down your heavy bag on the floor and come and sit next to me.
The waiter put down the tea tray gently so that none of the cups would break.
She put the cat down on the carpet, and it immediately ran under the sofa.
After the long walk, he put down his umbrella by the door and sat on the step.
The porter put the luggage down beside the bench and asked us to wait for the bus.

form_sentences.sentence: The waiter has put down the tray gently on the table.
She is putting down her bag to tie her shoelaces.
Putting down a deposit now will secure your place on the course.
The nurse puts down the patient's file after checking the results.
Please try to put down the shopping bags before you open the door.

definition: To suggest an idea, plan or name for others to consider.
extra_senses: insist on having one's opinions and rights recognized
summon into action or bring into existence, often as if by magic
examples: Our class representative put forward a plan to raise money for the school library.
The engineer put forward three options for repairing the bridge before the monsoon.
Several members put forward their names as candidates for the club secretary position.
My uncle put forward an idea for a small business selling handmade bags online.
The committee will consider the proposal that was put forward by the teachers last week.

form_sentences.sentence: The students are putting forward new ideas for the school garden.
Putting forward a clear proposal early helps the committee decide.
The manager puts forward a new plan at every monthly meeting.
Each member is allowed to put forward one name for the annual award.

definition: To place or fit something into a space, or to install a device in a building.
extra_senses: keep or lay aside for future use
break into a conversation
examples: The landlord put in a new water tank on the roof after the old one began to leak.
We had a small window put in above the kitchen sink to let in more light.
Our office put in a new air conditioner, so the room is much cooler now.
The electrician put in extra sockets near the study table for the students' laptops.
My father put in a steel gate to protect the front garden from stray animals.

form_sentences.sentence: The council has put in new street lights along the main road.
The workers are putting in extra hours to finish the bridge.
Putting in extra hours before exams can help you feel prepared.
My uncle puts in long hours at his shop during the festival.
You need to put in regular effort to learn a new language.

definition: To decide to do something at a later time instead of now.
extra_senses: cause to feel intense dislike or distaste
take away the enthusiasm of
examples: The principal put off the sports day because heavy rain was forecast for the whole week.
Do not put off studying for the exam until the last night, because you will be too tired.
The shop put off the sale until next month, when the new stock arrives from Chittagong.
He keeps putting off his dental check-up, even though his tooth has been hurting for weeks.
They put off the wedding reception by two weeks so that more relatives could come.

form_sentences.sentence: The concert has been put off until the weather improves.
Putting off the dentist appointment will only make the pain worse.
The noise from the building site puts off many potential buyers.
Do not try to put off studying until the night before the test.

definition: To place a piece of clothing or an item on your body, or to start a light or machine.
extra_senses: adopted in order to deceive
add to something existing
examples: It is getting cold in the evening, so please put on a warm jacket before you go out.
My little sister put on her red shoes and ran to the door to greet the guests.
Can you put on the fan? The room has become very hot this afternoon.
Before the exam, I always put on my favourite blue shirt for good luck.
She put on her spectacles to read the small print on the medicine bottle.

form_sentences.sentence: She has put on a warm jacket before going out into the cold morning.
He is putting on his shoes to leave for the airport.
Putting on a show for the school needs many volunteers.
The local theatre puts on a play every Saturday evening.
I need to put on some sunscreen before the beach trip.

definition: To stop a fire or light from burning, or to cause someone trouble or inconvenience.
extra_senses: put out considerable effort
deprive of the oxygen necessary for combustion
examples: The firefighters quickly put out the fire that started in the kitchen of the old market.
Please put out the candle before you go to sleep, so that nothing catches fire.
We did not want to put out our neighbours, so we kept the music very quiet.
My aunt was put out when the wedding caterer arrived two hours late to the house.
He put out the light on the veranda and walked slowly back into the house.

form_sentences.sentence: The firefighters are putting out the flames on the third floor.
Putting out a small kitchen fire needs a lid or a damp cloth.
The shopkeeper puts out fresh bread every morning at six.
The fire crew worked hard to put out the blaze quickly.

definition: To connect a telephone call to a particular person, or to make someone go through an unpleasant experience.
extra_senses: connect by telephone
examples: Could you put me through to the accounts department, please? I have a question about my bill.
The receptionist put the caller through to the manager, who was waiting for the news.
The exam board put the students through a difficult oral test before the final results.
Our mobile operator put my call through in less than a minute, which was very helpful.
The hospital put the old patient through several tests before the doctor decided on the treatment.

form_sentences.sentence: The operator has put my call through to the accounts department.
The staff are putting the orders through the new system today.
Putting the applicants through a written test helps the company choose.
The receptionist puts through every call to the manager's office.
The manager wants to put through the new schedule next week.

definition: To assemble something from separate parts, or to organise a plan or group of people.
examples: My brother spent the whole Friday putting together a wooden bookshelf for his study.
The teacher asked us to put together a short presentation on the water cycle for Monday.
The students put together a team of volunteers to clean the park on Sunday morning.
It took two hours to put together the new cooker, because the instructions were confusing.
The editor put together a special magazine section about the history of Dhaka University.

form_sentences.sentence: The team has put together a useful guide for first-year students.
Putting together a good CV takes time and careful editing.
The librarian puts together reading lists for each course.
We need to put together a budget before the next meeting.

definition: To raise something upright, or to attach something so people can see it.
extra_senses: mount or put up
construct, build, or erect
examples: The club put up a notice on the board announcing the date of the new football trials.
We put up a large tent in the field for the wedding guests during the cold season.
The shopkeeper put up a sign saying that the shop would close early on Friday.
The villagers put up bamboo poles to make a shelter for the travellers during the storm.
My cousin put up posters for the school debate competition on every wall near the gate.

form_sentences.sentence: The neighbours have put up a fence along the shared garden.
The workers are putting up the tent for the wedding party.
Putting up posters on the notice board is part of the job.
The family puts up guests during the festival season every year.
Could you help me to put up the shelves this weekend?

definition: Generally believed or supposed to be a certain thing, though this has not been proved.
examples: The putative cause of the fire was an old wire, but investigators are still checking.
Scientists are testing the putative health benefits of the herb in a large study.
The putative author of the poem lived five hundred years ago, though historians doubt it.
The club's putative leader never attends meetings, so others make the decisions.
The putative winner of the contest has been announced, but the judges may still change the result.

form_sentences.sentence: The old letter's writer remains putative, since no signature survives.

definition: Attractive or interesting because it is old-fashioned or unusual.
extra_senses: very strange or unusual; odd or even incongruous in character or appearance
attractively old-fashioned (but not necessarily authentic)
examples: We stayed in a quaint cottage with a thatched roof and a small garden.
The narrow lanes of Old Dhaka have a quaint charm that visitors love.
The shop sells quaint wooden toys that look like those from a hundred years ago.
He has a quaint way of speaking, using words nobody uses any more.
The village has a quaint market where traders still weigh goods on brass scales.

form_sentences.sentence: The village square looks quaint, with its wooden shops and old clock tower.
Compared with the city, the riverside village felt more quaint than I had expected.
Tourists often love the quaintness of old bazaars, with their narrow lanes and handmade goods.
The guesthouse was decorated quaintly, with lace curtains and tiny painted tiles.

definition: An official certificate or diploma that shows someone has completed a course or has the skills for a job.
extra_senses: the act of modifying or changing the strength of some idea
a statement that limits or restricts some claim
examples: Most of the jobs at this company require a university degree or another professional qualification.
My cousin has a teaching qualification and works at a private school in Sylhet.
The bank asked for the applicant's qualifications, including the certificates from her last two years of study.
Good qualifications can help you find work abroad, but you also need strong English skills.
Students who want admission to the medical college must show the right qualifications in their exam results.

form_sentences.sentence: Only graduates who meet the criteria qualify for the scholarship.

definition: Limited by conditions or reservations, rather than fully approving, complete or absolute.
extra_senses: limited or restricted; not absolute
holding appropriate documentation and officially on record as qualified to perform a specified function or practice a specified skill
examples: The committee gave only qualified approval to the plan, with several conditions attached.
The new bus route was a qualified success: busy in the morning but nearly empty at night.
She offered qualified support for the idea, provided the cost stayed under budget.
The doctor gave a qualified yes: I could travel, but only if I avoided carrying heavy bags.
His qualified apology, full of ifs and buts, made his sister even angrier.

form_sentences.sentence: Her approval of the plan was qualified and depended on the budget.
The doctor's second answer was more qualified than the first, with several warnings.

definition: To limit or adjust a statement so that it is less general or less strong.
extra_senses: pronounce fit or able
make more specific
examples: I should qualify my praise: the food was good, but the service was very slow.
The scientist qualified her claim by adding that more tests were needed.
He qualified his promise with a warning that bad weather could delay the trip.
Please qualify your answer, because not every student in the class agrees.
Writers often qualify a strong statement with words such as “usually” or “in most cases.”
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The statement has been qualified by a note saying the figures are estimates.
The report is qualifying its claims, admitting that the sample was small.
Qualifying a strong statement with careful evidence makes it more convincing.
The teacher always qualifies praise with a small criticism, so students stay humble.
The reviewer praised the book without qualification, and the publisher was delighted.

definition: Relating to the quality or nature of something rather than its amount or number.
extra_senses: relating to or involving comparisons based on qualities
examples: The survey combined numbers with qualitative feedback, such as comments from customers about how they felt.
There is a qualitative difference between a good meal and just a full stomach.
Qualitative research uses interviews to understand why people choose one brand over another.
The teacher gave qualitative comments on my essay instead of just a mark.
A qualitative analysis of the poem looks at its imagery and tone, not at word counts.

form_sentences.sentence: The survey results were qualitative, so the team explained them through interviews.
The second phase of the study was more qualitative, relying on detailed interviews.
The report compared the schools qualitatively, looking at teaching quality rather than scores.

definition: How good or bad something is, or a feature that makes a person or thing special.
extra_senses: a degree or grade of excellence or worth
a characteristic property that defines the apparent individual nature of something
examples: The quality of the rice from this market is much better than the cheap rice sold in bulk.
Nobody wants to buy a shirt with poor quality stitching that falls apart after one wash.
My grandfather always says that honesty is the most important quality in a good friend.
The quality of teaching in the new college has improved a lot since last year.
The restaurant is famous for its quality food, friendly service and reasonable prices.

form_sentences.sentence: Honesty and patience are the qualities a good teacher needs.
Anyone who passes the test will qualify for a place at the college.

definition: A state of not knowing what to do in a difficult situation where every choice has problems.
extra_senses: state of uncertainty or perplexity especially as requiring a choice between equally unfavorable options
examples: Nadia was in a quandary: she had two job offers and only one day to decide.
The shop owner faced a quandary when the supplier doubled prices just before Eid.
I am in a quandary about whether to study abroad or stay close to my parents.
The driver faced a quandary when both roads to the airport were blocked by floodwater.
Choosing between a job she loved and a better-paid one she disliked put Mina in a real quandary.

form_sentences.sentence: Many students face quandaries about choosing science or arts after the SSC results.

definition: An amount or number of something, especially a measurable or countable one.
extra_senses: an adequate or large amount
the concept that something has a magnitude and can be represented in mathematical expressions by a constant or a variable
examples: The shopkeeper sells rice by the kilogram, but he gives a discount for a large quantity.
Please add a small quantity of salt to the soup, and taste it before you serve it.
The factory produces a huge quantity of plastic bags every single day for the market.
Doctors say that the right quantity of medicine must be taken at the right time each day.
The school bought a large quantity of exercise books for the new session.

form_sentences.sentence: Smaller quantities of sugar make the tea less sweet and more healthy.
It is hard to quantify the benefits of a good teacher.

definition: To argue angrily with someone about something.
extra_senses: an angry dispute
an arrow that is shot from a crossbow; has a head with four edges
examples: My brother and I quarrel over the TV remote almost every evening.
The neighbours quarrelled about a tree whose branches hung over the wall.
Good friends may quarrel, but they usually make up within a day.
The two shopkeepers quarrelled loudly over a parking space outside their stores.
Don't quarrel with the referee; the decision will not change.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The two brothers quarreled over the old bicycle until their mother stepped in.
The neighbours have quarreled about the boundary wall for three years.
The children are quarreling over who gets the last piece of cake.
Quarreling in front of customers makes a shop look unprofessional.
My cousin quarrels with his sister almost every day about the television.

definition: One of four equal parts of something, or a particular district of a town or city.
extra_senses: a district of a city having some distinguishing character
provide housing for (military personnel)
examples: Please cut the watermelon into quarters, so that each child gets an equal share at the party.
The bus will arrive in about a quarter of an hour, so please wait at the stop.
The old quarter of the city is full of narrow lanes, small shops and crowded tea stalls.
Three quarters of the students passed the exam, which was better than last year.
My aunt lives in the quieter quarter of town, near the mosque and the primary school.

form_sentences.sentence: The hostel quarters near Dhaka University are small but very clean.
The company publishes a quarterly report on its sales and costs.

definition: Seeming to be something but not completely; partly or almost so.
examples: The group is a quasi-government body, funded by taxes but run privately.

The club has a quasi-official role in organizing the school fair.
Her quasi-scientific explanation sounded smart but had no real evidence.

definition: A platform built beside the water where boats can stop to load and unload.
examples: Fishermen unloaded their boxes of fresh fish onto the quay at dawn.
We waited on the quay for the ferry to arrive.
Cargo ships lined up beside the quay, and cranes lifted containers all day.
Tourists strolled along the quay in the evening, eating ice cream.
The old quay by the river was repaired before the launch service started.

form_sentences.sentence: Fishing boats were tied up along the quays, waiting for the morning tide.

definition: A female ruler of a country who inherits the throne, or the wife of a king.
extra_senses: a female sovereign ruler
the wife or widow of a king
examples: The queen gave a short speech about the importance of education to the crowd at the palace.
My history teacher showed us pictures of the old royal palace and the queen's throne room.
Our school chose a girl from class seven to be the queen of the annual cultural festival.

definition: To put an end to something, especially trouble or strong feelings, by firm action or effort.

form_sentences.sentence: The headmaster has quelled the rumours with a short, honest announcement.

definition: To satisfy your thirst by drinking something.
extra_senses: put out, as of fires, flames, or lights

The hikers stopped at a stream to quench their thirst before the final climb.

form_sentences.sentence: The cold lemonade has quenched our thirst after the long walk.
The farmers are quenching the dry fields with water from the new well.
Quenching your thirst with plain water is better than drinking sugary sodas.

definition: Often complaining, in a weak, irritated or whining way.

form_sentences.sentence: Of all the passengers, the most querulous complained about the seat, the food and the noise.

definition: A question, especially one asking for information or expressing doubt about something.
extra_senses: an instance of questioning
examples: If you have any query about the exam schedule, please email the office.

A customer sent a query asking whether the shoes come in a larger size.

form_sentences.sentence: The bank answered several customer queries about the new card fees on Monday.

definition: A sentence or word that asks for information, or a matter that needs to be discussed or solved.
extra_senses: the subject matter at issue
challenge the accuracy, probity, or propriety of
examples: Do you have any question about the homework, or should I explain the last example again?
The teacher answered every question from the students before the bell rang for lunch.
The main question is whether the new bridge will be finished before the rains arrive.
During the interview, the manager asked me a difficult question about my experience with teamwork.
Students should write their answers clearly, because the examiner will check each question carefully.

form_sentences.sentence: The police questioning of the witnesses lasted until after midnight.

definition: A line of people or vehicles waiting for something, one behind the other.

(information processing) an ordered list of tasks to be performed or messages to be transmitted

form_sentences.sentence: The team quibbled over a small point in the rules instead of playing.

definition: Done or moving very fast, or taking only a short time.
extra_senses: with little or no delay
hurried and brief
examples: Could you take a quick look at my essay before I submit it to the teacher tomorrow?

form_sentences.sentence: The train is quicker than the bus during the evening rush hour.

definition: At a fast speed, or within a very short time.
extra_senses: with little or no delay
without taking pains
examples: The children finished their drawings quickly, because they wanted to go out and play in the rain.

Please eat your breakfast quickly, because the school bus will leave in ten minutes.
The traffic on the bridge began to move quickly after the police cleared the blocked lane.

form_sentences.sentence: The nurse gave me a quick check of my blood pressure.

definition: Something given or done in return for something else, as an equal exchange of favors or benefits.
examples: I'll help you with maths, and in return you'll teach me guitar; it's a fair quid pro quo.

form_sentences.sentence: The contracts involved several quids pro quo, with each side gaining a favour.

definition: Quiet, still or inactive for a period of time, but able to become active again.
extra_senses: marked by a state of tranquil repose
being quiet or still or inactive
examples: The volcano has been quiescent for centuries, but scientists still monitor it closely.
After the exams, the usually busy hostel became quiescent for the whole holiday.
The disease can stay quiescent in the body for years before any symptoms appear.
The stock market remained quiescent in August, with few people buying or selling.
Her anger lay quiescent until her brother brought up the old argument.

form_sentences.sentence: The quiescent factory sat silent during the long holiday.
After the crowds left, the stadium became more quiescent with each passing hour.

definition: Making little or no noise, or having little activity or disturbance.
extra_senses: free of noise or uproar; or making little if any sound
not showy or obtrusive
examples: Please be quiet in the library, because some students are studying for the university exam.
The village was quiet at night, except for the sound of frogs and the wind in the trees.
My grandmother prefers a quiet room with a soft fan and a book by the window.
The office became quiet after the manager left, and everyone went back to their work.
We found a quiet corner of the park where we could talk without the noise of the traffic.

form_sentences.sentence: The library is the most quiet place on campus during exam weeks.
The quietness of the village at night is very peaceful.
She closed the door quietly so the baby would not wake.

definition: In a way that makes little or no noise, or without drawing attention.
extra_senses: with little or no sound
with little or no activity or no agitation (`quiet' is a nonstandard variant for `quietly')
examples: Please speak quietly, because the baby has only just fallen asleep in the next room.
The cat crept quietly across the kitchen floor and jumped onto the table.
My father closed the door quietly so as not to wake the children who were sleeping.
The students left the classroom quietly, so the teacher did not have to raise her voice.
She quietly handed the teacher a note, and nobody else in the class noticed it.

form_sentences.sentence: A quiet room is best for reading and taking careful notes.

definition: Being the most perfect or typical example of a particular quality or type of thing.
examples: Hilsa fish with rice is the quintessential Bengali meal.

That film is the quintessential road movie: two friends, an old car and an endless highway.
A rainy afternoon with tea and a good book is my quintessential idea of relaxing.
This café, with its wooden tables and strong coffee, is the quintessential student hangout.

form_sentences.sentence: The village tea stall looks quintessential, with its clay cups and loud chatter.
Of all the cafés in the old town, this one is the most quintessential.
Simplicity is the quintessence of good design, according to many architects.
The Eid market felt quintessentially Bangladeshi, with bright lights and crowded lanes.

definition: To stop doing something, or to leave a job or school permanently.
extra_senses: give up or retire from a position
go away or leave
examples: My uncle decided to quit his job at the bank and open a small grocery shop near home.

She wanted to quit the course, but her parents convinced her to finish the semester.
