Please quit making so much noise in the corridor, because the exam hall is just next door.

form_sentences.sentence: My father has quit smoking after twenty years of trying.
He quits the gym every winter but returns to it in spring.
Many people try to quit sugar to improve their long-term health.

definition: To some extent, or completely in a particular way, depending on how it is used.
extra_senses: to the greatest extent; completely
of an unusually noticeable or exceptional or remarkable kind (not used with a negative)
examples: The film was quite long, so we left the cinema hall feeling tired but very happy.
Your answer is quite correct, although the spelling of the last word needs a small change.
The river has become quite shallow this year, and the boats now carry fewer passengers.
My sister was not quite ready when the taxi arrived, so we waited for her in the lobby.
The new road to the airport is quite wide, and the traffic moves smoothly in the morning.

definition: Very idealistic and generous but impractical, with little thought for reality.
examples: His quixotic plan to plant a million trees all by himself made everyone smile.
It seems quixotic to start a free library in a village with no electricity, but she did it.
Rafi's quixotic dream of becoming a world champion with no coach was admirable but unrealistic.
The start-up's quixotic promise of free phones for everyone ran out of money in a month.
She made a quixotic gesture, giving her last taka to a stranger who needed a bus fare.

form_sentences.sentence: Her plan to plant a forest on the roof was the most quixotic idea the committee had heard.

definition: Showing mild surprise or puzzlement in a questioning, slightly amused way.
extra_senses: perplexed (as if being expected to know something that you do not know)
examples: She gave me a quizzical look when I said I had finished all the homework in ten minutes.
The teacher raised a quizzical eyebrow at the unusual excuse.
With a quizzical smile, Rafi asked why the cat was sitting in the empty box.
A quizzical expression crossed the shopkeeper's face as the stranger asked for a rare coin.
The puppy tilted its head with a quizzical air every time we said the word walk.

form_sentences.sentence: Her teacher's expression seemed quizzical when I explained my unusual answer.
After the third question, the examiner looked more quizzical than before.
He raised one eyebrow quizzically when the waiter brought the wrong dish.

definition: To repeat the exact words that someone else has said or written.
extra_senses: a punctuation mark used to attribute the enclosed text to someone else
a passage or expression that is quoted or cited
examples: In her essay, she quoted a famous poem about the river.
The newspaper quoted the shopkeeper as saying that prices had doubled.
Please don't quote me on this, because I'm not completely sure.
My grandfather loves to quote old proverbs whenever we make a mistake.
The report quotes several students who say the library should stay open late.

form_sentences.sentence: The article has quoted two doctors who disagree about the new treatment.
The reporter is quoting the coach's statement word for word.
Quoting sources accurately is an important skill in academic writing.
The quotation from the poem fits well in your introduction.

definition: Happening every day; ordinary and routine, sometimes to the point of being dull.
examples: Cooking, cleaning and paying bills fill most of our quotidian life.
The novel finds beauty in quotidian events, such as boiling tea or catching a bus.
After the wedding excitement ended, the family returned to its quotidian routine.
She uses her phone for quotidian tasks like checking the weather and paying electricity bills.
The photographer's pictures of quotidian street scenes, like a boy selling peanuts, won a prize.

form_sentences.sentence: Cooking rice and lentils seems quotidian to my mother, but it is an art to me.
Our classes in the morning are the most quotidian part of the week, with the same routine each day.

definition: A noisy, disorderly crowd of people who are hard to control.
extra_senses: disparaging terms for the common people
examples: A rabble of fans pushed past the guards and rushed onto the field.
The teacher walked into the classroom and found a noisy rabble instead of students.
Shoppers fought for sale items, and the store soon looked like a rabble.
The unhappy rabble outside the ticket counter refused to leave without refunds.
The wedding hall turned into a rabble when the food ran out.

definition: A competition to find out who is the fastest in reaching a place or finishing a task.
extra_senses: any competition
a contest of speed
examples: Our school holds a running race every year on Sports Day.
She won the swimming race by less than a second.
The boat race on the river drew thousands of cheering spectators.
The two cyclists were neck and neck for most of the race.
Registration for the charity race opens next week.

form_sentences.sentence: The young racer won the bicycle race by two full seconds.

definition: The sport of taking part in contests of speed, usually with cars, horses or bicycles.
examples: Horse racing is a popular sport in some parts of Bangladesh, especially during the winter season.
My brother watches motor racing on television every Sunday afternoon with his friends.
The boys organised a small bicycle racing event on the village road during the school holiday.
Car racing requires great skill, quick reflexes and a very strong understanding of the track.
Many young people dream of racing professionally, but few of them win a place in a famous team.

definition: A person who is good at telling interesting or amusing stories.
examples: My uncle is a wonderful raconteur, and the whole family gathers when he starts a story.
The old fisherman was a gifted raconteur who could keep the tea stall silent for an hour.
As a raconteur, she turned a simple bus ride into a hilarious adventure.
The dinner guest was such a witty raconteur that nobody noticed the food getting cold.
Every school needs a raconteur like Mr. Hasan, who makes history lessons feel like adventures.

form_sentences.sentence: The village has several raconteurs who entertain the tea-stall crowd every evening.

definition: Very different from what is usual, especially in a way that brings major change.
extra_senses: (chemistry) two or more atoms bound together as a single unit and forming part of a molecule
markedly new or introducing radical change
examples: The school made a radical change by starting classes an hour later.
Doctors recommended a radical change in his diet.
Smartphones brought radical changes to the way people pay bills.
The architect proposed a radical redesign of the city's bus stations.
Her radical idea of teaching math through games surprised the other teachers.

form_sentences.sentence: The new teacher's ideas seem radical, but they might actually work.
The second plan was more radical, and it changed the entire school timetable.
The company radically changed its menu after customers complained about the prices.

definition: A device that receives sound broadcasts through electromagnetic waves, or the broadcasting system itself.
extra_senses: an electronic receiver that detects and demodulates and amplifies transmitted signals
a communication system based on broadcasting electromagnetic waves
examples: My grandfather still listens to the cricket commentary on the radio every evening in the veranda.
The taxi driver had the radio on loudly, playing old songs as we crossed the busy bridge.
During the flood, the government used the radio to warn people about the danger in low areas.
The new radio station broadcasts news and music for students and young workers in the city.
I bought a small battery radio for the village trip, because the power often goes off there.

form_sentences.sentence: Old radios still work well in rural Bangladesh without a reliable power supply.

definition: A long horizontal bar that acts as a barrier, guard or support, such as a handrail beside stairs.
extra_senses: short for railway
complain bitterly
examples: Please hold the rail firmly when you walk down the steep stairs of the old bridge.
The balcony has a low iron rail, so small children should be watched carefully near it.
My father painted the wooden rail of the veranda white before the Eid guests arrived.
The workers fixed a new metal rail beside the pedestrian path to stop people from falling.
She grabbed the rail of the bus as the driver braked suddenly at the busy crossing.

form_sentences.sentence: Hold the metal rails when you walk down the wet stairs.
The railing on the balcony was repaired after the storm.

definition: A system of metal tracks along which trains run to carry passengers and goods.
extra_senses: compel by coercion, threats, or crude means
a line of track providing a runway for wheels
examples: The old railroad through the countryside was built by the British more than a century ago.
Children often walk along the railroad tracks near the station, which is very dangerous.
The government plans to extend the railroad to connect the port with the northern districts.
My grandfather worked for the railroad company as a signal operator for almost thirty years.
The railroad crosses the river on a long iron bridge, and trains move slowly across it.

form_sentences.sentence: Many old railroads in the country were built during colonial times.
Railroading shaped how goods were moved across the United States.

definition: A system of metal tracks along which trains run, and the organisation that operates them.
extra_senses: a line of track providing a runway for wheels
examples: We travelled from Dhaka to Rajshahi by railway, because the train was faster than the bus.
The railway station was crowded with families returning home for the Eid holidays.
The government wants to build a new railway line to connect the capital with the port city.
My uncle works for the railway as an engineer, checking the tracks and signals every week.
The railway journey through the paddy fields was calm, and the children waved at the farmers.

form_sentences.sentence: Several railways in Bangladesh were upgraded to carry more passengers.
Critics said the company would railroad the new fares through the board.

definition: Water that falls in drops from clouds to the ground.
extra_senses: precipitate as rain
drops of fresh water that fall as precipitation from clouds
examples: Heavy rain started in the afternoon, and the streets of Dhaka were full of water within minutes.
We carried umbrellas because the weather forecast said there would be rain before the evening.
Farmers were happy about the rain, since the rice seedlings needed water after the dry weeks.
The children jumped in the puddles after the rain and came home completely muddy.
Light rain fell on the village all night, and the roads were slippery in the morning.

form_sentences.sentence: We packed umbrellas because the forecast says the week will be rainy.

definition: To make an amount, level or price higher than it was before.
extra_senses: raise from a lower to a higher position
cause to be heard or known; express or utter
examples: The shop plans to raise the price of cooking oil because the cost of imports has gone up.
The government may raise the tax on imported cars to protect local manufacturers.
My father asked his boss to raise his salary, and the manager agreed after the annual review.
Doctors warned that eating too much salt can raise your blood pressure over the years.
The school hopes to raise enough money to repair the roof before the monsoon begins.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The school raised the fee for lab equipment at the start of last year.
The shop in Dhanmondi has raised its prices twice this year because of inflation.
The bank is raising interest rates to slow down rising inflation.
Raising money for the flood relief fund took only one week.
The company raises its salaries every January after a yearly review.

definition: A possible, often complicated result or consequence of an action or decision.
extra_senses: a part of a forked or branching shape
a development that complicates a situation
examples: Before quitting your job, think about the financial ramifications for your whole family.
The new law has serious ramifications for small shop owners.
Nobody understood the ramifications of closing the road until traffic stopped in every nearby street.
Cheating in an exam can have ramifications for your future that last for years.
The ramifications of a single data leak can reach thousands of customers.

definition: Spreading or growing very quickly in a way that is difficult to control.
extra_senses: rearing on left hind leg with forelegs elevated and head usually in profile
(of a plant) having a lush and unchecked growth
examples: Dengue was rampant in the city that summer, and the hospitals were full.
Cheating became rampant when the invigilators stopped checking the hall.
Rumours were rampant on social media after the match was cancelled.
Weeds grow rampant in the garden after the monsoon rains.
Rampant inflation forced many families to cut their food budgets.

form_sentences.sentence: Rust seemed more rampant on the old boats after the monsoon.
Factories often ramp production up quickly before the Eid festival season.

definition: A wide wall of earth or stone built around a castle or town to defend it.
examples: Tourists walked along the ramparts of the old fort and took photographs of the city.
Soldiers once stood guard on the ramparts, watching the road for enemies.
The ramparts of the old fort are crumbling, and workers are repairing them stone by stone.
The children climbed the grassy rampart behind the village and watched the sunset.
In the game, players must defend the castle's rampart from attacking soldiers.

definition: Deep, lasting bitterness and anger toward someone because of past wrongs.
examples: Years after the quarrel, the brothers still spoke to each other with rancor.
She forgave her friend without rancor and never mentioned the matter again.
The debate was fierce but free of rancor, and everyone shook hands afterward.
Rancor between the two families began over a small land dispute and lasted a generation.
There was no rancor in his voice when he congratulated the winner.

form_sentences.sentence: The two families carried old rancors into the wedding, but everyone tried to stay polite.
The rancorous argument at the committee meeting ended with two members walking out.

definition: Done or chosen without a plan, pattern or reason; left to chance.
examples: The teacher chose a random student to read the answer aloud.
A random check at the gate found two tickets that were fake.
Please don't ask me such a random question when I'm busy cooking.
The survey used a random sample of five hundred households from across the city.
The password generator creates a random mix of letters and numbers for your account.

form_sentences.sentence: The choice of winners seems random, so everyone has an equal chance.
The randomness of the test questions makes it hard to guess the answers.
The teacher chose students randomly to answer questions during the lesson.

definition: The set of different things, amounts or sizes that fall between a lower and an upper limit.
extra_senses: change or be different within limits
the limits within which something can be effective
examples: The shop sells a wide range of phones, from cheap models to expensive ones.
Tickets are available in a price range of five hundred to two thousand taka.
This course suits students in the age range of sixteen to nineteen.
The doctor explained that a normal heart rate falls within a certain range.
Her interests cover a surprising range, from chemistry to classical music.

definition: A person's or thing's position in a group, usually based on importance, quality or seniority.
extra_senses: relative status
the ordinary members of an organization (such as the enlisted soldiers of an army)
examples: She was promoted to a higher rank in the company after five years of hard work.
The students were ranked according to their marks, and Rafi came in the top position.
Military officers of high rank usually have more responsibilities than the ordinary soldiers.
The team moved up the league rank after winning four matches in a row this month.
The rank of a clerk in the office is lower than that of a section officer in the same department.

definition: The members or people who make up an organization, group or army, considered together.
examples: Thousands of new graduates join the ranks of job seekers every year.
The club's ranks grew quickly after its first charity football match.
Several teachers in the school's ranks volunteered to run the free evening classes.
Illness thinned the ranks of the cricket team just before the final.
The company's ranks include engineers, designers and drivers from twelve different districts.

definition: Extremely greedy for money or possessions and willing to take them unfairly from others.
extra_senses: excessively greedy and grasping
devouring or craving food in great quantities
examples: The rapacious moneylender charged poor villagers so much interest that they could never repay him.
A rapacious landlord raised the rent three times in one year and ignored every complaint.
Critics accused the company of rapacious pricing during the shortage of cooking oil.
In the story, a rapacious king taxed his people until nobody had anything left.
A rapacious builder cut down every tree on the plot to squeeze in more flats.

form_sentences.sentence: The landlord's demands were rapacious, raising the rent twice in one year.
The company became more rapacious after it bought its main rivals.
The rapacity of the online lenders trapped many students in heavy debt.
The bidders grabbed the auction stalls rapaciously, leaving smaller traders with nothing.

definition: Happening or moving very quickly, in a short period of time.
extra_senses: a part of a river where the current is very fast
characterized by speed; moving with or capable of moving with high speed
examples: Dhaka has seen rapid growth in the number of high-rise buildings over the last decade.
The doctor noticed a rapid improvement in my father's health after the new medicine started.
Rapid changes in technology mean that students must keep learning new skills every year.
The river rose at a rapid rate after the heavy rain, and the villagers moved to higher ground.
Due to the rapid response of the fire service, the damage to the market was kept small.

form_sentences.sentence: The spread of the new messaging app has been rapid across the campus.
Phone charging is now more rapid thanks to the newer cables.
The rapidity of the changes surprised many local businesses.
Prices of vegetables rose rapidly during the long flood season.

definition: At a very fast speed, or within a short space of time.
examples: The city's population has grown rapidly, so the buses on the main roads are always crowded.
Mobile phone use has spread rapidly across the villages in the last ten years.
The price of vegetables rose rapidly during the first week of Ramadan.
The fire spread rapidly through the dry grass, but the firefighters stopped it before midnight.
Prices of imported goods can change rapidly when the exchange rate moves up or down.

form_sentences.sentence: The rapid growth of the city has created new traffic problems.

definition: A feeling of extreme joy and excitement that fills your mind completely.
extra_senses: a state of elated bliss
examples: The children watched the fireworks in rapture, their eyes wide.
She read her admission letter again and again, her face full of rapture.
The audience listened in rapture as the violinist played the last piece.
He described his first view of snow with rapture.
The baby giggled with rapture when her father blew soap bubbles.

form_sentences.sentence: Visitors described the sunset in raptures, filling pages with praise.
The crowd gave the singer a rapturous welcome, cheering for several minutes.

definition: Not seen or happening very often, or found in only small numbers.
extra_senses: recurring only at long intervals
not widely distributed
examples: The Bengal tiger is a rare animal, and only a few hundred are left in the Sundarbans.
It is rare for the power to stay on all day in our village during the summer months.
Her grandmother's silver necklace is a rare piece, made by a craftsman from Old Dhaka.
Such a clear sky is rare in the monsoon season, so we went out to enjoy the sunshine.
A rare disease affects only a few people, which makes it difficult for doctors to study.

form_sentences.sentence: Snow is rarer in Bangladesh than in the mountains of Nepal.
Sunlight rarely reaches the floor of the dense forest.
A clear view of the night sky is a rarity in big cities.

definition: Belonging to or understood by only a small, privileged or highly educated group, and remote from ordinary life.
extra_senses: of high moral or intellectual value; elevated in nature or style
examples: She grew up in the rarefied world of private schools and holidays abroad.
The professor's rarefied language left most first-year students completely lost.
Few people ever enter the rarefied circle of top chess champions.
Fashion week takes place in a rarefied atmosphere where ordinary shoppers feel out of place.
His rarefied taste in wine meant the restaurant manager always came to his table.

form_sentences.sentence: Her circle of friends seemed rarefied, with only artists and critics.
The academic debate became more rarefied as the speakers used technical terms.

definition: Not very often, or only on a few occasions.
examples: My uncle rarely visits his village in winter, because the cold weather makes his knees ache.
She is a careful driver, and she rarely gets into an accident on the crowded roads.
The electricity rarely goes off in our area, so we seldom use the generator at night.
He rarely eats outside, because he prefers the simple food his mother cooks at home.
Students rarely finish the whole syllabus before the final exam, so revision is very important.

form_sentences.sentence: A rare disease can be difficult to diagnose at the first visit.

definition: How fast or how often something happens, measured against a unit of time or a set standard.
extra_senses: amount of a charge or payment relative to some basis
assign a rank or rating to
examples: The bus travelled at a steady rate along the highway, so we reached the city quickly.
The bank has raised the interest rate on savings accounts to attract more customers.
The number of students passing the exam has increased at a good rate this year.
Doctors measure your heartbeat rate to check whether your heart is working normally.
The unemployment rate in the district fell slightly after the new factory opened last year.

definition: To some extent, or more than usual; used when you want to soften a statement.
extra_senses: to some (great or small) extent
more readily or willingly
examples: The hotel was rather expensive, so we decided to stay at a cheaper guesthouse instead.
The homework was rather difficult, and I spent almost two hours solving the last problem.
I would rather walk home than wait for a rickshaw in the heavy traffic.
Her English pronunciation is rather good, although she still makes small mistakes with grammar.
The market was rather crowded on Friday, so we bought vegetables from the stall near the gate.

definition: To approve an agreement or decision officially, so that it becomes valid.
examples: The members voted to ratify the new club rules at the annual meeting.
Both countries must ratify the agreement before it takes effect.
The workers will ratify the pay deal if more than half of them vote yes.
The committee’s decision needs the principal’s signature to be ratified.
The board ratified the manager’s plan after a short discussion.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The board is ratifying the new budget at tomorrow's meeting.
Ratifying the agreement took longer than the negotiators expected.
The national assembly ratifies every budget before the new financial year begins.
Before the ratification, the club's members argued for hours about the new rules.

definition: The relationship between two amounts, showing how many times one contains the other.
extra_senses: the relation between things (or parts of things) with respect to their comparative quantity, magnitude, or degree
examples: The ratio of boys to girls in our class is three to two.
To make the mixture, use water and cement in a ratio of four to one.
A teacher-student ratio of one to twenty allows more attention for each child.
The recipe uses a rice-to-water ratio of one to two.
The bank looks at the ratio of your monthly income to your debts before giving a loan.
collocations: the ratio of A to B

form_sentences.sentence: The bank looks at debt-to-income ratios before approving a home loan.

definition: The process of thinking carefully and logically in order to reach a conclusion.
extra_senses: logical and methodical reasoning
examples: The detective solved the case through careful ratiocination rather than luck.
Chess rewards patient ratiocination, because you must think several moves ahead.
Mathematics teaches students the habit of ratiocination: stating each step and giving a reason for it.
After hours of ratiocination, the engineers found that the fault was in the cooling pump.
Her decision came not from ratiocination but from a sudden feeling.

form_sentences.sentence: The detective paused to ratiocinate, weighing each clue before naming the thief.

definition: Based on clear thinking and reason rather than feelings; able to think sensibly.
extra_senses: of or associated with or requiring the use of the mind
an integer or a fraction
examples: There must be a rational explanation for why the lights keep flickering.
Try to make a rational decision about money, not one based on a sudden mood.
Even when she was angry, she stayed rational and explained her side clearly.
Humans are rational beings, yet we often buy things we do not need.
It isn't rational to be afraid of a tiny lizard, but my sister screams every time.

form_sentences.sentence: After a calm discussion, she became more rational about the cost of the trip.
The rationality of her decision was clear after she compared all the options.
We should decide rationally, not emotionally, when we choose a university.

definition: The reasons or logical thinking behind a decision, action or belief.
examples: The headmaster explained the rationale for moving the exams to the morning.
I don't understand the rationale behind charging more for the smaller size.
The report sets out the rationale for building a new bridge over the river.
Parents asked about the rationale behind the new homework policy.
The doctor explained the rationale for the treatment before the patient agreed.

form_sentences.sentence: The manager explained the rationales behind each decision during the meeting.

definition: Loud, rough and harsh in sound, often with noisy, disorderly behavior.
extra_senses: disturbing the public peace; loud and rough
examples: A raucous crowd filled the stadium and cheered every goal as loudly as it could.
The raucous laughter from the next room kept me from sleeping.
Crows made a raucous noise at dawn outside my window.
The wedding party got raucous after midnight, and the neighbors had to ask for the music to be lowered.
A raucous argument over parking spaces broke out in the apartment lobby.

form_sentences.sentence: The party grew more raucous after midnight, with loud music and shouting guests.

definition: Not cooked, processed or refined, and in its natural state.
extra_senses: having the surface exposed and painful
not treated with heat to prepare it for eating
examples: Raw cotton from the northern districts is sent to the mill, where it is spun into thread.
Some people eat raw vegetables as a salad, but chicken should always be cooked well.
The factory buys raw jute from farmers and turns it into bags, rope and carpets.
Raw mango pickle is a favourite food in many Bangladeshi homes during the summer season.
Crude oil is raw material, and it must be refined before it can be used in engines.

form_sentences.sentence: The rawness of the wound made her wince when she touched it.

definition: To arrive at a place, or to get as far as a particular point, amount or level.
extra_senses: reach a point in time, or a certain state or level
move forward or upward in order to touch; also in a metaphorical sense
examples: We reached the bus terminal just before sunset, and the last bus had already left.
The price of onions has reached its highest level this year, so families are buying less.
The two sides finally reached an agreement after days of long and tiring negotiations.
Please keep the medicine on a high shelf, out of reach of small children in the house.
My cousin hopes to reach the final round of the national quiz competition next year.

form_sentences.sentence: Onion prices are reaching record highs in Dhaka's markets this month.
Reaching the top of the mountain took the team all morning.
The river reaches its highest level during the monsoon season.

definition: To behave or feel in a particular way as a result of something that has happened.
extra_senses: act against or in opposition to
undergo a chemical reaction; react with another substance under certain conditions
examples: How did your parents react when they saw your exam results?
Some people react badly to certain foods, such as shrimp or peanuts.
The crowd reacted with loud cheers when the team scored the winning goal.
She stayed calm and reacted quickly when the pot caught fire.
Shoppers reacted angrily when the shop raised its prices overnight.

form_sentences.sentence: Customers have reacted strongly to the price change on social media.
My younger sister is reacting badly to the new medicine, so we called the doctor.
Reacting too quickly to bad news can lead to poor decisions.
Sodium reacts with water, so it must be stored carefully in oil.
Try not to react angrily when someone criticizes your essay.

definition: A substance that is present at the start of a chemical reaction and is changed by it.
examples: In the equation, hydrogen and oxygen are the reactants that combine to make water.
In the exam, I forgot to balance the reactants and lost two marks.
Baking soda and vinegar are the two reactants that make a kitchen volcano fizz.
The fertilizer plant buys ammonia as a reactant and turns it into urea.
When one reactant runs out, the reaction stops even if plenty of the other remains.

form_sentences.sentence: Some chemicals react violently when they are mixed, so labels must be read carefully.

definition: What someone says or does in response to a thing that has happened or been said.
extra_senses: an idea evoked by some experience
a bodily process occurring due to the effect of some antecedent stimulus or agent
examples: Her first reaction to the bad news was silence, and then she quietly left the room.
The teacher's strong reaction surprised the students, who had not expected such a harsh response.
The announcement of the new bus fare caused a loud reaction from the commuters at the station.
My father's reaction to the cricket match was a big smile, because our team finally won.
Some medicines can cause an allergic reaction, so check the label carefully before you take it.

form_sentences.sentence: Customers had mixed reactions to the new menu at the cafe.
Some students react badly to pressure during the final exams.

definition: Strongly opposed to change and wanting to return to old rules, ideas or ways of doing things.
extra_senses: opposed to political or social liberalism or reform
examples: Reformers faced reactionary opposition from people who wanted to keep the old rules.
The headmaster's reactionary views on school uniforms surprised the younger teachers.
In the old film, the reactionary landlord refuses to let the village build a school.
Critics called the proposal reactionary because it would bring back rules abandoned decades ago.
A reactionary attitude to technology made the office slow to adopt computers.

form_sentences.sentence: The club's older members were reactionary, refusing every new idea from younger players.
Over the years, the board grew more reactionary, resisting every new proposal.
Her calm reaction to the bad news surprised everyone in the office.

definition: To look at written or printed words and understand what they mean.
extra_senses: have or contain a certain wording or form
look at, interpret, and say out loud something that is written or printed
examples: I read the newspaper in the morning, especially the pages about education and the economy.
Please read the instructions carefully before you switch on the new washing machine.
My little sister reads aloud to our grandmother every night before she goes to sleep.
The students read the question paper twice, because the examiner had changed the format.
Can you read this text message for me? My eyes are too tired to see the small letters.

form_sentences.sentence: I have read the entire novel in just three days.
My sister is reading a book about space science tonight.
Reading every day improves your vocabulary and your writing skills.
Try to read one short article in English each morning.
Every reader of the magazine can send a question to the editor.

definition: A person who enjoys reading books, or who reads a particular book or magazine.
extra_senses: someone who contracts to receive and pay for a service or a certain number of issues of a publication
a person who can read; a literate person
examples: My brother is an avid reader, and he finishes at least one novel every week.
The library has a special corner for young readers, with picture books and simple stories.
The newspaper thanks its loyal readers for their support during the difficult year.
A good book can keep a reader awake late at night, even after a long day at work.
She is a careful reader who notices every small detail in the stories she studies.

form_sentences.sentence: The newspaper has a large readership among university students.
Students read the instructions carefully before they start the test.

definition: The activity of reading written words, especially books, or a piece of writing studied for pleasure or class.
extra_senses: a particular interpretation or performance
a datum about some physical state that is presented to a user by a meter or similar instrument
examples: Reading every evening has improved my vocabulary a great deal since I started at the university.
The teacher gave us a long reading list for the summer, including two novels and some poems.
Good reading skills are important for the IBA admission test, especially for passages with long sentences.
Her favourite reading is a magazine about travel and wildlife, which she buys every month.
Regular reading of English newspapers helps students understand how sentences are built in real life.

form_sentences.sentence: The teacher asked us to read the passage aloud in class.

definition: Fully prepared and able to do something immediately, or willing to do it.
extra_senses: (of especially money) immediately available
poised for action
examples: Please get ready quickly, because the bus to the airport leaves in twenty minutes.
The food is ready, so please come to the table before the rice becomes cold.
Are you ready for the exam tomorrow, or do you need to revise the last two chapters?
The shop has ready cash for the customers who want to pay for their goods today.
My mother was ready with a warm meal when we returned from the long journey to Sylhet.

form_sentences.sentence: Of all the teams, ours was the most ready for the competition.
The readiness of the hospital staff helped during the emergency.
Rice is readily available at every market in the district.

definition: Existing in fact and not imagined, false or copied.
extra_senses: no less than what is stated; worthy of the name
used as intensifiers; `real' is sometimes used informally for `really'; `rattling' is informal
examples: The story seems like fiction, but it is based on the real experiences of a rickshaw puller.
Be careful when you buy electronics, because many cheap phones are fake and not the real brand.
He wanted to know whether the trip to Cox's Bazar was real or just a rumour from his friends.
The village market sells real honey from the hills, which is much better than the bottled kind.
Students need to think about the real problems in their community when they write an essay.

form_sentences.sentence: I really enjoyed the lecture about climate change yesterday.

definition: Based on what is possible or probable in real life, rather than on hopes or fantasies.
extra_senses: representing what is real; not abstract or ideal
of or relating to the philosophical doctrine of realism
examples: Set realistic goals for your revision, so that you can study steadily without feeling exhausted.
The budget for the school trip is realistic, because it covers the bus, lunch and entry tickets.
It is not realistic to expect a perfect score in the exam without regular practice every week.
The architect made a realistic plan for the new bridge, taking the monsoon floods into account.
Her expectations of the new job were realistic, so she was not disappointed by the long hours.

form_sentences.sentence: A more realistic budget is much easier to follow every month.
As a realist, he always plans for problems before they happen.
Realistically, we can finish the report by Friday if we start today.

definition: The true state of things as they actually exist, rather than as they are imagined or wished to be.
extra_senses: the state of being actual or real
the state of the world as it really is rather than as you might want it to be
examples: After months of waiting, he finally faced the reality that the company would not hire him.
In reality, the trip took much longer than we expected because of the heavy traffic.
Many students dream of studying abroad, but the reality of the costs can be very different.
The film shows the reality of life in a crowded slum, without any dramatic exaggeration.
Watching the news every day helps us understand the reality of the economic situation.

form_sentences.sentence: Students must face the harsh realities of job hunting after graduation.
Being a realist helped him accept the lower salary at first.
The real reason for the delay was a shortage of cement.

definition: To become fully aware of something, or to understand a situation that you had not noticed before.
extra_senses: perceive (an idea or situation) mentally
make real or concrete; give reality or substance to
examples: I realized my mistake only after I submitted the form, and then it was too late to change it.
She realized that her bag was missing when she reached the bus stop in the rain.
The students did not realize how important the grammar lessons would be until the exam.
When he finally realized the shop was closed, he walked back home with the groceries.
The teacher realized that many students were tired, so she ended the lesson a little early.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: I have realized that my study plan needs more regular breaks.
She is realizing how much effort the exam will need from her.
Realizing your mistake early can save time and money.
My brother realizes his mistakes quickly and apologises without fuss.
The realisation that she had failed the exam hit her very hard.

definition: Truly or actually, or used to emphasise how strongly you feel about something.
extra_senses: in actual fact
in fact (used as intensifiers or sentence modifiers)
examples: Do you really want to go to the cinema tonight, or would you rather stay at home?
The food at the new restaurant was really delicious, and the staff were very friendly.
I am not really sure whether the bus will come on time, so let us wait a little longer.
The teacher really wanted the students to understand the difference between these two tenses.
It was really hot in the afternoon, so we stayed indoors with the fan turned on.

form_sentences.sentence: The real problem is that the bus timetable changes every single week.

definition: To cut and gather a crop, or to receive a result or reward from your own efforts or actions.
extra_senses: get or derive
examples: Farmers in the village reap the rice in late autumn, when the fields turn golden.
Workers used sickles to reap the wheat before the rain arrived.
If you study a little every day, you will reap the rewards at exam time.
Companies that train their staff often reap the benefits in better service.
He reaped a handsome profit when the land he bought years ago doubled in price.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The farmers have reaped the paddy early this year because of the heavy rain.
Our family is reaping the benefits of the solar panels we installed last year.
Reaping the harvest before the flood was hard work, but the family managed it.
A patient student reaps the rewards of regular revision when the exam day arrives.
The reaper in the field worked from dawn until noon, cutting the jute by hand.

definition: The back part of something, or the part furthest from the front.
extra_senses: stand up on the hind legs, of quadrupeds
the side of an object that is opposite its front
examples: Please sit at the rear of the bus, so that the women's seats at the front remain free.
The children stood at the rear of the classroom, where the window let in the cool breeze.
A small garden lies at the rear of the house, where my mother grows chilli and brinjal.
The rear of the car was damaged in the accident, but the engine was still working well.
The security guard stood near the rear gate of the school to check every bag.

definition: A cause or explanation for something that happens, or a motive for doing something.
extra_senses: an explanation of the cause of some phenomenon
decide by reasoning; draw or come to a conclusion
examples: For some reason, the lights in the classroom went off in the middle of the lesson.
The main reason for the traffic jam was a broken bus that blocked the lane near the bridge.
There is no good reason why the library should be closed on a Sunday during the exam period.
My sister gave a clear reason for her decision, so the whole family accepted it quickly.
The doctor asked about the reason for my cough, because it had lasted more than three weeks.

form_sentences.sentence: Her reasoning was clear, so the judge accepted the argument.
The shop owner offered a reasonable price for the old bicycle.

ipa: /ˈri zə nə bəl, ˈriz nə bəl/
definition: Based on good sense and fair judgement, or not too expensive or excessive.
extra_senses: not excessive or extreme
marked by sound judgment
examples: The rent for the small flat near the university is reasonable, especially compared with the city centre.
It is a reasonable request to ask for a few extra minutes to finish the test paper.
The shopkeeper charged a reasonable amount for the rice, so we did not argue about the price.
My teacher made a reasonable point, and the whole class agreed to change the schedule.
It is reasonable to expect the bus company to repair the broken seats within a week.

form_sentences.sentence: The second proposal is more reasonable for a small team.
The reasonableness of the request was clear to the whole committee.
The hotel is reasonably priced and close to the beach.

definition: To a fair or sensible degree, neither too much nor too little.
extra_senses: with good sense or in a reasonable or intelligent manner
examples: The new restaurant near our office serves reasonably priced lunches that are good enough for students.
My sister is reasonably sure that she passed the job interview, although the result will come next week.
The buses on this route run reasonably well in the morning, but they are very crowded after five.
We bought reasonably good sarees for Eid at the market, and the shopkeeper gave us a small discount.
Our landlord agreed to fix the broken water pump reasonably quickly after we complained last week.

form_sentences.sentence: A reasonable amount of sleep helps you concentrate in class.

definition: To refuse someone's offer, request or attempt at friendship in a blunt or unfriendly way.
extra_senses: a deliberate discourteous act (usually as an expression of anger or disapproval)
force or drive back
examples: She rebuffed his repeated requests for money with a firm no.
The manager rebuffed our proposal without even reading it.
The tenant rebuffed the landlord's offer of a small payment to leave early.
Rafi tried to apologise, but his cousin rebuffed every attempt to make peace.
The proud old man rebuffed all offers of help from his neighbours.

form_sentences.sentence: She has rebuffed every offer to join the new team, saying she prefers her current job.
The shopkeeper is rebuffing customers who ask for a discount during the sale.
Rebuffing a friendly invitation without explanation can hurt a new friendship.
My sister rebuffs any attempt to plan a holiday, claiming she is too busy.
He was too polite to rebuff the offer of help from his neighbours.

definition: To speak sharply to someone because they have done something wrong.
extra_senses: an act or expression of criticism and censure
examples: The principal rebuked the students for littering the school ground.
She gently rebuked her son for not saying thank you.
The referee rebuked the player for arguing with his decision.
My manager rebuked me sharply for sending the email without checking it.
Neighbors rebuked the young men for playing loud music at midnight.

form_sentences.sentence: The principal has rebuked the students for shouting in the corridor.
The coach is rebuking the striker for missing an easy goal in the first half.
Rebuking a student in front of the whole class rarely helps him improve.
My manager rebukes anyone who arrives late to the morning meeting.
I did not want to rebuke my friend, so I spoke to her gently instead.

definition: To argue against a statement or accusation and show that it is false or wrong.
extra_senses: prove to be false or incorrect
examples: In the debate, Tania calmly rebutted every point her opponent had made.
The company released a statement to rebut claims that its product was unsafe.
He brought his bank records to rebut the accusation that he had hidden income.
The lawyer asked for time to rebut the witness’s statement with new evidence.
Scientists rebutted the rumor by showing data from three independent studies.

form_sentences.sentence: The company's claims were rebutted by three independent experts.
The lawyer is rebutting the witness's claim with a set of detailed receipts.
Rebutting a rumour takes far more effort than starting one.
The report rebuts the earlier theory with new data from the survey.
Her rebuttal of the critics was calm, clear and supported by facts.

definition: Stubbornly refusing to obey rules or accept control, and therefore difficult to manage.
extra_senses: marked by stubborn resistance to authority
examples: The recalcitrant toddler refused to put on his shoes, however gently his mother asked.
A few recalcitrant members of the club kept ignoring the new safety rules.
The recalcitrant printer jammed again, just minutes before the presentation began.
The teacher spent months working with one recalcitrant student who skipped most classes.
Recalcitrant tenants who still refused to pay were finally taken to court by the owner.

form_sentences.sentence: The old printer seemed recalcitrant, refusing to print anything without a restart.
My old laptop grew more recalcitrant each day before the exam.
The recalcitrance of the stubborn cat made the vet's job difficult.

definition: To bring back a piece of information, a memory or an experience from your mind.
extra_senses: go back to something earlier
call to mind
examples: I cannot recall the name of the doctor who treated my father, but I remember his clinic.
She could recall every detail of the wedding, from the food to the songs played by the band.
As far as I recall, the library closes at six o'clock on weekdays during the exam period.
My grandmother still recalls the old village market where she bought fish as a young girl.
Try to recall the formula from last week's lesson before you look at the answer sheet.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: My grandmother recalled the great flood of 1988 in vivid detail.
The company has recalled thousands of faulty phone chargers this month.
She is recalling her childhood in the village near the river.
Recalling old friends from school made him smile during the reunion.

definition: To say publicly that you no longer hold a belief or statement that you made earlier.
examples: The witness recanted her earlier statement after admitting she had not seen the accident clearly.
After a storm of angry comments, the blogger recanted his claims and apologized.
The researcher recanted his findings once other laboratories failed to repeat his results.
Under pressure from his friends, Tanvir recanted his harsh words about the team.
She refused to recant, insisting that every word in her article was true.

form_sentences.sentence: The witness has recanted his earlier statement to the police.
The journalist is recanting her earlier story after new facts emerged.
Recanting a mistake in public takes courage, but it builds trust.
The critic recants whenever new evidence proves his first opinion wrong.

definition: To go over the main points of something again, briefly.
extra_senses: repeat stages of evolutionary development during the embryonic phase of life
repeat an earlier theme of a composition
examples: Before the quiz, the teacher recapitulated the main points of yesterday's lesson.
Let me recapitulate what we agreed so that nobody leaves the meeting confused.
At the end of her speech, she recapitulated her three key proposals.
The news anchor recapitulated the day's top stories before the weather report.
Could you recapitulate the instructions? I missed the part about the password.

form_sentences.sentence: The teacher has recapitulated the main points of the chapter before the test.
Our coach is recapitulating the tactics on the whiteboard before the match begins.
Recapitulating the lesson at the end of each class helps weak students catch up.
The podcast recapitulates each week's news in five minutes, so listeners stay informed.
Before the exam, it helps to recapitulate the formulas you learned in class.

definition: A written or printed statement that shows that money has been paid for goods or services.
extra_senses: an acknowledgment (usually tangible) that payment has been made
report the receipt of
examples: Always ask the shopkeeper for a receipt, so that you can return the item if it is faulty.
I kept the receipt for the new phone in my wallet, in case the warranty needs to be checked.
The clerk gave us a printed receipt after we paid the school fees at the bank counter.
Please show the receipt when you collect your repaired laptop from the service centre.
Without a receipt, the shop could not refund the money for the broken pressure cooker.

form_sentences.sentence: Keep all your receipts in a folder for the annual tax return.
I did not receive the parcel, so I called the courier company.

definition: To be given, sent or paid something, or to come into possession of it.
extra_senses: receive a specified treatment (abstract)
register (perceptual input)
examples: My cousin received a letter from the university, telling him that he had been accepted.
Every month, the workers receive their salary on the seventh day, after the office closes.
The school received a donation of books from an old alumni group in the United States.
We received the wedding invitation a week before the ceremony, so we booked the bus tickets.
The villagers received food packets and clean water after the cyclone hit the coastal area.

form_sentences.sentence: The office has received hundreds of job applications this week.
The hospital in Barisal is receiving more patients after the cyclone.
Receiving honest feedback from teachers helps students improve quickly.
Our school receives a small grant from the government each year.
Students expect to receive their results by the end of July.

definition: Having happened or appeared a short time ago, not long in the past.
extra_senses: of the immediate past or just previous to the present time
approximately the last 10,000 years
examples: The newspaper reported recent changes to the admission rules for the public universities this year.
My brother bought a recent model of smartphone with a better camera for his school projects.
There has been a recent rise in the price of onions, and many families are cutting back on them.
She is a recent graduate of the medical college, so she is still learning the hospital routine.
Have you seen any recent photographs of the old bridge over the Buriganga river?

form_sentences.sentence: The change in the bus timetable seems recent, but I am not sure.
This is the most recent version of the study guide for the exam.
Recently, the city council approved a new park near the lake.

definition: A short time ago, or not long before the present moment.
examples: My family recently moved to a new flat near the university, so the commute is much shorter now.
Have you recently visited the new park in Uttara, or are you still waiting for the weekend?
Until recently, most of the students in our class used to travel to school by rickshaw.
The shop has recently changed its opening hours, so please check the timing before you go.
I recently finished reading an excellent novel about a village teacher, and I want to share it.

form_sentences.sentence: The recent storm damaged several bridges across the district.

definition: The way in which people react to or accept a new film, book, product or idea.
extra_senses: a formal party of people; as after a wedding
quality or fidelity of a received broadcast
examples: The new film received a warm reception from critics and was praised for its simple story.
The proposal was given a mixed reception, with some teachers supporting it and others objecting.
The local team's new coach was given a cold reception by the fans after their defeat.
Her debut novel had a very positive reception, and many readers recommended it to friends.
The young singer's song got a surprisingly enthusiastic reception on social media this week.

form_sentences.sentence: The couple hosted two receptions after the wedding ceremony.
The receptionist at the clinic gave me a form to fill in.
The hotel will receive guests after two o'clock in the afternoon.

definition: The tendency of a person who has been punished for a crime to commit crimes again.
examples: The prison runs education classes to reduce recidivism among released inmates.
Studies show that job training lowers recidivism, because former prisoners can earn an honest living.
The judge was worried about the high recidivism among young offenders.
A social worker said recidivism often follows when released prisoners find no work or housing.
The documentary explores why recidivism remains a problem in so many countries.

form_sentences.sentence: Judges sometimes give longer sentences to a recidivist who has broken the law before.

definition: Given, felt or done by each of two people or groups toward the other.
extra_senses: something (a term or expression or concept) that has an inverse relation to something else
(mathematics) one of a pair of numbers whose product is 1: the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2; the multiplicative inverse of 7 is 1/7
examples: The friendship works because the respect between them is reciprocal.
The two schools signed a reciprocal agreement that lets students attend each other's classes.
I helped him with math, and he did me a reciprocal favor by helping me with English.
Trust must be reciprocal; one person cannot build it alone.
The gym and the swimming pool offer reciprocal discounts to each other's members.

form_sentences.sentence: Their friendship has become more reciprocal over time, with both of them helping each other.
Trade relies on reciprocity, where each side gives something it values.

definition: The act of giving or doing something in return for what someone has given or done to you.
extra_senses: alternating back-and-forth movement
mutual interaction; the activity of reciprocating or exchanging (especially information)
examples: She invited us to dinner in reciprocation for our help with her move.
Friendship grows through the reciprocation of small kindnesses, such as sharing notes or lending books.
He gave generous gifts without expecting any reciprocation.
The two countries agreed to the reciprocation of visa-free travel for each other's citizens.
Her reciprocation came as a plate of homemade pitha for taking in her parcels.

form_sentences.sentence: If your friends help you move house, you should reciprocate when they need it.

definition: To think or believe that something is true or likely, based on what you know.
extra_senses: judge to be probable
deem to be
examples: I reckon the exam will be difficult, so we should revise the whole syllabus carefully.
My uncle reckons that the rain will stop by the evening, so we can go to the market.
How long do you reckon it will take to reach the village by boat in this season?
Most of the teachers reckon that practice is more important than memorising grammar rules.
We reckon the new bridge will reduce the travel time to the port by almost an hour.

form_sentences.sentence: The engineers reckoned the bridge would last for fifty years.
Experts have reckoned the total cost at about two million taka.
The shopkeeper is reckoning the total on a small calculator.
Reckoning the costs carefully is essential for any small business.
It is difficult to reckon the true cost of a long delay.

definition: A person who chooses to live alone and avoids meeting or talking to other people.
extra_senses: withdrawn from society; seeking solitude
examples: After his wife passed away, he became a recluse and rarely left the house.

form_sentences.sentence: Some recluses in the mountains rarely see anyone for years.

definition: Preferring to live alone and avoid other people.
extra_senses: providing privacy or seclusion
examples: The reclusive author rarely left his house and refused all interviews.
After her illness, she became reclusive and stopped answering calls from friends.
Our reclusive neighbor only comes out at night to feed the stray cats.
Some programmers prefer a reclusive routine, working alone in a quiet room for hours.
The reclusive artist lived on a small island and sold his paintings only by mail.

form_sentences.sentence: As he grew older, the old painter became more reclusive and rarely left his studio.
My grandfather lived like a recluse in the hills, seeing only his closest family.

definition: Public praise or formal acknowledgement of someone's skills, achievements or contribution.
extra_senses: the process of recognizing something or someone by remembering
approval
examples: The young scientist finally received recognition for her research on water quality in the delta region.

His long service to the hospital earned him recognition from the government at a ceremony in Dhaka.

form_sentences.sentence: Teachers should recognize every student's effort, not only the top scores.

definition: To know someone or something again because you have seen, met or experienced them before.
extra_senses: be fully aware or cognizant of
detect with the senses
examples: I recognized my old classmate immediately, even though he had grown a thick beard.
The guard did not recognize the visitor, so he asked for her identity card before opening the gate.

The police could not recognize the man in the blurry photograph taken at the crowded railway station.

Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The university has recognized the certificate from our training centre.
She is recognizing old friends at the school reunion party.
Recognizing a scam message can protect your bank account.
My phone recognizes my face and unlocks in a second.
The recognition of hard work is important for team morale.

definition: To tell someone that a person, product or course of action is good and worth choosing.
extra_senses: express a good opinion of
make attractive or acceptable
examples: My English teacher recommended a short guide to writing essays, which helped me improve a lot.

example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The doctor has recommended more rest after the operation.

definition: To find a way to make two different ideas, facts or needs fit together without conflict.
extra_senses: bring into consonance or accord
come to terms
examples: It is hard to reconcile a full-time job with preparing for the admission test.

She tried to reconcile her love of music with her family's wish that she become a doctor.

form_sentences.sentence: The accountant reconciled the bank statement with the company's receipts.
The two accounts have been reconciled, and the missing payment has been found.
The auditor is reconciling the figures from three different branches this week.
Reconciling two different ideas in one essay takes skill and careful planning.

definition: The act of becoming friends again after a quarrel or disagreement.
extra_senses: getting two things to correspond
examples: After years of silence, the two brothers finally achieved reconciliation.

Her visit to the hospital led to a reconciliation with her estranged father.
The counselor helped the couple move toward reconciliation.
Reconciliation takes time, but a sincere apology is a good first step.

form_sentences.sentence: The family had several reconciliations after years of silence and small arguments.

definition: Helping to end a disagreement and bring people or ideas back into harmony.
examples: Her reconciling smile ended the long silence between the two sisters.
The headmaster's reconciling speech helped the rival groups sit together again.
He sent a reconciling message after their argument and offered to meet for tea.
A reconciling tone in the negotiations made both sides more willing to compromise.
The elders played a reconciling role, bringing the two families back to the table.

form_sentences.sentence: After the apology, the atmosphere in the room became reconciling and calm.
She tried a more reconciling tone during the second round of talks.

definition: Hard to understand because it deals with a very obscure or specialized subject.
examples: The lecture on recondite points of medieval law lost most of the audience within ten minutes.
Her essay was full of recondite references that only a handful of scholars could follow.
I could not use the manual because its instructions were written in recondite technical language.

His recondite hobby of studying ancient maps bored his friends at dinner.

form_sentences.sentence: The footnotes became more recondite as the professor described ancient scripts.

definition: To explore or observe an area to gather information about it, often before going there with others.
examples: Before the group hike, two volunteers went ahead to reconnoiter the trail.

form_sentences.sentence: The scouts have reconnoitered the forest trail before the school trip.

definition: To write, film or store information so that it can be kept and looked at later.

definition: A piece of sound or video that has been captured and stored so that it can be played back later.
extra_senses: the act of making a record (especially an audio record)
a storage device on which information (sounds or images) have been recorded
examples: I made a recording of the lecture on my phone so that I could listen to it again at home.

definition: To return to a normal, healthy or stable condition after an illness, injury or problem.
extra_senses: get over an illness or shock
regain a former condition after a financial loss
examples: My brother is recovering well after his knee operation.

form_sentences.sentence: Recovering from surgery takes patience, so follow the doctor's advice closely.

definition: A bitter accusation made in answer to an accusation, often leading to angry blaming on both sides.
examples: After the exam results came out, the roommates traded recriminations about who had kept the room too noisy.
The business partners parted ways with bitter recriminations about who had wasted the company's money.

definition: Breaking out again after a period of calm, as a disease or a problem does.
examples: Health officials warned about a recrudescent outbreak of dengue after the early rains.

A recrudescent argument over money spoiled the family's happy Eid dinner.

Recrudescent worries about the exam kept her awake the night before the results.

form_sentences.sentence: The fever seems recrudescent, so the doctor wants us to return for another test.

definition: To put something right that is wrong or has been done badly.

examples: The bank promised to rectify the error on my statement within two days.

form_sentences.sentence: The shop has rectified the billing error and refunded the extra amount.
The engineer is rectifying the fault in the water pump this afternoon.
Rectifying a small mistake early is much easier than fixing a large one later.
A good editor rectifies errors in the text before it goes to print.
The rectification of the drainage problem will take at least two months.

definition: Having the colour of blood, fire or a ripe tomato.
extra_senses: red color or pigment; the chromatic color resembling the hue of blood
characterized by violence or bloodshed
examples: The mother bought a bright red sari for her daughter's wedding, with gold embroidery on the border.
Ripe tomatoes turn red in the sun, and the farmers pick them early in the morning.
The traffic light turned red just as the bus reached the crossing near the stadium.
My cousin painted the front door of the house red to match the decorations for the festival.

form_sentences.sentence: The redness on his cheek was caused by the cold wind.

definition: To remove or hide private or secret parts of a document before it is shared.
extra_senses: formulate in a particular style or language
prepare for publication or presentation by correcting, revising, or adapting
examples: The bank will redact your account number before sharing the document.

filling again by supplying what has been used up
examples: The renewal of my passport takes about two weeks.
Please pay the renewal fee before your library card expires.
The renewal of the old market brought new shops and fresh paint to the area.
Spring is a season of renewal, when the trees grow new leaves.
The tenant asked for a renewal of the lease for another year.

form_sentences.sentence: Our library membership needs two renewals each year, so set a reminder.

definition: To formally give up a claim, belief, habit or position, or to reject it publicly.
extra_senses: leave (a job, post, or position) voluntarily
turn away from; give up
examples: The prince chose to renounce his title and live as an ordinary citizen.
After the heart attack, he renounced smoking and began to walk every morning.
She renounced her claim to the family land so that her brothers would stop fighting.
The monk renounced all his possessions and moved to a small hut by the river.
The company renounced its old policy of unpaid overtime after workers complained.

form_sentences.sentence: She has renounced smoking after twenty years and feels much healthier.
The company is renouncing its old practices after a public scandal.

definition: To repair and improve an old building or room so that it looks new again.
extra_senses: make brighter and prettier
give new life or energy to

definition: Money paid regularly to a landlord for the use of a house, flat, shop or other property.

form_sentences.sentence: We found a rental flat in Mohammadpur at a reasonable price.

definition: To make something that is broken or damaged work properly again.
extra_senses: the act of putting something in working order again
a formal way of referring to the condition of something

The council will repair the potholes on the main road before the rainy season begins.

definition: Money or help given to make up for a wrong or damage that someone has suffered.

definition: Quick, clever and amusing conversation, especially when people answer each other with witty remarks.

definition: A meal, especially a good or large one.

We enjoyed a light repast by the river before heading back to the city.

definition: To say, do or make something again, often because it has already happened or been said.
extra_senses: make or do or perform again
happen or occur again

definition: Happening again and again, over and over, often in the same way.
examples: After repeated attempts, the young boy finally managed to ride his bicycle without falling down.
The doctor gave a repeated warning to my father about the danger of eating too much sugar.

definition: Many times, one after another, or over and over again.
examples: The teacher repeatedly asked the students to check their spelling before they handed in the essays.

definition: An indirect, usually unwelcome result of an action or event that happens later.

definition: Relating to a repertory or repertoire, meaning the set of plays, songs or pieces a performer or company can perform.
examples: The theater company's repertorial range goes from ancient Greek tragedy to modern comedy.

definition: To put something new in the place of something old, broken or missing.
extra_senses: take the place or move into the position of

form_sentences.sentence: The garage has replaced the broken battery in my car.

definition: To fill something up again after it has been used or emptied.

definition: Filled with a large amount of something; well supplied.

definition: To make an exact copy of something, or to repeat it in exactly the same way.
extra_senses: reproduce or make an exact copy of

examples: Other laboratories tried to replicate the experiment but got very different results.
The tailor replicated the old shirt so perfectly that nobody could tell the two apart.
The restaurant chain replicates the same menu and decor in every city.

form_sentences.sentence: The lab has replicated the experiment, and the results match the original study.

definition: A state of rest, sleep or calm, free from worry or activity.
