(used in combination) sized
examples: Could you bring me a larger size of this shirt, please?
The size of our new flat is perfect for two students who share the rent.
Our class size is forty students, which makes the lectures quite crowded.
The size of the crowd at the cricket match surprised the organizers.
Check the shoe size on the box before you buy the sandals online.

definition: A person who doubts claims or beliefs that most people accept and wants proof first.
examples: My father is a skeptic about miracle diets and always asks to see the evidence.
Even the biggest skeptics changed their minds after seeing the test results.
As a skeptic, Tania never trusts online offers that sound too good to be true.
The reporter, a natural skeptic, checked every number before publishing the story.
The teacher encouraged us to be skeptics and ask for proof instead of accepting everything we read.

form_sentences.sentence: A skeptical reader checks the sources before believing a headline.

definition: Doubting whether something is true or useful, and needing proof before you believe it.
extra_senses: marked by or given to doubt
examples: I am skeptical about any diet that promises quick weight loss.
The teacher was skeptical when Rafi said the dog had eaten his homework.
Many investors are skeptical of schemes that promise huge profits.
Scientists remain skeptical until the results have been tested again.
My father was skeptical about buying a used laptop from a stranger online.

form_sentences.sentence: The skeptical customers asked to see the receipts before paying the bill.
After the third broken promise, he became more skeptical of the company's claims.
A skeptic would want to see the test results before believing the claim.
She listened skeptically to the salesman's promises and asked for a written guarantee.

definition: A long thin stick of metal or wood used to hold pieces of food together while they are cooked.
extra_senses: drive a skewer through
examples: The cook pushed pieces of chicken and onion onto a metal skewer.
Soak wooden skewers in water first so they don't burn on the grill.
At the winter picnic, my uncle turned the skewers over the hot charcoal.
She tested the cake with a thin skewer to see if it was baked inside.
Street vendors sell grilled corn and spicy chicken on a skewer near the lake.

definition: Able to do something well because you have the knowledge, training and practice.
examples: My aunt is a skilful cook who can make biryani without measuring anything.
The surgeon was skilful and calm, so the operation finished in under an hour.
A skilful driver can weave through heavy Dhaka traffic without losing patience.
Our captain is a skilful batsman who plays well on difficult pitches.
He is skilful at explaining difficult math problems in simple words.

form_sentences.sentence: The surgeon is more skilful with difficult cases than her colleagues.
The mechanic skilfully repaired the engine without needing any new parts.

definition: In a way that shows skill, care and good judgment when doing something.
examples: The waiter skilfully carried six cups of tea without spilling a single drop.
She skilfully changed the topic when the question about the exam dates came up.
The rickshaw puller skilfully wove through the crowded market street.
My sister skilfully stitched the torn school bag before I left for class.
The nurse skilfully calmed the child and finished the injection in seconds.

definition: An ability to do something well, usually gained through practice, training or experience.
extra_senses: ability to produce solutions in some problem domain
examples: Learning to type quickly is a useful skill for any university student.
She has a real skill for drawing portraits, and she sells them online.
My father taught me the skill of fixing a bicycle chain.
Good communication skills can help you get a job in a busy office.
Swimming is a skill that everyone should learn, especially in a river town.

definition: Having the training, knowledge or experience needed to do something well.
examples: The factory needs skilled workers who can operate the new sewing machines.
My uncle is a skilled electrician, so he fixed our fan in ten minutes.
The hospital hired two skilled nurses for the night shift in the emergency ward.
Our team is skilled in web design, so the project should finish on time.
Only skilled tailors can stitch such fine embroidery on a wedding sari.

form_sentences.sentence: Experienced electricians are more skilled than new trainees on the job.

definition: The outer covering of the body, which protects it and can show health or feelings.
extra_senses: an outer surface (usually thin)
body covering of a living animal
examples: Apply sunscreen before you go out, because the sun can burn your skin.
In winter, my skin gets dry, so I put a thick cream on every night.
The mango skin was so thin that it tore while I peeled it.
The tailor said the new shirt's fabric is soft and gentle against the skin.
The biology lab showed us how the skin protects the body from germs.

form_sentences.sentence: Skinny jeans are back in fashion again this season.

definition: A short, small fight or argument, usually part of a larger conflict.
extra_senses: engage in a skirmish
examples: A brief skirmish broke out between rival fans outside the stadium, but police stopped it quickly.
The two sisters had a small skirmish over who would use the bathroom first.
The meeting began with a skirmish between the sales and accounts teams over the budget.
Border guards reported a skirmish that ended within minutes, and nobody was seriously hurt.
A skirmish over a parking space delayed the whole line of cars.

form_sentences.sentence: Small skirmishes broke out between rival fans before the match, but police calmed them quickly.

definition: To go around or along the edge of something, or to avoid dealing directly with a problem or topic.
extra_senses: avoid or try to avoid fulfilling, answering, or performing (duties, questions, or issues)
a garment hanging from the waist; worn mainly by girls and women
examples: The road skirts the edge of the lake before it enters the town.
We skirted the flooded market by taking a narrow lane behind the shops.
The minister skirted the question about rising prices and talked about education instead.
She skirted around the subject of money, hoping her friend would bring it up first.
The new highway skirts the city, so trucks no longer pass through the center.

form_sentences.sentence: The manager has skirted the question about overtime pay, offering only vague replies.
The road is skirting the lake, so the drive takes an extra twenty minutes.
Skirting the marketplace at rush hour saves time, though the path is narrow.
Drivers often try to skirt the flooded road by taking a longer route through the fields.

definition: Easily frightened or nervous, and likely to react suddenly or unpredictably.
examples: Rafi grew skittish whenever the teacher mentioned a surprise test.
Our new kitten is skittish and hides whenever someone walks in.
Skittish investors sold their shares at the first sign of bad news about the company.
She felt skittish before the interview and kept checking her phone.
The stray dog was skittish at first, but it finally took the food from my hand.

form_sentences.sentence: Of the three cats, the smallest is the most skittish, hiding whenever guests arrive.
The skittishness of the young deer made it hard for the photographer to get close.

definition: The area above the earth where you see clouds, sun, moon and stars.
extra_senses: throw or toss with a light motion
examples: The sky turned dark grey, and we knew the monsoon rain would arrive soon.
Look at the stars in the clear sky tonight; you can see the Milky Way.
The sky above Cox's Bazar turned orange as the sun went down over the sea.
The kids flew colorful kites across the sky during the Eid holiday.
The sky was crowded with planes waiting to land at the airport.

form_sentences.sentence: The skies over the Bay of Bengal turned orange as the sun went down.

definition: Loose and not pulled tight, or careless and not strict enough about work or rules.
extra_senses: dust consisting of a mixture of small coal fragments and coal dust and dirt that sifts out when coal is passed over a sieve
avoid responsibilities and work, be idle
examples: The rope was slack, so the boat drifted away from the riverbank.
He pulled the slack cable tight and fixed it to the wall.
Because security was slack at the entrance, anyone could walk in without a ticket.
The manager warned that slack work would no longer be accepted in the office.
Her slack attitude toward deadlines caused problems for the whole team.

form_sentences.sentence: The rope is most slack near the bottom, so the climbers must tighten it again.
The slackness of the security guards let two intruders walk into the warehouse.

definition: To satisfy a need, especially thirst, completely.
extra_senses: make less active or intense
cause to heat and crumble by treatment with water
examples: After the long walk, he drank a glass of cold water to slake his thirst.
Street vendors sell fresh sugarcane juice to slake the thirst of passersby in summer.
She read three books about space to slake her curiosity about the stars.
Only a big bowl of rice could slake his hunger after the long football match.
The documentary slaked my desire to know how old cities were built.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The cool coconut water has slaked our thirst after the long walk home.
The students are slaking their curiosity with every book in the library.
Slaking a thirst with sugary drinks in the heat can leave you feeling worse.
The cold rain at last slakes the dry earth after months of heat.

definition: To say false things about someone in order to damage their good name.
extra_senses: charge falsely or with malicious intent; attack the good name and reputation of someone
an abusive attack on a person's character or good name
examples: Someone slandered the shopkeeper online, claiming he sold expired food, and his sales dropped quickly.
She was upset that her former friend had slandered her to the whole neighborhood.
You should not slander a rival candidate just because you lost the school election.
The company threatened to sue anyone who slandered its products in public.
He felt slandered when coworkers spread a false rumor that he had stolen money.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary
Past participle · used as an adjective

form_sentences.sentence: The gossip website is slandering local shopkeepers with false claims about their prices.
Slandering a colleague behind their back can destroy trust in an office.
Whenever he loses an argument, my uncle slanders his opponents on social media.
The anonymous post contained slanderous claims that embarrassed the club's treasurer.
Courts can punish a slanderer who spreads false rumours about a business.

definition: To kill an animal for its meat.
extra_senses: kill (animals) usually for food consumption
kill a large number of people indiscriminately
examples: The farmer slaughtered two chickens for the family's Friday lunch.
Animals must be slaughtered only in clean, licensed slaughterhouses.
Many families buy cattle in the weeks before Eid, planning to slaughter an animal and share the meat.
The butcher slaughters only a few animals each morning so the meat stays fresh.
New rules require farmers to slaughter animals humanely.

form_sentences.sentence: The farmers are slaughtering goats for the festival feast this weekend.
Slaughtering animals for meat is regulated by strict hygiene rules.

definition: Dishonest or morally low in a way that seems cheap and unpleasant.
extra_senses: of very poor quality; flimsy
morally degraded
examples: The detective met his informant in a sleazy hotel near the bus terminal.
Customers complained about the sleazy tricks of a company that hid fees in tiny print.
The newspaper printed a sleazy story about the private life of a local businessman.
I did not want to rent that sleazy room, with its dirty walls and broken lock.
Journalists exposed a sleazy deal in which a contractor bribed building inspectors.

form_sentences.sentence: The hotel near the station looked sleazy, so we found another place to stay.
The advert became sleazier with each new version, so the company withdrew it.
The sleaze behind the fake lottery ticket scheme shocked the whole town.

definition: To rest with your eyes closed and your mind unaware of what is happening around you.
extra_senses: a natural and periodic state of rest during which consciousness of the world is suspended
a torpid state resembling deep sleep
examples: I usually sleep by eleven, because I need to wake up early for college.
The baby finally went to sleep after we sang a lullaby for an hour.
Try to sleep at least seven hours before a big exam.
The noisy construction next door kept us awake, so we could not sleep.
Our dog likes to sleep on the warm rooftop during winter afternoons.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The baby slept soundly throughout the long journey home.
She has slept for only four hours because of the exam stress.
The dog is sleeping peacefully in the shade of the porch.
Sleeping seven to eight hours a night helps memory and focus.
My younger brother sleeps with the window open every summer.

definition: The part of a shirt, blouse or jacket that covers the arm.
extra_senses: small case into which an object fits
examples: Roll up your sleeves before you wash the dishes, so they stay dry.
The sleeve of my kurta tore while I was climbing onto the crowded bus.
On hiking trips, a shirt with long sleeves protects your arms from mosquito bites.
The tailor shortened the sleeves of the jacket, and it fits me perfectly now.
The coach had a surprise plan up his sleeve for the final match.

definition: A large number or amount of people or things.
extra_senses: turn sharply; change direction abruptly
move obliquely or sideways, usually in an uncontrolled manner
examples: I received a slew of messages congratulating me on my admission result.
The new law brought a slew of changes for small businesses.
A slew of tourists arrived at the beach as soon as the rain stopped.
The teacher gave us a slew of homework before the holidays.
The restaurant has a slew of dishes on the menu, so choosing takes ages.

form_sentences.sentence: Our office received slews of complaints after the new billing system went live.

definition: A thin piece cut from a larger item of food, such as bread, cake or fruit.
extra_senses: make a clean cut through
a serving that has been cut from a larger portion
examples: Have a slice of watermelon; it is cold and sweet from the fridge.
My mother cut a thick slice of bread for my breakfast before school.
The baker gave us a free slice of cake to celebrate the grand opening.
I ate a slice of pizza on the train, and it was still warm.
A slice of the company's profit went to the employees as a bonus.

form_sentences.sentence: The bakery bought a new slicer for cutting bread quickly and evenly.

definition: To move smoothly over a surface, or to slip and move sideways out of control.
extra_senses: to pass or move unobtrusively or smoothly
move smoothly along a surface
examples: The car began to slide on the wet road, so the driver braked gently.
Children slide down the metal slide in the park every afternoon.
Please slide the door open slowly, because the handle is loose.
The baby tried to slide off the bed, so I held her tightly.
Our rickshaw began to slide on the muddy road after the monsoon rain.

form_sentences.sentence: The bag slid off the seat when the bus braked suddenly.
The price of rice has slid steadily over the past few months.
The boys are sliding down the hill on pieces of cardboard.
Sliding down the stairs is dangerous and should always be avoided.
The drawer slides open smoothly on its metal rails.

definition: Small in degree or amount; not serious or important.
extra_senses: pay no attention to, disrespect
(quantifier used with mass nouns) small in quantity or degree; not much or almost none or (with `a') at least some
examples: There is a slight chance of rain this evening, so take a small umbrella.
The train arrived after a slight delay, and nobody was upset.
He had a slight fever and stayed home from school for a day.
Even a slight change in the recipe can alter the taste of the curry.
I felt a slight pain in my back after lifting the heavy box.

form_sentences.sentence: The damage to the wall seems slight, so we can fix it this weekend.
I did not have the slightest idea what the lecturer meant by that formula.
The slightness of the difference between the two models convinced us to buy the cheaper one.
The price rose slightly this month, but the quality of the rice is still good.

definition: To a small or limited degree; only a little.
extra_senses: in a slim or slender manner
examples: The soup tastes slightly salty, so please add a little more water.
My brother is slightly taller than me, although we are the same age.
The price of onions rose slightly this week, but it is still affordable.
The road to Sylhet is slightly bumpy near the bridge, so drive carefully.
The new software looks slightly different, but the buttons work the same way.

form_sentences.sentence: There was a slight delay at the Benapole border checkpoint this morning.

definition: To move or leave quietly and secretly so that other people do not notice.
extra_senses: insert inconspicuously or quickly or quietly
move obliquely or sideways, usually in an uncontrolled manner
examples: I slipped out of the classroom quietly while the teacher was writing on the board.
The cat slipped into the kitchen and stole a piece of fish.
My uncle slipped away from the party before the speeches began.
A stray dog slipped through the gate while the guard was having tea.
She slipped a note into my bag during the lunch break.

form_sentences.sentence: The phone has slipped from my hand and cracked on the floor.
The little boy is slipping on the wet tiles near the swimming pool.
Slipping on wet tiles can cause serious injuries at home.
The key slips out of my pocket whenever I bend down.
Try to slip the letter under the door quietly so nobody notices.

definition: A surface or piece of land that rises or falls at an angle, like a hill or a ramp.
extra_senses: the property possessed by a line or surface that departs from the horizontal
be at an angle
examples: The children rode their bicycles down the grassy slope behind the school.
The road up the slope was slippery after the heavy rain.
Be careful on the steep slope near the waterfall, because the rocks are wet.
Our math teacher explained that the slope of this line is positive.
The tea garden covers a gentle slope that faces the morning sun.

definition: Unwillingness to work or make an effort; laziness.
extra_senses: any of several slow-moving arboreal mammals of South America and Central America; they hang from branches back downward and feed on leaves and fruits
apathy and inactivity in the practice of virtue (personified as one of the deadly sins)
examples: Sloth kept him in bed until noon, and he missed the morning class.
After the holidays, the whole family had to fight against sloth and get back to a routine.
The manager blamed the team's sloth for the missed deadlines.
Too much television can lead to sloth and a lack of exercise in children.
She overcame her sloth by setting small daily goals and rewarding herself.

form_sentences.sentence: His slothful habits, such as sleeping until noon, frustrated his hardworking parents.

definition: Unwilling to work or make any effort; lazy.
examples: After a slothful weekend on the sofa, he had no energy to study.
The manager warned that slothful workers would not receive a bonus.
Her slothful habits meant that dishes piled up in the sink for days.
A slothful approach to revision will not help you in the admission test.
On hot afternoons, the slothful cat did nothing but sleep on the warm tiles.

form_sentences.sentence: After months of doing nothing, he felt slothful and unfit.
The second half of the match was more slothful than the first, with few chances.

definition: Moving or happening at a low speed, or taking a long time to do something.
extra_senses: lose velocity; move more slowly
at a slow tempo
examples: The rickshaw was slow on the crowded bridge, so we walked the rest of the way.
My laptop is slow when I open too many tabs in the browser.
The queue at the bank was slow because only one counter was open.
Please drive slowly near the school, because children cross the road often.
My grandfather is slow to walk these days, but his mind is still sharp.

form_sentences.sentence: The slow train to Rajshahi stops at every small station on the way.
The slowest runner finished the race with a big smile on her face.
The slowness of the internet is frustrating for students taking online classes.

definition: At a low speed, or over a long period of time rather than quickly.
extra_senses: in music
examples: Please walk slowly on the wet stairs, because the floor is very slippery.
The patient is recovering slowly, but the doctor is hopeful.
Traffic moved slowly through Mohakhali because of the road repairs.
My English is improving slowly, but I practice every day with my friend.
The monsoon rain fell slowly on the rice fields and soaked the soil.

form_sentences.sentence: The slow progress of the project worried the new director.

definition: Clever at getting what you want in a quiet, secret way, often by tricking people.
examples: The sly shopkeeper hid the damaged items at the bottom of the box.
With a sly smile, she hid the surprise gift behind her back.
The fox in the story was so sly that it tricked the crow out of its food.
My uncle gave a sly wink to show he knew the real plan.
The sly driver took the long route to raise the fare.

form_sentences.sentence: The fox grew more sly each time the farmer tried to catch it.

definition: Not large in size, amount or importance; of a limited or below-average size.
extra_senses: relatively moderate, limited, or small
(of children and animals) young, immature
examples: My new room is small, but it has a window facing the garden.
The bakery sells small cakes that are perfect for a birthday tea party.
A small amount of salt makes the soup taste much better.
The village school has only a small library, but the students read eagerly.
The small boat carried three fishermen across the wide river.

form_sentences.sentence: The new flat is smaller than the old one, but it is much brighter.
The smallness of the kitchen made cooking a little difficult.

definition: Quick to learn, understand and solve problems; clever and sensible in what you do.
extra_senses: elegant and stylish
characterized by quickness and ease in learning
examples: My cousin is smart enough to solve difficult algebra problems in minutes.
It was smart of you to book the bus tickets a week early.
She has a smart way of saving money from her small salary.
The new app is smart enough to remind you when your bills are due.
Our manager made a smart decision to hire two more people before the rush.

form_sentences.sentence: My cousin is smarter at mathematics than anyone else in our class.
The smartness of his uniform impressed the visiting officials.
The guests were smartly dressed for the wedding reception.

definition: To break something into pieces with a sudden, hard blow, or to hit something very hard.
extra_senses: break into pieces, as by striking or knocking over
a vigorous blow
examples: I accidentally smashed a glass while washing the dishes this morning.
The tennis player smashed the ball over the net to win the point.
The storm smashed several branches off the old mango tree.
Careful, or the heavy suitcase will smash the phone in your bag.
The rising price of petrol smashed the family's monthly budget.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The glass has smashed into pieces on the kitchen floor.
The waves are smashing against the rocks at the harbour mouth.
Smashing the old record took the athlete three years of training.
The tennis player smashes the ball across the court with great power.
That goal was a real smasher, straight into the top corner.

definition: To notice an odor or scent using your nose, or to give off a particular odor.
extra_senses: emit an odor
the sensation that results when olfactory receptors in the nose are stimulated by particular chemicals in gaseous form
examples: I can smell fresh bread from the bakery across the street.
Please smell the milk before you pour it into the tea.
The kitchen smelled of cumin and roasted garlic on Eid morning.
The dog smelled the stranger's bag and started barking loudly.
Can you smell the rain in the air before a monsoon storm?
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The fish has smelled bad since the freezer stopped working.
The kitchen is smelling of fresh bread this morning.
Smelling fresh bread in the morning makes me hungry for breakfast.
The garden in our Dhaka flat smells of jasmine after the evening rain.
Her sense of smelling returned slowly after the long cold.

definition: To move your lips upward at the corners to show that you are happy or amused.
extra_senses: a facial expression characterized by turning up the corners of the mouth; usually shows pleasure or amusement
express with a smile
examples: The shopkeeper smiled at me and offered a glass of cold water.
My little sister smiled proudly when she got the highest marks in class.
Please smile for the camera, because we want a nice photo for the wedding album.
The nurse smiled gently and told me the injection would not hurt much.
Our driver smiled when we gave him an extra tip at the end of the trip.

form_sentences.sentence: The little girl has smiled at everyone she met today.
The shopkeeper is smiling at every customer who walks in.
Smiling at strangers can make the whole neighbourhood feel friendlier.
My teacher smiles whenever a student answers a question correctly.
It is nice to smile at people, even on a busy day.

definition: The grey or black cloud of gas and tiny particles that rises from something burning.
extra_senses: inhale and exhale smoke from cigarettes, cigars, pipes
a hot vapor containing fine particles of carbon being produced by combustion
examples: Thick smoke rose from the kitchen chimney, so we opened all the windows.
The smoke from the brick kilns makes the morning air hard to breathe.
A smoke detector in the hallway beeped because the toast had burned.
Smoke from the bonfire drifted over the village during the winter festival.
Stale smoke hung in the air of the tea stall long after the cooks had gone home.

form_sentences.sentence: The restaurant was smoky after the grill had been running all evening.
A smoker is at higher risk of several serious lung diseases.

definition: The habit or act of breathing in smoke from tobacco cigarettes, cigars or pipes.
extra_senses: emitting smoke in great volume
a hot vapor containing fine particles of carbon being produced by combustion
examples: No smoking is allowed inside the hospital, so please step outside.
Smoking near a petrol pump is very dangerous and must always be avoided.
My uncle decided to quit smoking after his doctor warned him about his heart.
Many restaurants and buses now have a smoking ban for the comfort of passengers.
Teachers asked the students to report any smoking near the school gate.

form_sentences.sentence: Doctors urge patients to smoke less and to exercise more often.
The smoky flavour of the grilled fish was absolutely delicious.

definition: Having a surface that is flat and even, without bumps, roughness or lumps.
extra_senses: make smooth or smoother, as if by rubbing
smoothly agreeable and courteous with a degree of sophistication
examples: Rub the wooden table with sandpaper until the surface feels smooth.
The new highway is so smooth that our bus ran without a single bump.
Her skin feels smooth after she started using a gentle face wash.
The chef mixed the lentils until the soup became thick and smooth.
The cricket pitch was smooth and dry, which helped the bowlers grip the ball.

form_sentences.sentence: The smooth surface of the new table feels pleasant to touch.
The second road is smoother than the rough track to the farm.
The smoothness of the ride impressed the passengers on the new bus.
The meeting went smoothly, and everyone agreed on the final plan.

definition: Without any problems, interruptions or unevenness; in a steady and even way.
extra_senses: in a smooth and diplomatic manner
examples: The wedding ceremony went smoothly, and every guest enjoyed the food.
The bus ride to Chattogram went smoothly, even though the road was crowded.
The new software runs smoothly on my old laptop, so I am very happy.
The job interview went smoothly because I had practiced my answers for a week.
Our new kitchen tap works smoothly now, and it no longer drips at night.

form_sentences.sentence: A smooth transition to the new software will save the team time.

definition: To cover someone or something so thickly or tightly that air is cut off, or to cover it completely.
extra_senses: deprive of oxygen and prevent from breathing
suppress in order to conceal or hide
examples: She smothered the oil fire with a damp towel.
The pancakes were smothered in honey and sliced banana.
Weeds soon smothered the young seedlings in the garden.
Don't smother your children with too many rules.
Thick smoke smothered the city for most of the morning.

form_sentences.sentence: The thick smoke is smothering the small fire before the fire engine arrives.
Smothering a grease fire with water can make it spread much faster.
The thick blanket of dust smothers the furniture every time the wind blows.
My mother tried to smother her laughter when the teacher slipped on the stairs.

definition: A long, legless reptile with a scaly body, some kinds of which are poisonous.
extra_senses: move smoothly and sinuously, like a snake
a deceitful or treacherous person
examples: Villagers were warned to be careful, because a snake had been seen in the paddy field.
In biology class, we learned how a snake sheds its old skin.
Keep the windows closed at night, so no snake can slip into the kitchen.
The snake charmer at the village fair played a flute while the cobra swayed.
Doctors say you should go to the hospital immediately after a snake bite.

form_sentences.sentence: The road wound in snaky bends up the steep hill to the village.

definition: To grab something quickly, often roughly or without permission.
extra_senses: to make grasping motions
a small fragment
examples: A thief on a motorbike tried to snatch her phone and speed away.
The child snatched the biscuit from the plate before anyone else could reach it.
The eagle swooped down and snatched a fish from the river.
He snatched the ringing phone off the table and answered it breathlessly.
She snatched her umbrella and ran out just as the rain began.

form_sentences.sentence: Someone has snatched my phone from the table while I was ordering tea.
The thief is snatching bags from passengers on the crowded platform.
Snatching a bag from someone in the street is a serious crime.
The cat snatches the sandwich from my plate whenever I look away.
The bag snatcher ran into the crowd, but a police officer caught him near the market.

definition: White, soft flakes of frozen water that fall from the sky and cover the ground in cold places.
extra_senses: a layer of snowflakes (white crystals of frozen water) covering the ground
fall as snow
examples: We have never seen snow in Dhaka, but the mountains of Nepal are full of it.
The children built a small snowman after heavy snow fell overnight.
Snow blocked the mountain road, so our bus stopped in a small village.
The snow melted quickly when the warm sun came out in the afternoon.
Doctors advise you to wear warm gloves when you walk outside in the snow.

form_sentences.sentence: The snowy mountains looked beautiful from the window of the plane.

definition: Used to show that you think a name or title is wrong or does not suit the person or thing.
examples: The so-called expert gave us advice that turned out to be completely wrong.
My so-called friends left the party early without telling me.
This so-called discount shop is actually more expensive than the supermarket.
The shop's so-called free gift came with hidden delivery charges.
Do not believe everything that so-called health experts say on social media.

definition: Completely wet, with water dripping from you or your clothes.
examples: We got caught in a sudden monsoon shower and arrived home soaked to the skin.
The soaked towel was too heavy to carry, so I wrung it out first.
Rafi's soaked shoes left wet footprints across the clean floor.
The riverbank was soaked after three days of heavy rain.
After the pipe burst, the soaked carpet had to be thrown away.

form_sentences.sentence: The children came home more soaked after playing in the monsoon rain.

definition: A substance used with water to wash and clean the skin, hands or clothes, often sold as a bar or liquid.
extra_senses: rub soap all over, usually with the purpose of cleaning

definition: The name that members of a family share, usually written after the given name.

Many people in our village share the same surname because they belong to one family.
The teacher called the roll using each student's surname, not their first name.
My surname is common in Bengal, so people often assume I come from Khulna.
Some women keep their own surname after marriage, and that is quite normal now.

form_sentences.sentence: Many Bangladeshi students share common surnames like Khan, Rahman and Ahmed.

definition: An amount of something that is more than is needed or used.
extra_senses: more than is needed, desired, or required
examples: The farmers had a surplus of rice, so they sold the extra in the city.
The shop sold its surplus stock at half price at the end of the season.
The government announced a budget surplus after collecting more tax than expected.
We gave our surplus clothes to a charity before moving to a smaller flat.
A surplus of graduates in one field can make it harder to find jobs.

form_sentences.sentence: The farmers sold their surpluses of rice at the market before the monsoon.

definition: A feeling of astonishment caused by something sudden or unexpected.
extra_senses: the astonishment you feel when something totally unexpected happens to you
a sudden unexpected event
examples: To my surprise, the professor agreed to extend the deadline by a whole week.
My sister gave me a birthday cake with a surprise party in the evening.
The result of the election was a big surprise to most of the analysts.
She looked at me with surprise when I told her I had passed the exam.
The sudden rain was no surprise, because the sky had been dark all morning.

definition: Feeling wonder or shock because something unexpected has happened.
examples: I was surprised to see my old school friend waiting at the railway station.
The children were surprised by the sudden burst of fireworks over the lake.
Everyone looked surprised when the teacher announced a test on the first day.
We were surprised that the shop was still open at midnight during the festival.
My father was surprised by how much the price of rice had gone up this month.

form_sentences.sentence: She gave a surprised smile when she saw her exam result.
I was more surprised by the price than by the quality of the meal.

definition: Unexpected or unusual, and therefore causing surprise or wonder.
examples: The surprising result of the test showed that most students had passed easily.
It is surprising how quickly the new bridge was finished, given the weather.
The news of her decision was surprising, because she had always loved the city.
The flight ticket was a surprising bargain, so we booked it for the holidays.
It was surprising to hear that the old school would close at the end of June.

form_sentences.sentence: The final result was more surprising than anyone predicted in the class.
The old bus ran surprisingly well despite the heavy rain and traffic.

definition: In a way that is unexpected, unusual, or hard to believe.
extra_senses: in an amazing manner; to everyone's surprise
examples: Surprisingly, the exam was easier than we expected, and most students finished early.
The soup tasted surprisingly good, even though it had only a few simple spices.
The market was surprisingly quiet this morning, so we bought our vegetables quickly.
Surprisingly, my younger brother passed the driving test on his very first try.
The apartment was surprisingly cheap, considering that it was in the city centre.

form_sentences.sentence: The surprising news about the bus fare cut delighted everyone in the class.

definition: Strange and dreamlike, so that it does not seem real.
extra_senses: resembling a dream
examples: Walking through the empty streets at dawn felt surreal, like a scene from a dream.
It was surreal to see my own name on the merit list.
The painter's surreal landscapes show clocks melting and fish floating through the sky.
After thirty hours without sleep, the airport lights and announcements seemed oddly surreal.
For someone who grew up in Dhaka, the silence of the mountain village felt surreal.

form_sentences.sentence: The city felt more surreal after the flood, with boats in the streets and empty roads.
Her paintings reflect surrealism, with melting clocks and floating animals.

definition: Done secretly and carefully so that no one notices.
extra_senses: conducted with or marked by hidden aims or methods
examples: He took a surreptitious glance at his phone during the lecture.
She slipped a surreptitious note to her friend across the classroom.
The child made a surreptitious grab for the last biscuit when no one was looking.
A surreptitious look at my neighbor's exam paper would have been cheating, so I looked away.
The detective took surreptitious photographs of the shop from across the street.

form_sentences.sentence: Her glance at the exam paper seemed surreptitious, so the invigilator watched her closely.
The second meeting was more surreptitious, held in a back room of the cafe.
She surreptitiously checked her phone under the desk during the lecture.

definition: In a secret, quiet way, so that other people do not notice.
examples: During the lecture, he surreptitiously checked his phone under the desk.
She surreptitiously slipped a note into her friend's bag before class.
The boy surreptitiously fed the stray cat from his plate under the table.
The guests surreptitiously looked at their watches while the speech dragged on.
He surreptitiously paid the bill while his friends were in the other room.

form_sentences.sentence: The students exchanged surreptitious notes under their desks during the lecture.

definition: A person or thing that takes the place of another, or acts on someone's behalf.
extra_senses: providing or receiving nurture or parental care though not related by blood or legal ties
a person appointed to represent or act on behalf of others
examples: Teachers sometimes become surrogate parents for students who live far from home.
The injured captain sent a younger player as his surrogate to the awards ceremony.
Many people use social media as a surrogate for real conversations with friends.
The company sent a surrogate to the meeting because the director was ill.
Soy milk is a common surrogate for dairy milk in many recipes.

form_sentences.sentence: Online classes served as surrogates for real classrooms when schools closed during the flood.

definition: Be or extend on every side of a person, place, or thing.
extra_senses: envelop completely
surround so as to force to give up
examples: A crowd of excited children quickly surrounded the cricket captain after the match.
High walls surround the old house, so you can see only the roof from the road.
Our village is surrounded by green paddy fields during the rainy season.
Police surrounded the market after the shop owners reported a robbery nearby.
Tall trees surround the small pond where the fishermen like to spend the mornings.

form_sentences.sentence: Thick fog is surrounding the old fort and the river this morning.
Surrounding the playground with tall trees made the school much cooler.
A high wall surrounds the university campus, with only two entrance gates.
Gardeners plan to surround the new pond with colourful flowers.
The quiet surroundings of the library help me concentrate on my reading.

definition: Located around or close to a particular place or thing.
examples: The surrounding area of the university is full of cheap tea stalls and bookshops.
Farmers in the surrounding villages grow mustard and potatoes during winter.
The hotel offers wonderful views of the surrounding hills and forests.
Traffic in the surrounding streets became heavy after the school bell rang.
The surrounding wall needs repairs, because part of it fell in last month's storm.

definition: The conditions, places, or things that are around a person or thing.
extra_senses: the area in which something exists or lives
examples: Children often learn better in calm surroundings, away from the noise of the street.
The restaurant was decorated with plants, and its surroundings felt peaceful and green.
After a long journey, I felt relaxed once I was back in my own familiar surroundings.
The old temple stood in beautiful natural surroundings, close to a shady forest.
Our hostel is in a quiet neighbourhood, so the surroundings are pleasant for studying.

form_sentences.sentence: Tall buildings surround the old bazaar, so it is always shady and cool.

definition: A study in which many people are asked the same questions to find out their opinions or behavior.
extra_senses: a detailed critical inspection
look over carefully or inspect
examples: A recent survey found that most students prefer studying in the evening.
We conducted a survey of fifty shoppers to learn which brands they trust.
The survey asks customers how satisfied they were with the delivery service.
A health survey in rural areas showed that many children need eyeglasses.
Please fill in the short survey at the end of the workshop.

form_sentences.sentence: The surveyor measured the land and marked the boundary with red poles.

definition: To continue to live or exist after a dangerous event, an illness or a difficult time.
extra_senses: continue in existence after (an adversity, etc.)
support oneself
examples: Everyone in the bus survived the crash with only small injuries.
The small shop survived the economic crisis by selling goods online.
Some plants can survive for weeks without water.
How do students survive on such a small allowance in a big city?
Only the strongest houses survived the cyclone in that coastal village.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: Several villagers have survived the flood by moving to higher ground.
The small shops are surviving the price rise by cutting their profit margins.
Surviving a long flight without sleep is hard, so pack a neck pillow.
The plant survives in dry soil because its roots store water for weeks.
Learning to swim is essential for the survival of anyone who lives near a river.

definition: Easily affected, influenced or harmed by something.
extra_senses: easily impressed emotionally
examples: Babies are more susceptible to colds during the winter months.
If you skip sleep before exams, you become susceptible to careless mistakes.
Old laptops are more susceptible to viruses, so keep your software updated.
Rice fields in low-lying areas are highly susceptible to flooding during the monsoon.
He is so susceptible to flattery that a few compliments can change his mind.

form_sentences.sentence: The susceptible files were stored on an old server with no encryption.
Children are more susceptible to colds than adults because their immune systems are still developing.
The susceptibility of old wooden boats to termites is a common problem in riverside towns.

definition: Think that something is probably the case, although you cannot prove it.
extra_senses: not as expected
regard as untrustworthy; regard with suspicion; have no faith or confidence in
examples: I suspect the power will go out again tonight, because the wind is getting stronger.
The teacher suspected that some students had copied answers from the same book.
We suspect the bus driver took a different route, because we arrived very late.
She suspects her phone battery is faulty, since it drains within a few hours.

form_sentences.sentence: The doctors have suspected a food allergy because of the rash.
My mother is suspecting that the milk has gone sour already.
Suspecting a friend without evidence can damage a relationship very quickly.
It is wise to suspect a scam when a stranger asks for your password.
The suspicion among villagers grew after the well water turned dark.

definition: To stop something for a period of time, or to officially stop a person from taking part for a while.
extra_senses: cause to be held in suspension in a fluid
bar temporarily; from school, office, etc.
examples: The railway suspended all trains for two hours because of the thick fog.
The school suspended two students for fighting in the playground.
I asked the bank to suspend my card after I lost my wallet.
Ferry services were suspended on the river during the cyclone warning.
The company suspended hiring until the new financial year begins.

form_sentences.sentence: The school is suspending classes for two days because of the heavy rain.
Suspending the account for a month can save money while you travel.
The bank suspends online transfers whenever it detects unusual activity.
The suspension of the bus service caused long queues at the station.

definition: A feeling that something is wrong or probably true, without clear proof.
extra_senses: doubt about someone's honesty
the state of being suspected
examples: The police placed the man under suspicion after he left the bank in a hurry.
I had a suspicion that the exam would be postponed, and it was.
Her strange behaviour aroused suspicion among the other members of the family.
Some villagers looked at the new shopkeeper with suspicion because they did not know him.
He told me in confidence that he had a suspicion about the candidate's real age.

form_sentences.sentence: The manager's sudden questions raised suspicions among the staff members.
I suspect the shopkeeper gave me the wrong change this morning.
The suspicious smell from the drain made the whole street uneasy.

definition: Causing you to think that something is wrong, or feeling doubt about someone's honesty.
extra_senses: not as expected
examples: The guard became suspicious when a man kept looking at the locked gate.
There was a suspicious package under the bench at the railway station.
She was suspicious of the offer because it seemed too good to be true.
The police asked the driver to step out, because his behaviour looked suspicious.
The taxi driver took a suspicious route, so I asked him to stop and explain.

form_sentences.sentence: The second email looked more suspicious than the first, with strange links.
Her sudden silence aroused suspicion, so the teacher asked her to stay behind.
The guard eyed the parcel suspiciously before he opened the gate.

definition: To keep something going over a long time, or to give someone or something what they need to survive.
extra_senses: undergo (as of injuries and illnesses)
provide with nourishment
examples: It is hard to sustain interest in a subject you find boring.
Rice and fish have sustained the people of this region for centuries.
The new factory sustained the village economy after the farms flooded.
Runners need a good breakfast to sustain their energy during a long race.
A small business must earn enough profit to sustain itself.

form_sentences.sentence: The new cafe is sustaining steady sales with cheap lunch deals.
Sustaining a long career in teaching requires patience and continuous learning.
The river sustains thousands of fishing families along its banks.
Using solar panels is a sustainable way to reduce electricity bills at home.

definition: Slim, smooth and elegant in shape, in an attractive way.
examples: The dancer looked svelte in her simple blue dress.
After months of swimming and walking, he became noticeably more svelte.
The new phone has a svelte design that slips easily into a pocket.
The model's svelte figure appeared on the cover of the fashion magazine.
A svelte black car glided silently past the crowded bus stop.

form_sentences.sentence: After a year of swimming, she looked more svelte and far more energetic.

definition: Make food, drink, or saliva pass from the mouth down into the stomach.
extra_senses: engulf and destroy
a small amount of liquid food
examples: Please swallow the tablet with a glass of water, not with tea or milk.
The child could not swallow the bitter medicine, so she made a face.
He swallowed a mouthful of rice and quickly took another spoonful of dal.
My throat felt sore, and it was painful to swallow for two whole days.
Be sure to chew the food properly before you swallow it at dinner.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The child has swallowed a coin, so the parents took him to the clinic.
He is swallowing the medicine with a glass of warm water.
Swallowing water while swimming in a dirty pond can cause stomach infections.
My dog swallows his food so fast that he sometimes coughs afterwards.

definition: Promise solemnly and firmly that you will do something or that something is true.
extra_senses: to declare or affirm solemnly and formally as true
promise solemnly; take an oath
examples: I swear that I will return the borrowed notes before the examination on Sunday.
The new officer swore to serve the people honestly and fairly.
She swore on her mother's name that she had not taken the money from the drawer.

form_sentences.sentence: The new officer has sworn to serve the public honestly and fairly.
The father is swearing that the old car still runs perfectly.
Swearing an oath before the judge is a serious step in any court case.
My grandfather swears that the old well never dried up, even in summer.
The coach asked the players to swear loyalty to the team.

definition: The use of rude or offensive words, usually when someone is angry or annoyed.
extra_senses: a commitment to tell the truth (especially in a court of law); to lie under oath is to become subject to prosecution for perjury
examples: The teacher warned the class that any swearing in the hallway would bring a punishment.

Our café has a clear rule against swearing, so families can enjoy their meals there.

Good manners at home mean no swearing, even when you are frustrated with traffic.

form_sentences.sentence: Please do not swear in front of the children at the family dinner.

definition: The salty liquid that comes out through your skin when you are hot, ill, or exercising.
extra_senses: excrete perspiration through the pores in the skin
agitation resulting from active worry
examples: Beads of sweat ran down his forehead after he walked up the hill in the heat.

Wipe the sweat from your face before you go into the air-conditioned office.
A cold sweat covered her face when she heard the results of the test.
The sweat on the rickshaw puller's back showed how hard he had worked all day.

form_sentences.sentence: Under the heavy sweater, sweat ran down his back during the long lecture.

definition: A warm knitted piece of clothing that covers the upper body, worn in cold weather.
extra_senses: a person who perspires
examples: Bring a warm sweater, because the evenings can be very cold in Sylhet in winter.
My mother knitted a bright red sweater for my little brother last December.
She put on her grey sweater before going out into the cool morning air.
The students wore thick sweaters to the early morning class during the winter break.

form_sentences.sentence: Wearing a wool sweater in the Dhaka heat makes me sweat within minutes.

sweep with a broom or as if with a broom

form_sentences.sentence: The street has been swept clean by the municipal workers this morning.

definition: Wide in range or effect, affecting or including very many things or people.

ignoring distinctions

form_sentences.sentence: The changes to the tax system are sweeping, affecting almost every business in the country.

form_sentences.sentence: This mango is sweeter than the one we bought last week at the market.

The baby smiled sweetly at her mother after waking from a long nap.

definition: Become larger or rounder in size, often because of injury or liquid collecting inside.
extra_senses: become filled with pride, arrogance, or anger
expand abnormally

Dried beans swell when you soak them in water overnight before cooking.

form_sentences.sentence: The river swelled rapidly after three days of heavy rain in the hills.

Swelling of the feet during long flights is common, so keep moving.
Her ankle swells every evening after she has been standing all day at work.

definition: An area of the body that has become larger than normal, often because of an injury or infection.

the increase in volume of certain substances when they are heated (often accompanied by release of water)

the act of swimming

definition: The sport or activity of moving through water by using your arms and legs.
extra_senses: filled or brimming with tears
applied to a fish depicted horizontally
examples: I go swimming at the club every Saturday morning, and it keeps me fit.
Swimming is a good exercise for people with sore knees and weak backs.

The new sports complex will include a swimming pool, a gym, and a tennis court.
My cousin works as a lifeguard at a swimming pool near the Gulshan lake.

definition: Move backwards and forwards or from side to side, following a curved path.
extra_senses: move or walk in a swinging or swaying manner
change direction with a swinging motion; turn

form_sentences.sentence: The gate has swung open in the strong wind, so please close it.

exchange or give (something) in exchange for

definition: Stop an electrical device from working by using its switch.

form_sentences.sentence: The lights have been switched off to save power during load shedding.

definition: Larger and rounder than normal, usually because of injury, illness, or liquid collecting inside.

form_sentences.sentence: My ankle looks more swollen today than it did yesterday.

definition: A person who loves luxury and pleasure and spends much time enjoying them.
examples: My cousin is a sybarite who spends his weekends in spas and five-star hotels.

definition: A person who praises powerful people too much in order to gain an advantage for themselves.
examples: The director was surrounded by sycophants who praised every idea, however bad.

definition: A close relationship in which two living things, or two groups, depend on each other and both benefit.
examples: Bees and flowers live in symbiosis: the bees get nectar and the flowers get pollinated.
A symbiosis exists between the street vendors and the office workers, since each depends on the other.
Fungi and tree roots live in a symbiosis that helps both of them grow.

form_sentences.sentence: Biologists study the symbioses between fungi and tree roots in forest soil.

definition: A sign, picture or object that represents something else, such as an idea, a quality or a quantity.
extra_senses: something visible that by association or convention represents something else that is invisible
examples: The dove is a symbol of peace in many cultures.
The symbol on the map shows where the hospital is.
In chemistry, H is the symbol for hydrogen.
The national flag is a symbol of the country's freedom and pride.
A heart emoji is a symbol of love in text messages.

form_sentences.sentence: The periodic table uses chemical symbols, such as H for hydrogen and O for oxygen.

In road design, red is used to symbolize danger, so drivers notice it quickly.

definition: Showing care and understanding for someone who is unhappy, sick, or in trouble.

showing or motivated by sympathy and understanding and generosity
examples: Our neighbour was very sympathetic when my father fell ill and could not work.

form_sentences.sentence: The new doctor was more sympathetic to my worries than the last one.
She received many messages of sympathy after her grandmother passed away.

definition: Feeling of sorrow for someone's trouble, together with a wish to help or support them.
extra_senses: sharing the feelings of others (especially feelings of sorrow or anguish)
a relation of affinity or harmony between people; whatever affects one correspondingly affects the other
examples: I felt great sympathy for the family who lost their home in the fire.
Many neighbours sent their sympathy when my grandfather passed away last month.
The teacher showed sympathy for the student whose father was in the hospital.

form_sentences.sentence: Please accept my sincere sympathies on the loss of your father.
A sympathetic neighbour brought us hot food when our power was cut.

definition: Happening at the same time or at the same speed, so that things move together.

examples: The dancers made synchronous movements, turning and bowing at exactly the same moment.

The two motors turn at a synchronous speed, so the machine stays balanced.
The traffic lights along the road are synchronous, letting cars pass on green for a long stretch.

definition: The main subject or idea that a speech, book, film or event is about.

provide with a particular theme or motive

Nadia chose a blue and gold theme for the decorations at her sister's wedding.

definition: The study of God and religious beliefs.

the learned profession acquired by specialized courses in religion (usually taught at a college or seminary)

The seminar examined the theological questions raised by the ancient text.

definition: An idea or set of ideas that is meant to explain why something happens or how something works.

a belief that can guide behavior

definition: As a result of that action; by that means.
examples: Rafi saved a little every month and thereby collected enough for a new laptop within a year.

definition: For that reason; as a result of what has just been said or done.

definition: A long piece of written research that a student submits to earn a university degree.

definition: Having a large distance between two opposite surfaces, or packed closely together.

relatively dense in consistency

definition: In a thick layer, or with many things growing or placed closely together.

with a thick consistency

extra_senses: indistinct articulation
used of a line or mark

definition: A person who secretly takes something that belongs to someone else.

definition: Having a small distance between two surfaces, or having little width or thickness.

very narrow

definition: Any object, item, or matter that you can see, touch, or refer to without naming it.

a special abstraction

form_sentences.sentence: Newcomers arrived at the university with trepidations about the first exam.

definition: A test of something to find out how well it works, or a formal examination of a case in court.
extra_senses: trying something to find out about it
the act of undergoing testing
examples: The shop offered a free two-week trial of the new vacuum cleaner before we paid.
The school began a trial of online homework to see whether students found it useful.
Before buying the bike, I asked for a short trial ride around the block.
The company launched a trial of the new bus route on a few busy roads.

definition: A flat shape with three straight sides and three angles.
extra_senses: something approximating the shape of a triangle
a small northern constellation near Perseus between Andromeda and Aries
examples: The teacher drew a triangle on the board and asked us to measure its angles.

form_sentences.sentence: Students drew several triangles and squares in their geometry notebooks.

definition: An action meant to deceive or cheat someone, or a clever way of doing something.

a period of work or duty

form_sentences.sentence: The trickster in the village folk tale fooled the greedy landlord.

definition: Of very little importance, value or size.
extra_senses: not worth considering

form_sentences.sentence: The printing error seemed trifling, but the whole batch of notes had to be redone.

definition: To make something start or happen, especially suddenly.

definition: Used so often that it has lost its freshness, interest and meaning.

form_sentences.sentence: The speaker's closing remarks were more trite than inspiring, sounding like every other speech.

definition: A group of three powerful people who share control or leadership.
examples: A triumvirate of experienced teachers ran the school after the principal retired.

definition: Of very little importance or value.
extra_senses: of little substance or significance

The cost of the repair was trivial compared with the price of a new machine.

form_sentences.sentence: Some students think spelling mistakes are more trivial than grammar errors, but both matter.

definition: A difficult situation, a problem, or something that causes worry or inconvenience.

definition: A piece of clothing that covers each leg separately, from the waist down to the ankles.

definition: Agreeing with the facts or the way things really are; not false or made up.

We promised to uphold the traditions of our school.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The judge has upheld the original decision, so the case is now closed.
The new principal is upholding strict rules about attendance and punctuality.
Many citizens believe that upholding the law matters more than popularity.

definition: Higher in place or position than something else, or the top part of something.
extra_senses: higher in place or position
the higher of two berths
examples: Our family lives on the upper floor of the building near the bazaar.
The upper shelf of the cupboard holds the books that we rarely use.
She has a small cut on her upper lip from the bicycle accident last week.
The upper part of the hill was covered with clouds during the morning.
The upper bunk on the train is cheaper, but it is harder to climb into.

definition: A sudden loud, confused noise or excited public reaction, usually because people are angry or upset.
extra_senses: loud confused noise from many sources
examples: The classroom was in an uproar when the teacher announced a surprise test.
News of the ticket price increase caused an uproar among fans.
The crowd burst into an uproar when the referee ignored the foul.
An uproar broke out in the market when two cars blocked the narrow lane.
The whole meeting fell into uproar after the manager's rude remark.

form_sentences.sentence: The unpopular bus fare hike caused several uproars across Dhaka last month.
The uproarious laughter in the classroom could be heard from the corridor.

definition: To make someone feel sad, angry or worried, or to knock something over by accident.
extra_senses: cause to lose one's composure
move deeply
examples: The bad news about the exam results upset my friends, so I tried to cheer them up.

The loud argument in the next flat upset the old man who was trying to sleep.
The cat jumped on the table and upset the tray of tea cups in the kitchen.
It upset my mother when she heard that her sister's house had been damaged by the flood.

form_sentences.sentence: The sudden price rise upset many families who were already struggling.
She was upset that nobody at the office remembered her birthday.
The news is upsetting my grandmother, so please speak gently about it.
Upsetting a friend with a careless joke is easy, but apologising takes courage.
Loud music from the neighbour's flat upsets my sleep almost every night.

definition: Making you feel sad, worried or distressed, often because of something shocking.
examples: The news of the fire in the market was upsetting, because many shops were destroyed.
It was upsetting to see stray dogs starving near the railway tracks.
The film had an upsetting ending, so I did not enjoy it as much as I expected.
Losing my favourite pen was upsetting, although it was not very expensive.
The upsetting letter from the bank said our loan application had been refused.

form_sentences.sentence: The second letter from the bank was more upsetting than the first one.

definition: With the top part at the bottom, or in a state of great disorder.
examples: The painting was hanging upside down on the wall, so the children laughed at it.
The bottle was upside down in the bag, so the water spilled over the books.
Someone turned the whole room upside down while looking for the lost key.
My little brother held the book upside down and pretended that he was reading.
The classroom was upside down after the storm blew open the windows and scattered the papers.

definition: On or to a floor of a building that is higher than the ground floor.
extra_senses: on or of upper floors of a building
the part of a building above the ground floor
examples: Please bring the extra blankets upstairs, because the guests will sleep in the top room.
My sister is studying upstairs, so please keep the music quiet this evening.
The shop's office is upstairs, above the tea stall at the corner of the street.
The children ran upstairs as soon as they heard the rain begin on the roof.
Our upstairs neighbours play loud music on Friday nights, so we cannot sleep.

definition: Moving or pointing towards a higher place, level or amount.
extra_senses: directed up
extending or moving toward a higher place
examples: The upward trend in rice prices has worried many families in the village this year.
The plane made an upward turn and climbed quickly above the clouds.
Water moves in an upward direction when the pump starts pushing it into the tank.
The bank reported an upward change in the interest rate for new loans.
The smoke rose in an upward direction from the kitchen chimney in the early morning.

form_sentences.sentence: The trend in fuel prices is upward again after a short drop.

definition: Towards a higher place, level or amount.
extra_senses: to a later time
examples: The smoke from the brick kiln drifted upwards into the grey sky.
Prices of vegetables have moved upwards during the monsoon season.
She looked upwards at the flock of birds flying over the river.
The children jumped upwards to reach the mango hanging from the branch.
The temperature climbed upwards all afternoon, so we stayed indoors.

definition: Relating to a town or city, rather than the countryside.
extra_senses: located in or characteristic of a city or city life
examples: Dhaka is one of the most crowded urban areas in the world.
Many young people move from villages to urban centers in search of jobs.
Rooftop gardens help urban families grow fresh vegetables.
Air pollution is a serious health problem in urban neighborhoods.
She grew up in a quiet village, so urban life felt noisy and fast at first.

form_sentences.sentence: The new housing project looks very urban, with tall towers and little green space.
Our town is more urban than my cousin's village, with shops open until midnight.

definition: Polite, confident and relaxed in social situations, with smooth and refined manners.
examples: The urbane host greeted every guest by name and made even shy visitors feel at ease.
Our new principal is urbane, speaking calmly and politely even when parents complain loudly.
He had an urbane way of turning a difficult interview question into a joke.
The hotel manager's urbane charm persuaded the angry guests to wait for another room.
My uncle, who has lived in several countries, is the most urbane person in our family.

form_sentences.sentence: The new hotel manager seemed more urbane than his predecessor at every reception.

definition: The process by which more people come to live in towns and cities, and cities grow larger.
extra_senses: the social process whereby cities grow and societies become more urban
examples: Rapid urbanization has made Dhaka one of the most crowded cities in the world.
Urbanization pulls young people from villages to cities in search of jobs and better schools.
Experts warn that unplanned urbanization can cause flooding when drains and canals get blocked.
Our geography teacher asked us to write an essay on urbanization and its effects on farmland.
Rising urbanization means cities need more buses, clean water and affordable housing.

definition: To strongly advise or encourage someone to do something.
extra_senses: push for something
an instinctive motive
examples: Doctors urge people to drink plenty of water during the summer heat.
My teacher urged me to apply for the scholarship.
Parents urged the school to repair the broken fence.
The police urged residents to stay indoors until the storm passed.
She urged her friend to see a dentist about the toothache.

form_sentences.sentence: The city council has urged residents to plant more trees along busy roads.
The teacher is urging students to revise the grammar chapter before Friday.
The bank runs ads that focus on urging customers to save for their future.
The head of the club urges members to pay their fees before the monthly meeting.
Friends often have to urge me to take a break before my exams.

definition: Needing to be dealt with quickly or immediately, because it is important or serious.
examples: The patient needs urgent medical attention, so please call an ambulance immediately.
I have an urgent message from my office, so I must reply before lunch.
The city faces an urgent need for clean drinking water after the flood.
The manager sent an urgent request for the budget report before the meeting on Monday.
The school sent an urgent notice asking parents to collect their children early.

form_sentences.sentence: The repairs to the school roof are urgent, because the rain is getting in.
Her call sounded more urgent than usual, so I picked up at once.
The urgency of the situation was clear when the water level rose again.
The doctor will urge the patient to rest for at least two weeks.
The villagers urgently needed clean water after the well was flooded.

definition: To take something and employ it for a particular purpose.
extra_senses: the act of using
what something is used for
examples: Please use the blue towel for your hands, and keep the white one for guests.
My sister uses her phone mostly to read the news and send messages to friends.
The mechanic used a special spanner to tighten the wheel of the bus.
Many students use online dictionaries to check new words while they read.
You can use the washing machine in the laundry room after nine in the morning.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: The old printer has been used for every mock test this year.
My classmates are using a free app to practise English vocabulary daily.
Using a calculator in the maths exam saves time but needs careful checking.

definition: To use all of something so that none of it is left.
extra_senses: require (time or space)
examples: Please don't use up all the hot water before I get to the shower.
We used up the last of the rice, so dinner will be simple tonight.
The students used up their data bundle during the first week of classes.
If you keep streaming videos all day, you will use up your phone's storage quickly.
The printer used up nearly every sheet of paper in the office by Friday.
example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

form_sentences.sentence: We have used up all the rice, so let's buy more from the bazaar.
The students are using up their mobile data during the video calls.
Using up leftover vegetables is a smart way to save money at home.
My mother always uses up every drop of oil before buying a new bottle.

definition: Not new; previously owned or used by someone else.
extra_senses: (of persons) taken advantage of
previously used or owned by another
examples: We bought a used motorbike from a neighbour, which saved us a lot of money.
The shop sells used books for students at half the price of new ones.
My cousin buys used clothes from the weekend market because they are cheap and still good.
The used laptop works well, although the keyboard is a little noisy.
Used furniture is often sold at a good price after families move to a new house.

form_sentences.sentence: The bicycle seemed used, but its brakes were new and reliable.

definition: Describes something that happened regularly, or was true, in the past but is no longer the case.
extra_senses: in the habit of doing something
examples: When I was a child, I used to play cricket in the field behind our house.
My grandfather used to tell us stories about the village before the bridge was built.
We used to live in Sylhet, but we moved to Dhaka when my father got a new job.
Students used to write letters by hand, but now they mostly send messages on their phones.
She used to hate spicy food, but now she eats green chillies with every meal.

definition: Able to help you or to be used for a good purpose; of real value.
extra_senses: having a useful function
examples: This dictionary app is very useful when I need to check new words during class.
The tip about saving data on mobile phones was useful for lowering my monthly bill.
A small torch is useful to carry on the road, because power cuts are common.
Our teacher gave us a useful list of words to learn for the admission test.
The old umbrella is still useful during the monsoon, so do not throw it away.

form_sentences.sentence: Practice tests are more useful than rereading notes before the IBA exam.
The use of the new library app has grown quickly among students.
She used her spare time usefully by revising vocabulary on the bus.

definition: Having no value or purpose, or not working properly at all.
examples: The old fan is useless now, because its motor has burned out completely.
Her advice about the exam was useless, because the questions were nothing like that.
Throwing plastic bags into the drain is useless, because they block the water flow.
My phone became useless after water spilled inside it at the beach.
It is useless to argue with the driver, because he never listens to the passengers.

form_sentences.sentence: Keeping a useless gadget in the drawer only creates more clutter.
The old printer became more useless after the cartridge finally ran out.
The uselessness of the rumour became clear once the facts were checked.
The alarm rang uselessly because the battery had been removed.

definition: A person who uses a product, service, or piece of equipment.
extra_senses: a person who uses something or someone selfishly or unethically
a person who takes drugs
examples: Every user of this app must create an account before saving any notes.
My cousin is a heavy user of the library's online database during exam season.
The phone company offers a discount to new users who switch from another provider.
Less experienced users often struggle to find the settings menu on their first day.
Before buying the printer, Rafi asked a few users whether the ink lasted long.

definition: Happening or done most often, or in the way that is normal in a situation.
extra_senses: commonly encountered
examples: I ordered my usual tea with milk, and the stall owner smiled at me.
Traffic was heavier than usual, so we reached the university an hour late.
After the exam, the teacher returned to her usual calm and cheerful manner.

The power went out again, but she carried on with her homework as usual.

form_sentences.sentence: It is more usual to arrive early for a job interview in Dhaka.

definition: In most cases, or as a general rule under normal conditions.
examples: I usually take the bus to campus, but today I walked because of the rain.
She usually studies at the library until closing time on weekdays.
Monsoon floods usually reach the low-lying fields in late June.

Do you usually check the price before buying clothes online?

form_sentences.sentence: Our usual breakfast is rice, eggs and a cup of hot tea.

definition: To take someone's position, power or right by force or without any legal right.
extra_senses: take the place of
examples: In the story, the prince's uncle tried to usurp the throne while the king was ill.

Some apps usurp your attention by sending alerts every few minutes.

form_sentences.sentence: The younger brother usurped his role as family spokesperson at the wedding.
The new group has usurped the old club's leadership without holding any vote.
The rival app is usurping the market share of older tools, year after year.
A clever manager sometimes usurps credit for other people's ideas at meetings.
The usurpation of the reporter's byline by a senior editor angered the newsroom.

definition: The practice of lending money at an extremely high, often illegal, rate of interest.
extra_senses: the act of lending money at an exorbitant rate of interest
examples: Lending money at forty percent a month is usury, and it is against the law.
Poor farmers once fell into deep debt to moneylenders who practiced usury.
The bank was fined after customers complained about usury hidden in the loan contract.
Many societies have passed laws against usury to protect people who borrow.
She learned about usury in her economics class when the teacher explained loan sharks.

form_sentences.sentence: Newspapers exposed several usuries that trapped small farmers in heavy debt.
Lawmakers want to ban usurious interest rates on payday loans.

definition: Designed to be useful and practical rather than attractive or comfortable.
extra_senses: someone who believes that the value of a thing depends on its utility

The utilitarian design of the bridge ignored beauty and focused on carrying traffic safely.
Our office furniture is utilitarian, so nobody expects comfort from those hard chairs.

form_sentences.sentence: The new bus shelters looked more utilitarian than the old ones, with plain metal benches.

definition: To use something, especially in a practical or effective way.
extra_senses: convert (from an investment trust to a unit trust)
examples: The school utilizes the empty hall in the evenings for adult literacy classes.

example_usage: Base form · after a modal or auxiliary

The utility company restored power to our street by evening.

a work of fiction describing a utopia
examples: No city is a utopia, but we can still work to make ours cleaner and safer.

form_sentences.sentence: Utopian plans for the new city ignored the cost of building roads and water supply.

definition: A period of time away from work or study, spent resting or travelling for pleasure.
extra_senses: spend or take a vacation
the act of making something legally void

form_sentences.sentence: Every vacationer at the beach resort wanted a room with a sea view.

definition: To keep changing your mind between different choices or opinions because you cannot decide.

form_sentences.sentence: The committee has vacillated between two venues for the wedding.

definition: Empty of thought, meaning or intelligence.
extra_senses: devoid of significance or force
devoid of matter

form_sentences.sentence: The reality show felt vacuous, with nothing interesting happening beyond loud arguments.

definition: An unexpected and unpredictable change in a situation or in the way a person behaves.
